But if the central claims were already circulating, in fixed verbal form, within a few years of the crucifixion—while hostile witnesses in Jerusalem could still object—then the “legend had time to grow” explanation loses much of its grip. The early-dating argument is a wager that the second picture is closer to the truth.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: Stating the Argument Carefully
text: The argument is usually run in three moves. First: a document produced within the lifetime of eyewitnesses is too early to be a fully developed legend that could circulate unchallenged. Second: the core New Testament material falls inside that eyewitness window—and its earliest layers fall startlingly early. Therefore: the New Testament must be assessed not as late mythology but as first-generation testimony.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: Stating the Argument Carefully
text: Two cautions are needed before we go further, because the argument is often overstated. The conclusion is modest: it tells us the material is early, not that it is accurate. And the second premise does not require the most aggressive possible dating of the four Gospels. As we will see, the strongest version of the case rests on the layers that almost everyone—believer and skeptic alike—already grants to be early: Paul’s undisputed letters of the 50s, and the pre-Pauline tradition embedded inside them.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: Stating the Argument Carefully
text: For much of the twentieth century, the regnant view—shaped by the form critics, above all Rudolf Bultmann—treated the Gospels as the deposit of decades of anonymous community storytelling, with the historical Jesus all but unrecoverable beneath the layers. The most dramatic challenge to that consensus came from an unexpected quarter. In 1976 the liberal Anglican bishop John A. T. Robinson—no friend of conservative apologetics, and famous for the radical theology of Honest to God—published Redating the New Testament, in which his fresh examination of the internal evidence led him to the startling conclusion that the entire New Testament may have been written before the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70.1 Robinson’s specific dates remain a minority position, but his deeper point landed: the textbook datings, he argued, rested on a foundation thinner and more circular than their confidence suggested.2 In parallel, work on the pre-Pauline creeds (reaching back to Joachim Jeremias) and, more recently, Richard Bauckham’s case for eyewitness sources behind the Gospels, has pushed the conversation toward closeness rather than distance.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: Premise One: An Early Date Starves a Legend
text: Why should earliness matter at all? The classic statement comes from the Oxford Roman historian A. N. Sherwin-White, who in his 1960–61 Sarum Lectures (published 1963) turned the historian’s eye on the Gospels. Working from how legends actually behave in the ancient sources—he used Herodotus as his test case—Sherwin-White argued that even two full generations was too short an interval for legend to wipe out a solid historical core; the mythologizing tendency, he observed, takes longer than that to triumph over hard fact.3 For the Gospels the interval is shorter still. Where living memory remains, an invented account does not float free; it collides with people who were present.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: Premise One: An Early Date Starves a Legend
text: That collision was not hypothetical. According to Acts, the earliest preaching of the resurrection happened in Jerusalem, weeks after the crucifixion, to crowds that included the very authorities who had engineered Jesus’s death. Claims about an empty tomb or public events could in principle have been falsified on the spot. Early dating keeps that adversarial check in force, which is exactly what a slow-growing legend needs to escape.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: Premise One: An Early Date Starves a Legend
text: The premise should not be oversold, and a careful critic will press it. The skeptic Richard Carrier and others have noted, rightly, that Sherwin-White’s “two-generation rule” was an aside about a particular body of Greek material, not a demonstrated law of folklore; rapid legendary embellishment is not impossible, and the rate at which stories mutate varies enormously.4 The honest reply is that Premise One does not need an iron law. It needs only the comparative point that more time and more distance make undetected legend easier, and that the New Testament window is unusually tight by the standards of ancient history—where our best surviving biographies of Alexander the Great, by Arrian and Plutarch, were written some four centuries after him and are still mined for a historical core.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: Premise Two: The New Testament Really Is Early
text: Here the case finds its firmest ground, and it must lead the way—because the popular objection that “the Gospels were written decades later” quietly assumes the narrative Gospels are the earliest evidence we have. They are not. In 1 Corinthians 15:3–7, writing in the mid-50s, Paul hands on what he himself had “received”: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve, then to more than five hundred, to James, and to all the apostles. The technical language of “delivering” and “receiving” tradition, the non-Pauline vocabulary, the rhythmic structure, and the Aramaic name Cephas all mark this out as a pre-formed oral creed that Paul is quoting, not composing—a formula already circulating before he wrote it down.5

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: Premise Two: The New Testament Really Is Early
text: How early? Paul’s own conversion is usually placed within a few years of the crucifixion, and in Galatians 1:18–19 he describes going up to Jerusalem to meet Cephas (Peter) and James—two of the named witnesses in the creed—three years later. The tradition he relays must predate that meeting. This is why the dating crosses ideological lines. The German New Testament scholar Gerd Lüdemann—who emphatically does not believe Jesus rose bodily and explains the appearances as visions—nonetheless concluded that “the elements in the tradition are to be dated to the first two years after the crucifixion… not later than three years.”6 Gary Habermas, who has surveyed the literature most exhaustively, reports that a wide range of scholars across the spectrum who address the question place the formula within the first few years—though this figure should be cited with care, since it is a count of published positions assembled by one researcher rather than a randomised poll.7

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: Premise Two: The New Testament Really Is Early
text: That meeting did more than fix a date; it turned Paul into a checkable link back to the eyewitnesses. Three years after his conversion he lodged for a fortnight with Cephas — the first name in the creed — and, as C. H. Dodd famously quipped of those fifteen days, “we may presume they did not spend all the time talking about the weather.”8 Fourteen years later he went up to Jerusalem again and this time deliberately “set before” its leaders — James, Cephas, and John, the reputed “pillars” — the gospel he had been preaching, “in order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain” (Galatians 2:2). The dispute in view there was about the terms on which Gentiles could be included, not a line-by-line audit of the tradition; so when Paul reports that the leaders “added nothing” to his message and gave him “the right hand of fellowship” (Galatians 2:6, 9), his point is that they required nothing further of him — no circumcision, no law — and recognised his gospel as one with their own. We should not overstate what this shows: in the same letter Paul is at pains to say that the gospel he preached was “not man’s gospel” but came “through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Galatians 1:11–12), so this is not a report of Paul being taught the tradition by Peter, nor of the eyewitnesses auditing his memory against theirs. What it shows is narrower and still weighty — that the message Paul preached independently was set before the leading men of the Jerusalem church, those who had known Jesus, and was endorsed by them rather than corrected. The line from the events to the creed does not vanish into anonymous hands; it runs through named people who had access to one another and to the events, and who publicly recognised that Paul preached the same gospel they did.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: Premise Two: The New Testament Really Is Early
text: The force of this is hard to overstate, and it reframes the whole debate. Whatever one decides about the date of Mark, the proclamation of Jesus’s death, burial, and resurrection appearances is not a late accretion that grew over generations. It sits at the very foundation, traceable to the believing community in Jerusalem within a handful of years of the events—and naming individuals, some still alive, who could be questioned.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: Premise Two: The New Testament Really Is Early
text: Paul’s undisputed letters—Romans, the Corinthian correspondence, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, Philemon—are dated by near-universal agreement to roughly AD 48–60See the evidenceThe evidenceSourcePaul’s seven undisputed letters — Romans, 1–2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, Philemon — placed by standard Pauline chronology at roughly AD 48–60. They are first-generation documents by a man who knew the original apostles, and they already presuppose the central narrative of cross and resurrection.Who holds itNear-universal across the spectrum, critical scholars and confessing Christians alike. That places the load-bearing claims well inside living memory. (This establishes early attestation — how soon the claims are on record — not, by itself, that their content is true, which is argued on separate grounds.). They are themselves first-generation documents, written by a man who knew the original apostles, and they already presuppose the central narrative of cross and resurrection. That alone places the load-bearing claims well inside living memory.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: Premise Two: The New Testament Really Is Early
text: A second clue concerns the book of Acts. Luke–Acts is a two-volume work, and Acts ends with remarkable abruptness: Paul under house arrest in Rome, awaiting trial, the gospel preached “with all boldness and without hindrance” (Acts 28:31). What it never narrates is striking. It does not report the martyrdom of Paul (c. AD 64–67), nor of Peter, nor the death of James the brother of Jesus (AD 62, recorded by Josephus9), nor the Neronian persecution, nor—most conspicuous of all—the destruction of Jerusalem and its Temple in AD 70. Luke, who narrates the martyrdoms of Stephen and of James son of Zebedee in detail, and who returns again and again to the theme of the Temple, would have had every reason to mention these catastrophes had they already happened. On this reading, Luke wrote Acts in the early 60s, which places his Gospel (and Mark, one of its sources) earlier still. This is the heart of Robinson’s case, and it was pressed in great detail by the classicist Colin Hemer.10

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: Premise Two: The New Testament Really Is Early
text: Not every argument for an early Acts is an argument from silence. The New Testament scholar David Seccombe has pressed two further considerations, neither of which turns on what Acts fails to mention. The first is one of political climate: from the outbreak of the Jewish revolt in AD 66, an intense anti-Jewish mood settled over the Roman world, and in that atmosphere the opening chapters of Luke read as dangerous material to own or circulate—a coming deliverer who “has brought down the mighty from their thrones” (Luke 1:52), the promised rescue “from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us” (1:71), those “waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem” (2:38), a disciple remembered as “Simon who was called the Zealot” (6:15), and a narrative that ends with Paul in chains “because of the hope of Israel” (Acts 28:20). Salvation cast so thoroughly in the terms of Israel’s national hope, Seccombe argues, fits far more naturally before the war than in the long aftermath of Jewish defeat. The second consideration concerns the book’s purpose: Acts devotes whole chapters (10–11 and 15) to arguing that Gentiles may be received without circumcision—a debate whose very shape presupposes a Jewish church in the position of strength, being asked to make room for Gentiles. After 70, with Judea crushed and the church increasingly Gentile, that argument had—on Seccombe’s reading—largely lost its occasion. Both points are contested: scholars who date Luke–Acts later read the same features as compatible with a post-70 setting, and Seccombe himself presents his case as a set of further, cumulative reasons rather than a proof. But unlike the silence of Acts, they point to positive features of the text rather than gaps in it (David Seccombe, “Dating Luke-Acts: Further Arguments for an Early Date,” Tyndale Bulletin 71.2 [2020]: 207–227).

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: Premise Two: The New Testament Really Is Early
text: Finally, the early church remembered who wrote the Gospels and traced them to the apostolic circle. The earliest such testimony comes from Papias of Hierapolis (writing c. AD 110–130), preserved by the church historian Eusebius. Papias reports, on the authority of “the Elder,” that Mark became Peter’s “interpreter” and accurately wrote down what Peter recounted of the Lord’s words and deeds, though “not in order,” and that Matthew compiled the sayings “in the Hebrew dialect.”11 Later writers—Irenaeus around AD 180—name all four Evangelists. This testimony is external corroboration that the church tied its Gospels to eyewitnesses and their associates, not to anonymous late authors.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: The Strongest Objection, Stated at Full Strength
text: The mainstream of critical scholarship does not accept the early-60s dating of the Gospels, and its case must be stated fully. The standard consensus, articulated by Bart Ehrman among many others, dates Mark to around AD 70, Matthew and Luke to roughly 80–85, and John to 90–95.12 Ehrman regards these dates as “not really particularly controversial.” The reasoning is layered: Matthew and Luke used Mark as a source, which requires Mark to have circulated first; and—the decisive point—Mark 13 (the “Olivet Discourse”) and its parallels have Jesus predicting the encirclement and destruction of Jerusalem. The simplest historical explanation, on this view, is that the Evangelist wrote after AD 70 and shaped the prophecy in light of what had occurred—a vaticinium ex eventu, a “prophecy after the fact.”

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: The Strongest Objection, Stated at Full Strength
text: This is not special pleading, and it is important not to caricature it. Historians as a rule do not assume miracles or genuine foreknowledge when an ordinary explanation is available, and the correspondence between Jesus’s words and the events of 70 is real. The great historian of Judaism E. P. Sanders, while granting that nothing in Mark must be dated after 70, still inclined to a date around 70 on broader grounds.13 Luke 21:20, with its talk of Jerusalem “surrounded by armies,” reads to many scholars as more specific than Mark—suggesting an author writing with the siege in view. To a critic, the early-dater looks like someone willing to multiply improbabilities (genuine prediction, a string of coincidental silences) to avoid the obvious.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry
text: The reply begins with a concession. The vaticinium ex eventu reading is a legitimate historical inference, and it cannot be refuted simply by insisting that Jesus could predict the future—that would smuggle the conclusion into the premise. The most one can say is that the argument is not as decisive as it sounds, for three reasons.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry
text: First, the prediction in Mark 13 is conspicuously unspecific about the manner of Jerusalem’s fall. It speaks of the Temple’s stones thrown down, of wars and rumors of wars, of flight to the mountains—but says nothing of the fire that gutted the Temple, the months-long siege, or the legions of Titus, the very details a writer narrating after the fact would find hard to omit. Some scholars—notably N. T. Wright and R. T. France—have noted that the discourse draws its imagery from the Old Testament and from earlier threats to the Temple rather than from the specifics of 70. Second, the silences in Acts remain hard to explain on a late date; a convergence of expected-yet-absent events (Paul’s death, James’s death, the fall of Jerusalem) is more telling than any single omission. Third, and most importantly, the early-dating case for the central claims does not stand or fall with Mark’s date at all. Even on Ehrman’s own chronology, the creed of 1 Corinthians 15 and Paul’s letters carry the death, burial, and resurrection proclamation back into the 30s and 50s. Whether Mark is 65 or 72 changes little here.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry
text: And here the limits must be stated plainly, in the critic’s favor. The argument from silence in Acts—as distinct from the political and apologetic arguments noted earlier, which do not depend on it—is genuinely an argument from silence, and such arguments are only as strong as the certainty that the author would have mentioned the missing event—a judgment about which reasonable scholars differ. Luke may have ended Acts where his narrative purpose was complete, with the gospel reaching Rome. The dissenting expert here is the consensus itself: most New Testament specialists are not persuaded that the silences outweigh the source-critical and Olivet-Discourse considerations, and they place the Gospels a decade or two later than Robinson did. The early-dating of the narrative Gospels to the pre-70 period is therefore a serious, defensible, but genuinely contested position—not a settled result.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry
text: So let the critic have the last objection before the reply. Ehrman would say: you have rescued the early creed, granted, but you have not rescued the early Gospels, and it is the Gospels that contain the miracles, the empty tomb, the detailed narratives—so the gap you most needed to close, you have left open. That is fair. The considered answer is that the argument never promised to close it. What the creed establishes is that the explanatory core—a crucified, buried, and (it was claimed) risen Jesus, attested by named witnesses—is too early to be slow legend. The narrative details are a further question, addressed by other lines of evidence, including the case that the Gospels themselves rest on named eyewitness testimony, and the finding — from a scholar who set out to disprove it — that the Gospels were composed in the recognisable genre of Graeco-Roman biography (bios), a literary form whose very purpose is to convey historical information about a real person. That is a claim about genre, not a guarantee of accuracy: ancient bioi still selected and shaped their material around a theme. But it means the Gospels ask to be read as testimony about a real life, not as free-floating myth.14

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: The Honest State of the Scholarship
text: Two things are true at once, and a responsible presentation holds them together. On the dating of the four Gospels, the mainstream consensus—Mark c. 70, the others in the 80s and 90s—remains the majority view, and the pre-70 dating championed by Robinson and Hemer—and restated more recently by Alexander Mittelstaedt (2006), Karl Armstrong (2017), and David Seccombe (2020)—is a respected minority position, not the field’s settled judgment; a centrist commentator like Craig Keener, no partisan of the early date, still places Luke–Acts in the early 70s, with the 60s and 80s among the live possibilities. But on the dating of the earliest tradition—the 1 Corinthians 15 creed and the undisputed Pauline letters—there is broad agreement across the ideological spectrum, sceptics included, that the material is remarkably early. The live debate is not about whether the central proclamation is early (it is) but about how much follows from that, and about where exactly the narrative Gospels sit within the eyewitness generation.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: Conclusion: What Early Dating Does and Does Not Establish
text: What the argument establishes is real and worth holding onto. The foundational Christian claims about Jesus’s death and resurrection appearances are not the residue of generations of mythmaking; they are demonstrably early, fixed in creedal form within a few years of the events, named to specific witnesses, and circulated while hostile parties in Jerusalem could have objected. Even on the mainstream (later) dating, the Gospels fall within living memory. The “legend had time to grow” hypothesis, in its strong form, simply does not fit the evidence.

title: How Early Was the New Testament Written? The Case for Closeness to the Events
section: Conclusion: What Early Dating Does and Does Not Establish
text: What it does not establish is equally important, and pretending otherwise would forfeit the reader’s trust. Early does not mean true. An early date rules out one explanation—slow, undetected legendary development—but it does not rule out sincere error or deliberate fabrication; people can and do invent things quickly. Nor does it prove the pre-70 dating of the narrative Gospels, which remains contested. The early-dating argument is best understood as removing a whole class of objection and clearing the ground—handing the central claims over to be assessed as first-generation testimony, where the harder questions of honesty, accuracy, and the resurrection itself can be taken up on their own terms. It does not win the war. It just makes sure the right battle gets fought.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
text: Sometime around the year 112, a worried Roman governor sat down to write to his emperor for advice. Pliny the Younger had been executing Christians in the province of Bithynia—on the Black Sea coast of what is now Turkey—and he wanted to be sure he was doing it correctly. To gather evidence he had interrogated suspects, two female deacons among them, “under torture.” What he learned about this stubborn sect he reported almost as a curiosity. Their habit, he told Trajan, was to gather before dawn on a fixed day and “to recite a hymn antiphonally to Christ, as to a god.”1

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
text: That single line, scribbled by a hostile pagan administrator more than two centuries before the Council of Nicaea, is the quiet undoing of one of the most popular myths about Christianity ever made: that the deity of Christ and the doctrine of the Trinity were invented in the fourth century—voted into existence by bishops at the command of the emperor Constantine. The line gained mass currency through Dan Brown’s 2003 novel The Da Vinci Code, whose characters announce that “until that moment in history, Jesus was viewed by his followers as a mortal prophet… a great and powerful man, but a man nonetheless,” and that his divinity was established at Nicaea by “a relatively close vote.”2 It is repeated in pubs and comment threads to this day. And it is, on the plain historical record, false.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
text: But there is a serious version of the developmental thesis—argued by scholars, not novelists—and it should be met at full strength. This essay does both: it sets out what the pre-Nicene church actually believed and prayed, distinguishes the real story of doctrinal development from the myth of invention, and then squares up to the strongest critic in the room.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: Stating the Question Carefully
text: Precision matters here, because two different claims are easily blurred. The first is the popular one: Nicaea invented the belief that Jesus is divine. The second is a scholarly one: the precise conceptual vocabulary of Trinitarian doctrine—one essence in three persons, the Son “of one substance” with the Father—developed over time, and was hammered into final form in the fourth century. The first claim is refuted by the evidence. The second is, in large part, simply true—and no informed Christian need deny it.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: Stating the Question Carefully
text: The thesis this essay defends is therefore narrower and more honest than triumphalism allows. It is that the early church worshipped and confessed Father, Son, and Holy Spirit from the earliest period we can document; that this devotion long predates Constantine; and that the councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381) did not create that faith but clarified its language under pressure from a genuinely new denial. Development of terminology is not invention of belief. The praying came first; the definitions came to defend the praying.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: The Pre-Nicene Church at Worship
text: The most important evidence is not a creed but a practice. Before there were technical terms, there was a pattern of devotion in which Jesus was reverenced alongside God the Father in ways Jews reserved for God alone. The late Larry Hurtado of Edinburgh—the leading historian of early Christian worship—called this a “binitarian” (later he preferred “dyadic”) shape of devotion, and argued that it emerged not after centuries of drift but within the first two decades of the movement, among monotheistic Jews who would have regarded worshipping a creature as blasphemy.3 This is what Hurtado meant by calling earliest Christianity a “mutation” within Jewish monotheism: Jesus was sung to, prayed to, baptized into, and invoked.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: The Pre-Nicene Church at Worship
text: The fingerprints of that worship are embedded in the New Testament itself, often in material that predates the documents quoting it. Paul preserves the Aramaic prayer marana tha—“our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22)—a petition addressed to Jesus that must have arisen in the first Aramaic-speaking churches of Judea. The hymn of Philippians 2:6–11, which most scholars regard as pre-Pauline tradition Paul is citing, applies to Jesus the words of Isaiah 45:23, where every knee bows to Yahweh. These are not fourth-century inventions; they are the oldest strata we possess.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: The Pre-Nicene Church at Worship
text: The same pattern continues seamlessly into the generation after the apostles. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, wrote seven letters around 107–110 while being marched under guard to his execution in Rome. He calls Jesus “our God” without apology or argument—in the opening greeting of his letter to the Ephesians he addresses a church “united… by the will of the Father and of Jesus Christ our God.”4 A man writing on his way to be eaten by beasts is not polishing an archive for posterity; he is recording the settled speech of his churches. And then there is Pliny—a Roman official with no stake in Christian theology—reporting that the worship of Christ “as to a god” was the defining habit of the sect. (Some scholars, noting Pliny’s Latin quasi deo, debate the precise force of “as to”; the classicist A. N. Sherwin-White argued the word here simply means “as,” not “as if.”)5

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: The Pre-Nicene Church at Worship
text: Three further structures of pre-Nicene faith confirm the threefold shape. Baptism was administered “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit”—the formula of Matthew 28:19, already prescribed as standard practice in the Didache, a church manual most date to the late first or early second century.6 The Rule of Faith—the summary of belief converts confessed before baptism—ran in a threefold, Father-Son-Spirit pattern in Irenaeus and Tertullian well before any council, the seed from which the later creeds grew.7 And doxologies praised the three together: the account of Polycarp’s martyrdom (c. 155–160) records Polycarp’s final prayer, which closes by giving glory to the Father through Jesus Christ, “with him and the Holy Spirit.”8 The grammar of worship was Trinitarian long before the metaphysics was defined.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: The Ante-Nicene Fathers: Real Development, Honestly Told
text: None of this means the early Fathers spoke with the polished precision of the later creeds. They did not, and pretending otherwise does the case no favors. The pre-Nicene writers were reaching for language adequate to an experience that outran their vocabulary, and their formulations are uneven.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: The Ante-Nicene Fathers: Real Development, Honestly Told
text: Justin Martyr, writing around 150–160, defends the worship of the Logos as God yet can also describe him as “another God” alongside the Father and as serving the Father’s will—language that sounds, to modern ears, subordinationist.9 Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 180), combating Gnosticism, gave the church its enduring image of the Son and the Spirit as the “two hands” of the Father, insisting the one God always acts through Word and Wisdom.10 Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–254), the most powerful mind of the era, made a decisive contribution by teaching the eternal generation of the Son—the Son is begotten of the Father not at some point in time but eternally, so that there never was a time when the Father was without his Word—yet Origen too used language that ranks the Son below the Father.11

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: The Ante-Nicene Fathers: Real Development, Honestly Told
text: The Latin contribution came from Tertullian of Carthage. Around 210, in a treatise against a teacher named Praxeas who had collapsed the distinctions between Father and Son (the error later called modalism), Tertullian forged the vocabulary the West would use forever after. He appears to be the first Christian writer to use the Latin trinitas—“Trinity”—and he described Father, Son, and Spirit as three persons (personae) of one substance (unius substantiae)—the idea later summed up as tres personae, una substantia.12 A full century before Nicaea, the substance of the formula the church would make standard was already on the page.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: The Ante-Nicene Fathers: Real Development, Honestly Told
text: So the honest picture is neither a pristine creed delivered intact from the apostles nor a fourth-century fabrication. It is a living tradition that knew what it worshipped—the Father, and the Son who is fully God and not a creature, and the Spirit—while still working out how to say it without lapsing into either modalism (one God wearing three masks) or tritheism (three gods). That is development. It is exactly what we should expect of a community thinking under pressure across generations.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: What Nicaea Actually Did—and the Real Vote
text: Into this tradition, around 318–320, a presbyter of Alexandria named Arius introduced something his own bishop regarded as new and alarming. Arius taught that the Son, though exalted above all creation, was a creature—made by the Father out of nothing before the ages. His slogan was stark: “there was when he was not.”13 The Son, on this view, was not eternal and not of the same divine being as the Father. It was a line the mainstream of the prior tradition—Origen’s eternal generation, the worship Ignatius and Pliny attest—had not crossed, even where its language wobbled (Tertullian could say there was a time when God was not yet Father, though he never made the Son a creature brought into being from nothing).

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: What Nicaea Actually Did—and the Real Vote
text: When Constantine, newly master of the whole empire and anxious for its unity, summoned the bishops to Nicaea in 325, the council’s question was never whether to use exalted language for Jesus—both sides already did. The question was narrower and sharper: is the Son a created being, or is he truly and fully God—uncreated, of one substance with the Father? To exclude Arius’s teaching, the council adopted into its creed the word homoousios—“of the same substance” (or essence) as the Father. The term was not biblical, and it was controversial even among the orthodox, since it had a checkered history in earlier disputes. But it had one decisive virtue: it was the one word Arius’s party could not sign while still meaning that the Son was a creature.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: What Nicaea Actually Did—and the Real Vote
text: And the vote? Of roughly 250 to 318 bishops present (the sources vary), all but two of those present subscribed; only two Libyan bishops, Theonas and Secundus, refused outright and were exiled with Arius—though several who signed would soon waver in the turbulent decades that followed.14 Dan Brown’s “relatively close vote” is the reverse of the truth: the margin was overwhelming. Nor were these men Constantine’s creatures. Some of the bishops at Nicaea bore the scars and missing eyes of the Great Persecution under Diocletian, which had ended barely a decade earlier—hardly a docile assembly inclined to vote on imperial command. The doctrine they affirmed was the one their churches had been praying.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: What Nicaea Actually Did—and the Real Vote
text: It is equally important to say what Nicaea did not do. It did not produce the creed most Christians recite today; the fuller “Nicene Creed,” with its developed clause on the Holy Spirit, comes from the Council of Constantinople in 381, which confessed the Spirit as “the Lord, the giver of life… who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified.”15 And Nicaea did not settle the matter. As the historian Lewis Ayres has stressed, homoousios was so far from being an instant slogan that for nearly twenty years after the council scarcely anyone—Athanasius included—even mentioned it; the decades after 325 were a chaos of competing parties, not a tidy triumph.16 The full Trinitarian synthesis was the achievement of the next two generations, above all the Cappadocian Fathers—Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa—who clarified the distinction between the one ousia (essence) and the three hypostaseis (persons). Development, here, is undeniable. The point is what was being developed: the language for a faith already held, not the faith itself.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: The Strongest Objection, Stated at Full Strength
text: The serious challenge does not come from Dan Brown. It comes from Bart D. Ehrman, the agnostic New Testament scholar whose How Jesus Became God (2014) gives the developmental thesis its best-known popular statement. Ehrman explicitly rejects the Constantine myth—he knows the devotion is early. His claim is subtler.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: The Strongest Objection, Stated at Full Strength
text: Ehrman argues that the historical Jesus did not claim to be God and was not worshipped as God in his lifetime. After the crucifixion, some of his followers had visionary experiences they took to be appearances of the risen Jesus, and concluded that God had exalted him to heaven. From there, Christology “evolved”: Christians progressively pushed the moment of Jesus’s divine status earlier and earlier—from the resurrection, back to his baptism, back to his conception—though Ehrman also finds a pre-existent Christ in material older than Paul’s letters.17 Crucially, Ehrman insists that the ancient line between human and divine was porous, populated by a spectrum of semi-divine beings; so calling Jesus “a god” in the second century need not mean what Nicaea later meant by it. On this reading, the high Christology of Ignatius and the worship Pliny reports are real—but they are way-stations on a road, not the destination, and the full-strength claim that the Son is the one God, co-equal and co-eternal, is a later and contestable theological construction.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: The Strongest Objection, Stated at Full Strength
text: This is the objection at its best, and parts of it must be conceded. The accurate observations in it should be granted: there was real development; early language is uneven; “god” carried a wider range in antiquity than in modern monotheism; and the technical vocabulary of Constantinople is not found on the lips of Jesus of Nazareth. None of those facts, though, carries Ehrman’s conclusion. The history is messier than a slogan.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry
text: Yet the developmental model strains against the very evidence Ehrman concedes. The disagreement is not really about dates—Ehrman himself finds a pre-existent Christ in material older than Paul’s letters—but about what kind of being the earliest Christians took him to be: on his account a pre-existent divine being of a lower order, an angel or something like one. Two features of the earliest Christian material are hard to place among the exalted intermediaries. The first is where Jesus is put. In 1 Corinthians 8:6 Paul takes Israel’s own confession that the LORD is one and divides its two divine titles, so that the “one God” is the Father and the “one Lord” is Jesus Christ, “through whom are all things.” That reading of the verse is influential, arguably dominant, and genuinely contested: James F. McGrath argues that “one Lord” is set alongside the creed rather than folded into it.18 Taken as the majority take it, it is not one more step up a ladder. Wisdom is praised; Enoch is exalted; but no Jewish writer took the creed of divine uniqueness and wrote a second figure into it. Paul did. Ehrman will not be moved by the objection that a “one Lord” who is not the one God leaves Paul confessing a second divine power; he takes that horn, holding that ancient Judaism had room for such a being.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry
text: The second is worship. To Ehrman’s point about the porous human-divine boundary, the reply is not that Judaism drew the Creator/creature line with every angel on the creature side—that is Bauckham’s contested thesis, and exactly what Ehrman denies. It is narrower: whatever room Judaism had for exalted intermediaries, those figures characteristically refuse worship and redirect it to God, while the earliest Christians were praying to Jesus and singing to him within the first two decades.3 That is exactly why Hurtado calls the worship of Jesus a startling “mutation” rather than an unremarkable promotion. The earliest Christians did not slot Jesus into a familiar category of exalted agents; they did the unthinkable thing of giving a recently crucified man the devotion their Scriptures reserved for Yahweh—and they did it almost at once.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry
text: But the critic should get the last word before the reply closes, because the strongest form of his case is not yet exhausted. Ehrman can grant everything above and still press: worship and full conciliar dogma are not the same thing. Granting that the earliest Christians revered Jesus extraordinarily, the specific metaphysical claim—one identical divine essence in three co-equal persons—is a fourth-century philosophical settlement that the New Testament neither states nor requires. You have shown early high devotion; you have not shown the Nicene Creed. The distinction is accurate, and it draws the honest boundary of the argument.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry
text: The reply is to grant the distinction and deny that it carries Ehrman’s conclusion. Yes, the conceptual apparatus of ousia and hypostasis is later than the New Testament; the Cappadocians’ precision is a genuine theological achievement, not a verse one can cite. But the doctrine those terms protect—that the Son is fully God and not a creature, worshipped with the Father, and that the one God is somehow Father, Son, and Spirit—is the very thing the earliest worship already presupposed. The councils did not add deity to a human Jesus; they supplied a grammar that could hold together the threeness and the oneness the church had been confessing all along, and could rule out the two ditches—Arius’s created Son on one side, the modalists’ collapse of the persons on the other. The development is real; what it developed was not the worship but the words. So the evolutionary account does not hold: the Nicene confession is not a later construction laid over a lower Christology, but the church’s precise statement of the worship it had offered from the start.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: Was It Borrowed from Paganism?
text: A second objection comes from a different direction, and it too should be stated fairly before a reply. The Trinity, it is said, was never Christian at all: it was lifted from the older paganism that surrounded the early church. Egypt had its family of Isis, Osiris, and Horus; Babylon and Sumer had their divine triads; Rome worshipped the Capitoline three—Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva—in a single temple on the Capitoline Hill; and Mithras is often thrown onto the pile for good measure. The doctrine of “three-in-one,” the argument runs, is simply a Christian recycling of a pattern the ancient world already knew by heart. The claim circulates widely—in documentaries, in comment threads, in the same neighborhood as The Da Vinci Code—and it is worth answering plainly rather than waving away.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: Was It Borrowed from Paganism?
text: Begin by conceding what is true. Ancient religion really was full of divine threesomes; grouping gods in threes was a genuine and widespread habit, in Egypt above all.19 No one need pretend otherwise. But a shared number is not a shared doctrine, and here the objection makes a category error that decides the case. Every one of these “trinities” is a grouping of separate gods—polytheism, not monotheism. Isis, Osiris, and Horus are mother, father, and son, three distinct deities bound by a family story. The Capitoline triad is three separate gods who happen to share a temple. These are collections of different beings. The Christian claim is the reverse: not three gods but one God, one being (ousia), who exists eternally as three co-equal, co-eternal persons (hypostaseis). To say “both have a three” is like saying a bicycle and a triangle must be the same thing because each involves a number. (Mithras, so often named in the list, was a single central figure rather than a triad of gods—which shows how loosely these parallels are drawn.)20

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: Was It Borrowed from Paganism?
text: The deeper problem is one of soil and direction. The Trinity was not confessed by pagans reaching for a fresh myth. It was confessed by Jews—people formed from childhood by the Shema, “Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4), for whom offering worship to any creature was the gravest blasphemy. Strict monotheists are the least likely people on earth to smuggle in a pagan triad; refusing exactly that was the thing their whole identity existed to do. As Larry Hurtado stressed, the earliest devotion to Jesus arose inside Jewish monotheism, among worshippers who would not bow to Caesar’s gods on pain of death. The doctrine grew not from monotheists abandoning monotheism but from monotheists who would not abandon it, and yet found they had to reckon with what they had received in Christ and the Spirit. That is the opposite of syncretistic borrowing.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: Was It Borrowed from Paganism?
text: Finally, a word about method. The move from surface similarity to genealogy—they both have a three, therefore one copied the other—is the same discredited reasoning behind the popular claim that Jesus was patched together from Horus and Mithras. Scholars of ancient religion long ago named and rejected it; the biblical scholar Samuel Sandmel called it “parallelomania,” the error of mistaking resemblance for dependence, and even a skeptic like Bart Ehrman has dismantled the pagan-copycat thesis at length.21 The point is not that no triads existed in the ancient world. They plainly did. The point is that borrowing is unfounded on every axis that matters: wrong religion, wrong structure, wrong direction.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: The Honest State of the Scholarship
text: Where does the live debate actually stand? On the popular claim, there is no debate among historians: no mainstream historian of any persuasion holds that Constantine or Nicaea invented Jesus’s divinity. That belief is documented in pagan and Christian sources alike for two centuries before the council, and the “close vote” is a fiction.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: The Honest State of the Scholarship
text: The genuine scholarly disagreement runs along a finer seam. The “early high Christology” scholars hold that Jesus was worshipped (Hurtado) and included in the divine identity of Israel’s God (Bauckham) essentially from the start—though Bauckham’s divine-identity category is itself debated. Ehrman and those influenced by older “history of religions” approaches hold to a more evolutionary model, even while conceding how early the devotion appears. Both sides agree the worship is early; they disagree over how to interpret it and how far it reaches toward later dogma. On the fourth century itself, the work of Ayres and the late R. P. C. Hanson has demolished the old caricature of a tidy fight between “Nicene” and “Arian” blocs, revealing instead a confusing field of overlapping theologies that took decades to resolve.22 This is the honest texture of the history—and it is far more interesting than either the apologist’s slogan or the skeptic’s.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not Establish
text: The historical record establishes, with as much confidence as the sources allow, that the early church worshipped and confessed Father, Son, and Holy Spirit from its earliest documented life—in its prayers, its hymns, its baptisms, and its rules of faith—long before any emperor convened a council. It establishes that Arianism, not Trinitarian faith, was the innovation Nicaea confronted, and that the council’s near-unanimous verdict was the defense of an inheritance, not the manufacture of a novelty. The popular claim that Nicaea invented the Trinity, or voted Jesus into godhood, simply cannot survive contact with the evidence.

title: The Early Church and the Trinity
section: Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not Establish
text: It is equally important to mark what this does not establish. It does not show that the doctrine sprang fully formed from the apostles’ lips; the technical language of one essence in three persons was a real development, refined across the fourth century and beyond. It does not, by itself, prove the doctrine true—that the triune God exists is a further question, argued from Scripture, reason, and the claims and resurrection of Jesus himself. What the history removes is a specific and very common objection: the charge that Christians worship a god assembled by a committee under political duress. They do not. They worship the one their forebears were already singing to before dawn, “as to a god,” while the empire was still trying to make them stop. We hold that this worship is rightly placed—that the one they sang to is, as Nicaea confessed, true God from true God, one God with the Father and the Spirit, a mystery we confess rather than a formula we have mastered. That case is argued from Scripture and the resurrection, and it begins where this one ends.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: A claim that could be checked
text: Of all the events the first Christians proclaimed, the empty tomb is the one that, in principle, anyone in Jerusalem could have falsified by a short walk. The appearances were experiences; you either had one or you did not. But a body either lies in a grave or it does not. When the apostles began preaching in the very city where Jesus had been executed weeks earlier — insisting that God had raised him — they were making a claim with a physical address attached. If a tomb known to the authorities still held a corpse, the simplest refutation in the history of religion was available: open it.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: A claim that could be checked
text: This essay is about that grave alone. It is not about whether the disciples saw the risen Jesus, nor about Paul's testimony, nor about the wider "minimal facts" method — those arguments are treated elsewhere in this library. Here the single question is narrower and prior: did the tomb of Jesus, on the third day, in fact stand empty? That the disciples believed it did is not in dispute. Whether the belief was rooted in a real, discoverable fact — and how a careful historian should weigh the evidence — is the matter at hand. The honest answer is that the empty tomb is well attested and accepted by a substantial body of scholars, that it is more contested than the appearances, and that the strongest sceptical alternative deserves to be stated in full before it is answered.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: The fact and its supports
text: The empty tomb is not a free-floating assertion. It is lodged inside a cluster of details — the burial, the man who performed it, the location, the witnesses — each of which can be examined on its own. Five lines of evidence are usually advanced. None is decisive alone; their force is cumulative.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: The fact and its supports
text: The empty-tomb tradition is anchored to a named, identifiable burial. According to all four Gospels, Jesus was interred not in a common grave but in the rock tomb of Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the Sanhedrin — the very council that had handed Jesus over.1 This detail carries weight precisely because it is awkward. Early Christian writing is, on the whole, sharply hostile to the Jewish leadership that secured Jesus' death; for a pious member of that body to step forward and do right by Jesus cuts against the grain. The Catholic scholar Raymond Brown, who was no apologist for the miraculous, judged the burial by Joseph "very probable," reasoning that a Christian fabrication of a Sanhedrist who honours Jesus is "almost inexplicable" given that hostility.2 A named tomb in a named owner's possession also means the claim was, in the language of historians, falsifiable: there was a specific place to point to.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: The fact and its supports
text: The tomb, moreover, was a real and identifiable kind of place, not a narrative convenience. Jodi Magness, a leading archaeologist of Roman-period Judaea, judges the Gospel descriptions of Jesus' burial consistent with how Jerusalem Jews of the period actually buried their dead — the body washed, wrapped in a shroud, and laid on a rock-cut shelf, the entrance closed by a blocking stone.3 That is precisely the sort of tomb a wealthy councilman such as Joseph would have owned, and precisely why the women returned after the Sabbath expecting to finish the burial rites — and found the shelf bare. This is consistent with the Gospel account rather than proof of an empty grave; the full archaeology is treated in the companion essay on the burial of Jesus.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: The fact and its supports
text: One of the strongest strands is that Jesus' opponents did not deny the tomb was empty — they offered a rival explanation for it. Matthew reports that the chief priests bribed the guard to say, "His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep," and adds that "this story has been spread among the Jews to this day."4 Whatever one makes of the guard narrative itself (which is unique to Matthew and which critics reasonably question), the telling datum is the polemic: the earliest recoverable Jewish response to the resurrection preaching was not "the body is still there" but "the body was taken." To bother explaining why a tomb is empty is most naturally read as conceding that it was empty. It should be granted, in fairness, that this counter-story is securely attested only from Matthew's period onward, so the datum is strong but not contemporaneous with the events themselves.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: The fact and its supports
text: This counter-story has an unusually long paper trail. Around 150, Justin Martyr records that Jewish authorities were sending emissaries to say the disciples "stole him by night from the tomb"; around 200, Tertullian in North Africa knows the same charge.5 A polemic that the opponents kept alive for over a century is hard to reconcile with the idea that there was simply no empty tomb to argue about.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: The fact and its supports
text: In every Gospel the discovery of the empty tomb is credited first to women — in the lead, Mary Magdalene.6 In first-century Judaea this was not a flattering choice. Josephus, reflecting the conventional attitude, writes: "Let not the testimony of women be admitted, on account of the levity and boldness of their sex."7 A movement free to compose its founding story for maximum credibility would naturally have put male disciples at the tomb. That the tradition instead makes women the first and primary witnesses — and shows the male apostles disbelieving their report as "an idle tale" (Luke 24:11) — is the kind of counter-productive detail the criterion of embarrassment marks as probably historical. The New Testament historian Richard Bauckham argues that the women are named so consistently across the sources precisely because they were known, public eyewitnesses whose testimony the tradition could not quietly drop.8

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: The fact and its supports
text: Bauckham presses the point further: the women are not a vague literary flourish but identifiable individuals — Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, Joanna, Salome — whose report could still be checked against living memory when the Gospels were written, and a movement inventing a story for maximum credibility would not have rested it on witnesses whose public word carried so little weight.8 N. T. Wright makes the same point from the other side: had the empty-tomb narratives been late apologetic fiction, casting women as the principal discoverers is the very last thing their authors would have done.9 The limit should be stated precisely: whether women were formally barred from giving legal testimony is itself disputed, and this essay rests only on Josephus's frank aside about how their word was regarded7 — but even that weaker claim is enough to make female first-witnesses a counter-productive choice for an inventor.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: The fact and its supports
text: The resurrection was first proclaimed in Jerusalem, not in distant Galilee a generation later. This matters because the tomb was local and accessible, and the authorities had every motive and every means to end the movement by producing the corpse. As the philosopher William Lane Craig has pressed the point, a resurrection proclamation in the same city, within weeks, would have been impossible to sustain if the body lay where everyone could find it.10

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: The fact and its supports
text: Craig has developed the point into a sustained argument. The site of the grave was known to Jew and Christian alike; a movement proclaiming a bodily resurrection could not have taken root in the very city of the public execution and burial unless that grave was empty. The authorities had both the motive and the means to strangle the preaching at birth by producing the body — and yet the counter-move the sources record is not a corpse but a story about a stolen one, which concedes the tomb rather than refuting it.11

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: The fact and its supports
text: The argument is not airtight — a body weeks dead might be hard to identify, and we cannot prove the authorities tried and failed — but the silence about any such refutation, in a context where one was so obviously wanted, is suggestive.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: The fact and its supports
text: The empty tomb is reported in Mark and, independently, in the special material of Matthew, Luke, and John, and the burial is presupposed in the pre-Pauline creed of 1 Corinthians 15 ("he was buried, … he was raised").12 A number of scholars judge that Mark drew his passion-and-burial account from an earlier connected source, pushing the tradition back well before the Gospel's composition.13 On this view the empty-tomb report belongs to the pre-Markan passion source and is therefore very early — and its earliest form is conspicuously plain: an open grave and frightened women, with none of the guards, angelic choreography, or spectacle the second-century apocryphal gospels would later heap on.11 A tradition that reports a puzzle rather than a triumph reads far more like early memory than like developed legend, a restraint traced further in the companion essay on the earliest resurrection narratives. Multiple independent lines reporting the same outcome — an empty grave — raise its probability above what any single witness could establish.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: What the evidence does and does not show
text: It is essential to state the limit plainly. None of this proves a resurrection. An empty tomb, by itself, is consistent with theft, relocation, confusion, or causes we cannot now recover; the leap from "the grave was empty" to "God raised him" depends on the appearances and on the failure of natural alternatives, argued separately. The empty tomb is a necessary feature of the bodily-resurrection claim and a serious historical datum in its own right — not, on its own, a demonstration of the miracle. Conversely, even firm establishment of the tomb leaves untouched the question that the rest of the case must answer: why was it empty?

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: The sceptical case, in its strongest form
text: The most formidable challenge does not quibble about who first reached the tomb; it denies that there was a known tomb to reach. John Dominic Crossan, the most prominent voice of the Jesus Seminar on this question, argues that the burial narratives are theological fiction. Rome crucified to terrify, and routinely left the dead on the cross or in shallow graves as carrion for scavenging dogs and birds; a condemned provincial like Jesus, Crossan contends, would most likely have met the same fate, his remains never recovered.14 On this reading Mark created the Joseph-of-Arimathea burial tradition, and the empty-tomb story is "neither an early historical event nor a late legendary narrative but a deliberate Markan creation."15 If Crossan is right, the entire structure above collapses: there is no tomb to be found empty, and the enemy polemic is simply a Christian literary device.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: The sceptical case, in its strongest form
text: It must be conceded what is true in the objection. Roman crucifixion was indeed a horror designed to deny the victim honourable burial, and non-burial was common. Bart Ehrman, on independent grounds, has likewise argued that the burial tradition is doubtful and that Romans typically left crucifixion victims unburied — so the sceptical case here is not Crossan's alone.16

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: The sceptical case, in its strongest form
text: Yet the case has real countervailing weight, and it can be met here rather than merely deferred (the fuller treatment, since it turns on the burial rather than the tomb itself, is in the companion essay on the burial of Jesus). Three considerations tell against Crossan's reconstruction. First, Jewish law required the burial of the executed before nightfall (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), and Josephus states that the Jews were so scrupulous on this point that they took down and buried even the crucified before sunset;17 Judaea was not a place where Roman non-burial customs went unchallenged. Second, the crucified man Yehohanan — whose heel-bone, still pierced by the nail, was recovered from a first-century Jerusalem tomb — is direct material proof that at least some victims of crucifixion in Jesus' city were given proper burial.18 Third, the very embarrassment of crediting the burial to Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council that condemned Jesus, and the discovery to the women, tells against pure invention. Crossan's thesis requires treating as fiction precisely the details — a Sanhedrist benefactor, the women witnesses — that bear the marks of awkward memory rather than invention. The dispute over the burial is genuinely live, and it is the hinge on which the strongest version of the sceptical case turns.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: The sceptical case, in its strongest form
text: If one grants the tomb but seeks a natural emptying, the classic candidate is theft — the very charge the ancient polemic preferred. The difficulty is motive and consequence: the disciples who would have to be the thieves then went on to suffer and, in several cases, die for proclaiming a resurrection they would have known to be staged. Sincere people die for false beliefs all the time; what is psychologically strained is a coordinated group dying for what they personally know to be a fraud. (This essay does not rest the point on the disciples' deaths, treated elsewhere; it notes only that simple theft must carry that burden.) Variants — the women erred to the wrong tomb, the authorities quietly relocated the body — each founder on the same rock: had the body existed anywhere recoverable, producing it would have been the obvious and devastating reply, and no source records anyone doing so. These are not knock-down refutations; they are reasons the natural theories have not commanded a consensus.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: The sceptical case, in its strongest form
text: A distinct and pointed objection observes that neither the pre-Pauline creed of 1 Corinthians 15 nor Paul anywhere mentions a tomb found empty; the discovery narrative first surfaces in Mark, a decade or more later, which is why critics read it as a Markan device rather than early tradition. The observation is accurate and should be granted: Paul nowhere narrates the discovery of an empty grave. But the inference does not follow, for three reasons. First, in a first-century Jewish frame the creed's own words — Christ "was buried" and "was raised on the third day" (1 Corinthians 15:3–4) — already entail an emptied grave. As N. T. Wright argues at length, no first-century Jew could have described a man as "raised" while his corpse still lay in the tomb; "resurrection" meant precisely the reversal of that state, so the creed presupposes the empty tomb rather than omitting it.19 Second, a compressed four-line kerygmatic formula, listing who died and to whom he appeared, would not pause to narrate a tomb-discovery regardless of what its author believed about the grave; silence in a summary is not denial. Third, the tradition Mark preserves — women as the first witnesses — bears the embarrassment marks discussed above, which tell against a late apologetic invention. Paul's silence, then, is the silence of a creed that assumes the empty tomb, not of a movement that had never heard of one.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: Where the scholarship stands
text: It is sometimes claimed that "about 75 percent" of scholars accept the empty tomb. That figure comes from Gary Habermas's ongoing bibliographic survey of resurrection literature since 1975, and it should be cited with care: it is a count of published positions assembled by one researcher, not a randomised poll, critics have questioned how the sample was drawn, and Habermas himself has leaned on it less in recent work.20 What can be said responsibly is more modest and still substantial: the empty tomb is affirmed by a wide range of mainstream scholars — among them Brown, Wright, and the agnostic classicist Michael Grant, who concluded that "if we apply the same sort of criteria that we would apply to any other ancient literary sources, the evidence is firm and plausible enough to necessitate the conclusion that the tomb was indeed found empty."21 Grant's "necessitate" in fact claims more than this essay does: the verdict defended here is the more cautious "more probable than not," not that the evidence compels the conclusion.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: Where the scholarship stands
text: It helps to name the scholars on the affirming side, since they are as real and as varied as the sceptics. The range spans the Catholic Raymond Brown, the Anglican N. T. Wright, the agnostic classicist Michael Grant, and the Lutheran ancient historian Paul Maier, who put the historian's verdict about as strongly as the evidence allows: "If all the evidence is weighed carefully and fairly, it is indeed justifiable, according to the canons of historical research, to conclude that the sepulcher of Joseph of Arimathea, in which Jesus was buried, was actually empty on the morning of the first Easter. And no shred of evidence has yet been discovered in literary sources, epigraphy, or archaeology that would disprove this statement."22 Maier’s “no shred of evidence would disprove” is an argument from the absence of disproof, and states the case more confidently than this essay does; the verdict defended here remains the cautious “more probable than not.” This is the position of a substantial majority of those who have worked closely on the question — how large a majority, as the previous paragraph cautioned, cannot be precisely quantified — and not a unanimous one.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: Where the scholarship stands
text: It is also genuinely disputed, with Crossan, Ehrman, and others on the other side. The empty tomb is better described as a strong, well-defended position than as a settled fact — and noticeably less secure than the near-consensus that the disciples had experiences they took to be appearances.

title: The Empty Tomb: How Strong Is the Case That the Grave Was Found Empty?
section: Conclusion
text: The case for the empty tomb is cumulative and circumstantial, in the way most ancient history is. A named burial by an awkward benefactor; an enemy polemic that explains the emptiness rather than denying it, traceable across a century; women as the embarrassing first witnesses; a proclamation launched in the one city where the body could most easily have been produced; and several independent strands of tradition converging on the same outcome — together these make the empty tomb more probable than not, and well worth defending. They do not, by themselves, prove the resurrection, and the most serious sceptical reply — that there was no honourable tomb to begin with — remains a serious objection, one the evidence answers on balance even if it cannot rule it out with certainty. The verdict a careful inquirer can reach is therefore confident but bounded: the grave was, in all probability, found empty; what emptied it is the next and larger question. That conclusion is best held the way Peter urged any such case be made — "with gentleness and respect" (1 Peter 3:15), sure of what the evidence shows and candid about where it stops.

title: Where Did Human Equality Come From?
text: You believe — almost without having to be told — that every human being is of equal worth. The newborn and the dying, the genius and the person with a profound disability, the celebrated and the destitute: whatever separates them, you assume that something makes them equal, and that this something outranks everything else about them. Strip away rank, usefulness, intelligence and strength, and a bare human worth remains, the same in each. We call the denial of this “dehumanising,” which is to say we treat it not as a mistake of fact but as a kind of blasphemy.

title: Where Did Human Equality Come From?
text: Here is the surprise. That conviction is not obvious, and it is not natural. It is a value, not a measurement — because as a measurement it is plainly false. Human beings are radically unequal in every capacity you can name: in strength, health, intellect, beauty, longevity, usefulness to others. Nothing you can weigh, count or test comes out equal. “Equal worth” is a claim about what a person is, laid over a mass of evidence that they are not equal in what they can do. So where did it come from? For most of recorded history almost no one believed it, and the civilisations that gave the West its philosophy believed something close to its opposite.

title: Where Did Human Equality Come From?
section: The world that ran the other way
text: The ancient Mediterranean was not merely hierarchical in the way every society is hierarchical, with some people richer or more powerful than others. It was hierarchical in its account of being. Some human beings were held to be higher and others lower not by accident of circumstance but by nature, from birth, in their very constitution. Aristotle states it without embarrassment, because to him it was simply description: “For that some should rule and others be ruled is a thing not only necessary, but expedient; from the hour of their birth, some are marked out for subjection, others for rule.”1 This is not a defence of a controversial thesis. It is a man pointing at what he takes to be the furniture of the universe.

title: Where Did Human Equality Come From?
section: The world that ran the other way
text: On this view, justice did not mean the levelling of persons; it meant the opposite. The intellectual historian Larry Siedentop puts the point flatly: “the core of ancient thinking” was “the assumption of natural inequality.”2 Greeks and Romans looked at the human race and instinctively saw a pyramid — men above women, free above enslaved, Greek above barbarian — and to give each his due, which is what justice was, meant keeping each in the tier nature had assigned him. Modern justice equalises; ancient justice ranked. They are nearly opposite ideas wearing the same word.

title: Where Did Human Equality Come From?
section: The world that ran the other way
text: Individual voices did dissent, and honesty requires naming them: some Stoics and Roman jurists reasoned toward a common humanity. Aristotle himself argues for natural slavery because others in his own day were calling slavery a mere human convention, contrary to nature; Seneca could write that a slave is a fellow human being; the jurist Ulpian recorded the principle that, by natural law, all are born equal.3 But — and this is the decisive fact — none of it became a movement, a law, or a settled conviction that the weak have a claim on the strong simply by being human. Seneca kept his slaves; Ulpian's maxim sat inside a legal code that enforced slavery. The dissent lived as an idea and never became anything more.

title: Where Did Human Equality Come From?
section: What the old stories took for granted
text: To feel how strange the equal-worth intuition is, look at what the ancient world's origin stories assumed a human being was for. In the Babylonian creation epic Enuma Elish, humanity is manufactured from the blood of a slain god, the traitor Kingu, and the purpose is stated in the making of us: mankind is charged with the service of the gods, so that the gods may be at ease.4 The older Mesopotamian poem Atrahasis is blunter still. The lesser gods have gone on strike, refusing the endless labour of digging the world's rivers and canals; so humanity is created to take the work over — “let man bear the load of the gods.”5 We are, in these stories, the gods' unpaid workforce, brought into existence for our usefulness and made from the blood of a murder.

title: Where Did Human Equality Come From?
section: What the old stories took for granted
text: That is not a slightly grimmer version of human dignity. It is a different kind of thing altogether. It is an anthropology in which a person's worth just is their utility, in which some exist to labour so that others may be at leisure — which is exactly the tiered world Aristotle described, now written into the cosmos at its origin. Against that background you can begin to measure the size of the reversal that was coming.

title: Where Did Human Equality Come From?
section: Four hundred crosses
text: What did that hierarchy cost an actual person? Consider one episode, reported by the Roman historian Tacitus. In AD 61 a senator named Pedanius Secundus, the prefect of the city of Rome, was murdered by one of his own slaves. Ancient custom prescribed the remedy: when a master was killed under his own roof, the entire household of slaves — in this case around four hundred men, women and children, nearly all of them innocent — was to be executed together. A crowd gathered in the streets to stop it, and the Senate debated. A minority recoiled. But the jurist Gaius Cassius carried the day, arguing that the old severity must stand, that so mixed a mass of slaves could be held down “only by terror,” and that — in the sentence that lays the whole logic bare — “in every great precedent there is some injustice, which is compensated, as against individuals, by the public advantage.”6 The four hundred went to their deaths.

title: Where Did Human Equality Come From?
section: Four hundred crosses
text: Read Cassius's principle slowly, because it is the precise inversion of the modern intuition. The individual is real but negligible; the collective is what counts; and an injustice done to particular persons is simply the price of the system, absorbed by the general good. A world that could reason like that, in its Senate, about hundreds of innocents, was not a world with a weak commitment to human equality. It was a world organised around the opposite commitment, and doing so in good conscience.

title: Where Did Human Equality Come From?
section: The claim that broke it
text: Into that world came a conviction with a different shape. Its root is not first of all Christian but Jewish: the opening page of Genesis says that God made humanity — not the king, not the free man, not the Greek, but humanity, male and female alike — in his own image. “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.”7 The claim is that worth is not earned or measured but conferred, bestowed on every human being by the Maker, and therefore identical in each regardless of capacity or rank. That doctrine developed in Jewish scripture and Jewish interpretation, and it stands on its own feet; the church did not invent it. What the church did was carry it into the Gentile world at scale, and weld it to a second claim that struck the ancient ear as insane.

title: Where Did Human Equality Come From?
section: The claim that broke it
text: The second claim was about the cross. Crucifixion was Rome's instrument for un-personing a human being: the death reserved for slaves and rebels, engineered to strip its victim of dignity in public.8 And Christians said that God himself, in the person of the Son, had been executed＊“God was executed” — in what sense Christians say itIs sayingThe one who suffered and died is a divine person, God the Son. Scripture speaks this way: it was “the Lord of glory” who was crucified (1 Corinthians 2:8), and God bought the church “with his own blood” (Acts 20:28).Not sayingNot that the divine nature suffered or died, and not that the Father suffered. Christ is one person in two natures, fully God and fully man; he died in his true human nature, and God did not cease to be God. by that very method. Paul knew how it sounded — he called the message of a crucified Messiah “a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles.”9 But follow the logic. The empire's supreme act of contempt, its way of declaring a human being worthless, had become the object of worship.
