Anthony has shown that Ibn Isḥāq was working from a Christian Palestinian Aramaic version of John, in which the Greek paraklētos had become the Aramaic menaḥḥemānā (“the comforter,” also evoking menaḥem, “comforter/consoler,” a messianic title in some Jewish texts).4 From this eighth-century seed, later Muslim writers assembled a fairly standard list of biblical “announcements” of Muhammad, which is still in circulation today. We will take the major ones in turn.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: Deuteronomy 18: “A Prophet Like Moses”
text: The flagship text is Deuteronomy 18:15–18. Moses tells Israel: “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers—it is to him you shall listen.” God then confirms it: “I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him” (ESV).5

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: Deuteronomy 18: “A Prophet Like Moses”
text: The Muslim argument here has real force and deserves to be stated without caricature. It has two parts. First, the phrase “from among their brothers.” Israel’s “brothers,” on this reading, are the Ishmaelites—the descendants of Abraham’s other son. The Bible itself describes Ishmael’s line as dwelling “over against all his kinsmen” (Genesis 25:18), so an Arab prophet, a cousin rather than a son of Israel, fits the wording naturally. Second, and more forcefully, the criterion “like Moses.” The Muslim points out that Muhammad resembled Moses far more closely than Jesus did: both Moses and Muhammad were lawgivers who brought a comprehensive code; both led their people in war; both married and had children; both died natural deaths and were buried; both began as ordinary men, not as divine figures. Jesus, by contrast, founded no state, fought no battles, and—on the Christian account—was no mere prophet but the incarnate Son. So if we are asked who, in history, was “like Moses,” Muhammad seems the more obvious answer.6

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: Deuteronomy 18: “A Prophet Like Moses”
text: The reply is not to dismiss these observations but to test them against what Deuteronomy actually says. Take “brothers” first. The word for “brothers” (Hebrew aḥim) is used throughout Deuteronomy for fellow Israelites, and the decisive parallel sits only one chapter earlier. In Deuteronomy 17:15 God commands that Israel’s king must be “one from among your brothers… You may not put a foreigner over you, who is not your brother” (ESV).7 The very same phrase, in the very same context, is explicitly defined to exclude the foreigner. To read “your brothers” as Ishmaelite Arabs in chapter 18 while it plainly means non-foreign Israelites in chapter 17 is to make the word mean opposite things in adjacent paragraphs. The plainer reading is that the coming prophet, like the coming king, would be an Israelite.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: Deuteronomy 18: “A Prophet Like Moses”
text: Now “like Moses.” The Muslim list of similarities—lawgiver, general, husband—is real, but it is a list the text never supplies. Deuteronomy gives its own criteria, and they are different. The prophet would have God’s words put in his mouth and speak in God’s name (18:18–19); Jesus says exactly this of himself: “I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment—what to say and what to speak” (John 12:49, ESV).8 More striking still is the book’s own closing verdict. Deuteronomy 34:10–11 ends: “there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face, none like him for all the signs and wonders that the LORD sent him to do” (ESV).9 The two marks of a Moses-like prophet are intimate knowledge of God and confirming miracles. These are not incidental to the Christian case: the Gospels present Jesus as doing precisely such signs, whereas the Qur’an itself records that Muhammad’s contemporaries challenged him for a confirming sign and were told none would be given of that kind (see Surah 6:37; 17:90–93). The Qur’an presents itself as the supreme sign, and later tradition does attribute miracles to Muhammad (Surah 54:1, for instance, is read by some as the splitting of the moon); so the point is the narrow one—that the Qur’an does not present Mosaic-type confirming sign-miracles, not that Muhammad is said to have worked no wonders at all.10

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: Deuteronomy 18: “A Prophet Like Moses”
text: Finally, the New Testament settles the question of its own intended referent. In Acts 3:22 Peter quotes Deuteronomy 18 and applies it directly to Jesus; in Acts 7:37 Stephen does the same.11 Whatever one makes of those identifications, they show that the earliest readers of this prophecy—Jews steeped in the Hebrew text—heard it as pointing to a single coming Israelite prophet, the Messiah, not to an Arabian one six centuries later.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: Deuteronomy 18: “A Prophet Like Moses”
text: Here, honesty requires a concession. Critical scholars such as the Jewish commentator Jeffrey Tigay read Deuteronomy 18 in its first sense not as a single end-time prophet at all, but as a standing institution—a promise that God would always raise up legitimate prophets for Israel, in contrast to the pagan diviners condemned in the surrounding verses.12 If that is the primary meaning, then the passage was not originally a prediction of one future individual. But notice that this reading helps the Muslim case no more than the Christian: a promise of an ongoing line of Israelite prophets, defined against foreign practice, is the last text to fit a non-Israelite. The Christian claim is the more modest and defensible one—that the immediate context and the New Testament’s own application converge on Jesus—not that the verse is a mathematical proof.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: The Paraclete of John 14–16
text: The second great proof-text is Jesus’ promise, in his farewell discourse, of “another Helper”—in Greek, paraklētos. “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever, even the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16–17, ESV).13 Surah 61:6, with its prophecy of “Ahmad,” has long been read by Muslims as Jesus foretelling this Helper—Muhammad.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: The Paraclete of John 14–16
text: Two versions of the argument exist, and the stronger one should be put first. The straightforward version simply notes that the Paraclete is described as a person who is sent, who teaches, who testifies, who will “convict the world concerning sin” (John 16:8)—language that, the Muslim argues, reads more naturally of a coming man than of an impersonal influence. Jesus even says, “if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you” (John 16:7), suggesting a successor.14 The bolder, linguistic version is the one associated with the convert ʿAbd al-Aḥad Dāwūd (formerly David Benjamin Keldani) in the 1920s: that the original Greek was not paraklētos (“comforter, advocate”) but periklytos—“famed, renowned, praised”—which is a precise Greek equivalent of Aḥmad, “the praised one.” On this view a Christian scribe, deliberately or by error, swapped periklytos for the similar-looking paraklētos, erasing Muhammad’s name from the text.15

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: The Paraclete of John 14–16
text: Begin with the linguistic claim, because it is the easier to settle and the more often abandoned even by Muslim scholars. There is no manuscript—not one—in which the word periklytos stands in John. Every Greek copy of these verses reads paraklētos; so do the ancient Latin, Syriac, and Coptic versions and the patristic quotations.16 The proposal is a pure conjecture with zero textual evidence behind it. Worse, it is self-defeating in the context of the larger Muslim–Christian debate: to claim the text was altered is to grant that the Bible is corrupted—which is exactly the premise needed to deny that the Bible can foretell anything reliably at all. One cannot cite the Gospel of John as a true prophecy of Muhammad and in the same breath say John’s wording cannot be trusted. (We treat this tension at length in our companion essay on the Islamic Dilemma.)

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: The Paraclete of John 14–16
text: The personal-language version is more interesting, and it is right that the Paraclete is spoken of as “he,” not “it.” But Jesus does not leave the identity open. He names the Helper four times over, and each time the same way. The Paraclete is “the Spirit of truth” (14:17); “the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name” (14:26); the one who “proceeds from the Father” (15:26).17 Three features of this Helper cannot be made to fit any seventh-century man, however praised. First, he is a Spirit, not a body. Second, his mode of presence is indwelling: “he dwells with you and will be in you” (14:17, ESV)—Muhammad did not live inside the disciples. Third, the timing is imminent and corporate: Jesus tells the eleven the Helper will come to them, and the risen Jesus dates it precisely—“you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts 1:5)—fulfilled at Pentecost in Acts 2, weeks later, not six centuries on.18 A figure who is a spirit, who indwells believers, and who arrives within days is not a description that an Arabian prophet of the 600s can satisfy.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: The Paraclete of John 14–16
text: The strongest critic here is not a polemicist but the historian Sean Anthony, whose work the Christian should engage rather than wave away. Anthony argues that Ibn Isḥāq’s identification was not a clumsy misreading but a sophisticated piece of late-antique exegesis: working from an Aramaic gospel in which paraklētos had become menaḥḥemānā, Ibn Isḥāq drew on a real stream of messianic expectation around the figure of the “Comforter” (menaḥem) and read Muhammad into it.19 The honest reply concedes the sophistication while denying the conclusion: the Aramaic menaḥḥemānā is itself simply a translation of “the Comforter,” the Holy Spirit; that a creative reader could later hear “Muhammad” in its consonants tells us about the ingenuity of the reader, not about the meaning of John.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: The Shorter List: Maḥamaddim, Isaiah’s Servant, Haggai’s Desire
text: Beyond the two flagship texts, a cluster of shorter claims recurs, and they can be answered briefly and calmly.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: The Shorter List: Maḥamaddim, Isaiah’s Servant, Haggai’s Desire
text: Song of Songs 5:16. The bride says of her beloved, in Hebrew, kullo maḥamaddim—rendered “he is altogether desirable” (ESV).20 Because the consonants of maḥamaddim resemble “Muhammad,” some Muslims hear the prophet’s name hidden in the verse. But maḥamaddim is a common Hebrew plural noun meaning “delights, desirable things”; the -im ending is simply the Hebrew plural suffix, and the word appears elsewhere in ordinary contexts (for example Lamentations 2:4, of “all that was delightful”). It is a description in a love poem, not a proper name—rather as the English word “commander” contains the sound “command” without naming anyone. This is said not to mock the reading, which is sincerely offered, but to explain the grammar plainly.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: The Shorter List: Maḥamaddim, Isaiah’s Servant, Haggai’s Desire
text: Isaiah 42. Isaiah’s “servant” songs speak of a chosen one in whom God delights, who will “bring forth justice to the nations” (42:1, ESV).21 Some Muslims apply this to Muhammad as the prophet to the Gentiles. But Isaiah defines the servant’s manner in the next breath: “he will not cry aloud or lift up his voice… a bruised reed he will not break” (42:2–3)—a gentle, suffering figure, who in the fuller arc of Isaiah 52–53 is “pierced for our transgressions” (53:5, ESV).22 The New Testament identifies this servant as Jesus (Matthew 12:18–21 quotes Isaiah 42 directly of him), and the portrait of one who suffers and bears others’ sins fits the crucified Christ, not a victorious statesman.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: The Shorter List: Maḥamaddim, Isaiah’s Servant, Haggai’s Desire
text: Haggai 2:7. The King James Version reads, “the desire of all nations shall come,” and this “desire” is occasionally claimed for Muhammad.23 The claim rests on a translation choice. The Hebrew verb is plural (“they shall come”) while “desire” (ḥemdat) is singular, so most modern versions render it “the treasures of all nations shall come in” (ESV)—the wealth of the nations flowing into God’s house, not a person at all. And the context is the second temple, which God promises to fill with glory—a temple destroyed in AD 70, long before Muhammad. The verse cannot be about a seventh-century man without rewriting both its grammar and its setting.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: Two Visions: Isaiah’s Riders and Daniel’s Stone
text: Two further passages come up less often than Deuteronomy 18 or the Paraclete, but both recur in written dawah, and both reward exactly the same discipline: read the vision through to its end, and it names its own subject.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: Two Visions: Isaiah’s Riders and Daniel’s Stone
text: The argument fastens on a single line in one of Isaiah’s night-visions. The prophet’s watchman is told to look for “riders on donkeys, riders on camels” (Isaiah 21:7).24 On the Muslim reading these are two prophets seen together: the rider on the donkey is Jesus, who entered Jerusalem on a donkey as all four Gospels record, and the rider on the camel is Muhammad, the prophet of the camel-riding Arabs who came after him. The pairing looks tidy—the Messiah and then the final Messenger, foreseen side by side in one verse—and it is offered sincerely.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: Two Visions: Isaiah’s Riders and Daniel’s Stone
text: The tidiness dissolves the moment the line is read with the ones around it. Isaiah 21 opens, “The oracle concerning the wilderness of the sea” (21:1), and it is a vision of the fall of Babylon. God tells the prophet, “Go, set a watchman; let him announce what he sees” (21:6). The watchman is posted to catch the first sign of an approaching army, and the riders—horsemen in pairs, some on donkeys and some on camels—are that army’s couriers, galloping in with news. What is the news? The watchman cries it out two verses later: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground” (21:9, ESV). The donkeys and the camels belong to one military scene—the messengers who announce that Babylon has fallen. They are not a timeline of two prophets six centuries apart; they are the mounts of a single report arriving on a single night.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: Two Visions: Isaiah’s Riders and Daniel’s Stone
text: Read in its own context, then, Isaiah 21 is about the collapse of an empire, and it says nothing about a future prophet at all—neither Jesus nor Muhammad is its subject. To lift one clause out of a Babylon oracle and hang a prophetic biography on it is to read past the very sentence the vision supplies as its own meaning.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: Two Visions: Isaiah’s Riders and Daniel’s Stone
text: Daniel interprets Nebuchadnezzar’s dream of a great statue—head of gold, chest of silver, on down to feet of iron and clay—as a succession of kingdoms. Then “a stone was cut out by no human hand,” struck the statue, and “became a great mountain and filled the whole earth” (Daniel 2:34–35).25 Daniel explains that this represents a final kingdom God will set up, one that crushes the others and endures. The Muslim argument identifies that last, world-filling, God-given kingdom with Islam: it arose after the empires of the ancient world, spread across the earth with remarkable speed, and—on this reading—stands as the everlasting kingdom the vision foretold. Put at its strongest, the case points to something genuinely in the text: Daniel does describe a final kingdom, divinely established, that outlasts the rest and covers the earth.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: Two Visions: Isaiah’s Riders and Daniel’s Stone
text: What settles the matter is the two things Daniel says about that kingdom—both of which cut against the identification. The first is its timing. The kingdom of God in this vision arises “in the days of those kings” (Daniel 2:44)26—that is, during the era of the fourth and last empire of the statue, not centuries after it has passed. Interpreters divide over that empire’s identity: the traditional Jewish and Christian reading is Rome, while much critical scholarship, dating Daniel to the second century BC, reads it as the Greek (Seleucid) kingdom; some dispensationalists expect instead a future, revived Roman empire. But the disagreement gives the Islamic reading no foothold—on every one of these timetables the fourth empire is either the ancient one (Rome or Greece) or, for dispensationalists, a still-future revival of it, never a power first appearing in seventh-century Arabia. A caliphate founded in the 600s arrives generations too late for the ancient readings and centuries too early for the futurist one; it fits no window of “the days of those kings.” And even if one relocates the kingdom from the political caliphate to the faith it founded, that faith still arose in the seventh century—too late on the very same timetable.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: Two Visions: Isaiah’s Riders and Daniel’s Stone
text: The second is its permanence. Daniel 2:44 says this kingdom “shall never be destroyed… and it shall stand forever” (ESV). The Aramaic word behind “forever” (ʿalam) carries the sense of unbroken perpetuity; the standard lexicons gloss the Biblical Aramaic term as “perpetuity, antiquity,” and list Daniel 2:44 among its occurrences.27 Whatever kingdom the vision means, it is one that does not end. The historical caliphate does not answer to that description: it arose in the seventh century and was formally abolished in 1924.28 A kingdom with a datable beginning and a datable end—however vast in between—is not the kingdom “that shall stand forever.” So the verdict here, held to what the text shows, is again no: Daniel 2 does not describe a kingdom founded in seventh-century Arabia. On its own terms it points to a kingdom that begins while the ancient empires still stand and never falls—which is why Christians have long read the stone cut without human hands as the kingdom of God inaugurated in Christ, the one kingdom that fits both marks.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: The Structural Problem Beneath the Whole Project
text: Step back from the individual texts, and a deeper difficulty appears—one of logic rather than language. To argue “the Bible foretells Muhammad,” one must treat the Bible as a reliable, God-given witness; otherwise its “prophecies” prove nothing. Yet the standard Muslim response to the embarrassing things the Bible actually does teach—Jesus’ deity, his crucifixion, his resurrection—is to say that the text has been corrupted (taḥrīf). These two moves sit in deep tension. A more sophisticated Muslim may distinguish textual corruption (taḥrīf al-naṣṣ) from corrupted interpretation (taḥrīf al-maʿnā)—holding that the words are intact but Christians misread them—which would let him cite the Bible as prophecy while rejecting its teaching on Christ. But that move only sharpens the asymmetry it hopes to escape: the alleged prophecies of Muhammad are supposed to be clear enough to recognize, while the Bible’s teaching on Jesus’ deity, crucifixion, and resurrection—stated far more plainly and far more often—would have to be so obscure that its first readers and every generation since misread it. A text lucid enough to foretell Muhammad is not opaque enough to hide the cross. This is not a debating trick but a genuine tension, and a charitable conversation can name it without hostility. It is the reason the prophecy argument, pressed hard, tends to lead a thoughtful Muslim back into the pages of the Gospels themselves—which is the best possible place for the conversation to go.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: What This Does and Does Not Establish
text: Honesty requires marking the limits of the case. It does not prove that every Christian messianic reading of the Old Testament is beyond dispute; messianic interpretation involves real interpretive judgment, and serious Jewish and critical scholars read several of these texts differently from how Christians do. The argument of this essay is narrower and firmer: that, read in their own literary and historical context and in their original languages, none of the cited passages naturally refers to Muhammad, and the two load-bearing ones—Deuteronomy 18 and the Paraclete—are, on their own internal criteria, the worst possible fit for a non-Israelite man who was neither a spirit nor a worker of confirming signs. The New Testament writers, reading their own scriptures, applied them to Jesus.

title: Does the Bible Predict Muhammad? The Prophecy Claims Examined
section: What This Does and Does Not Establish
text: So the honest answer to the question is no: the texts standardly advanced in support of the Qur’an’s appeal to the Torah and Gospel do not, on inspection, predict Muhammad—and are unsupported by any manuscript that has ever been found. That is a significant result, reached not by attacking Islam’s prophet but by doing the one thing the Qur’an itself invites: opening the Bible and reading what is written. For the Christian, the goal of that reading is never to win a point but to introduce a Muslim friend to the prophet like Moses who knew God face to face, the Spirit of truth who dwells within, and the suffering Servant pierced for our transgressions—to let a conversation that began about Muhammad become, gently, a conversation about Christ.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
text: Walk into a mosque in Cairo or Istanbul and pick up the Quran on the shelf, and you will almost certainly be holding a text printed in the reading of Hafs ‘an ‘Asim. Walk into a mosque in Rabat, Nouakchott, or much of West Africa, and the Quran in your hands may instead be printed in the reading of Warsh ‘an Nafi‘. Open them side by side and you will find them overwhelmingly the same book—the same surahs, the same order, the same overarching message. But you will also find, scattered across the pages, hundreds of small differences: a lengthened vowel here, a different verb form there, occasionally a different word altogether, and in a handful of places a difference that changes what a verse means or even what it commands a believer to do.1

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
text: Both of these texts are printed and certified as authentic by Muslim authorities, including Saudi Arabia’s King Fahd Complex for the Printing of the Holy Quran.2 Neither is a forgery or a sectarian deviation. They are two of the canonical qira’at—the readings of the Quran—and they raise a question that deserves to be asked carefully and answered honestly: in what sense is there one Quran?

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: Stating the Question Carefully
text: It is worth being precise from the outset, because this topic is easy to overstate in both directions. This essay is not about whether the Quran has been wildly corrupted or rewritten beyond recognition—it has not been. The Arabic consonantal text (the rasm) is remarkably stable, and the readings differ within a narrow band. Nor is this the broader question of the Quran’s overall preservation history, the Uthmanic standardisation, or the companion codices; that is treated in a separate deep dive.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: Stating the Question Carefully
text: The narrow question here is the qira’at themselves. The popular apologetic claim—heard often in dawah (Islamic outreach)—is that the Quran has been transmitted letter-for-letter, dot-for-dot, identical across the centuries and across the world, and that this perfect preservation is itself a proof of its divine origin. The aim of this essay is to test that specific claim charitably against the Islamic tradition’s own data. The honest finding, stated plainly, is this: one perfectly identical text is a more complicated claim than the popular version allows. There is one Quran in the sense that matters most to a Muslim—one message, one stable skeleton—but there is genuine, divinely sanctioned variety in how it is read, and the system that defines which readings count was the work of named human scholars over several centuries. That is the whole of the claim, and it is enough to be worth examining.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: The Foundation: The Hadith of the Seven Ahruf
text: Any fair account must begin where the Islamic tradition itself begins: not with later scholars but with Muhammad. The most authoritative hadith collections record that the Quran was revealed in multiple forms. In Sahih al-Bukhari, ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab reports that he heard Hisham ibn Hakim reciting Surah al-Furqan in a manner different from his own, seized him, and dragged him to the Prophet. After both men recited, Muhammad responded: “It was revealed thus,” and then, “This Quran has been revealed to be recited in seven ahruf, so recite of it whichever is easy for you.”3

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: The Foundation: The Hadith of the Seven Ahruf
text: The word ahruf (singular harf) is notoriously difficult. It can mean “letters,” “modes,” “dialects,” or “ways”—and the Islamic tradition never settled on a single meaning. The tradition itself preserves an extraordinary range of views: the hadith scholar Ibn Hibban (d. 354 AH) listed some thirty-five different opinions on what the seven ahruf actually were, and later scholars round the figure to around forty.4 This is not a Christian polemic; it is the tradition’s own record of its disagreement. What the hadith establishes, on the tradition’s own terms, is that variation in recitation was permitted by the Prophet from the beginning—and that even the earliest community did not agree on how to classify it.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: From Ahruf to Qira’at: How the System Was Built
text: The qira’at are not simply the seven ahruf preserved intact. They are a later, scholarly system, and tracing how it was assembled is the historical heart of the matter.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: From Ahruf to Qira’at: How the System Was Built
text: When the third caliph Uthman standardised the written text around 650 AD, the manuscripts he produced recorded only the consonantal skeleton. Early Arabic script had no vowel signs and few of the dots (diacritics) that distinguish otherwise identical consonants. A single written word could therefore be vocalised in several legitimate ways. For roughly the next three centuries, reciters across the Muslim world transmitted a wide variety of readings, in a period scholars call ikhtiyar—“choosing.” Master reciters in Medina, Mecca, Kufa, Basra, and Damascus each had their own systems.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: From Ahruf to Qira’at: How the System Was Built
text: The decisive narrowing came in Baghdad around 936 AD, when the scholar Abu Bakr Ibn Mujahid (d. 324 AH) wrote his Kitab al-Sab‘a fi al-Qira’at, “The Book of the Seven Readings.” Ibn Mujahid selected seven reciters as canonical and treated readings outside this set as shadhdh (anomalous, non-canonical).5 The Harvard-trained scholar Shady Nasser, in the standard academic study of this process, documents that Ibn Mujahid’s choice of exactly seven was controversial in its own day: some contemporaries objected that it caused confusion by inviting people to conflate his seven readings with the seven ahruf of the hadith—which were not the same thing.6 Three further readings (those of Abu Ja‘far, Ya‘qub, and Khalaf) were later raised to canonical status, chiefly through the work of Ibn al-Jazari, to give the ten readings recognised today; a wider set of fourteen is sometimes discussed.7

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: From Ahruf to Qira’at: How the System Was Built
text: Each of the ten readings is transmitted through two principal rawis (transmitters), giving the familiar pairs: ‘Asim of Kufa is transmitted by Hafs and by Shu‘ba; Nafi‘ of Medina by Warsh and by Qalun. So the “readings” a Muslim encounters in print—Hafs ‘an ‘Asim, Warsh ‘an Nafi‘—are reader-plus-transmitter combinations.8 The point to grasp is simply that the authoritative list of how the Quran may be recited was assembled, debated, and revised by named scholars over centuries; it was not delivered complete and fixed at the start.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: What the Differences Actually Look Like
text: Honesty cuts both ways here, and the first thing to concede is that the great majority of differences between the readings are minor. They concern vowel length, points of pronunciation, the assimilation of letters, and rules of elongation—features that disappear entirely in translation. A reader of the King Fahd Hafs text and a reader of the King Fahd Warsh text are reciting the same surah, and a listener who did not know the technical system might hear only a difference of “accent.”

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: What the Differences Actually Look Like
text: But not all the differences are merely phonetic. Some reach the consonants, the words, and the meaning.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: What the Differences Actually Look Like
text: In the opening chapter, al-Fatiha—the most recited passage in all of Islam—verse 4 is read by ‘Asim and al-Kisa’i as mâliki yawmi al-din, with a long vowel, “Owner of the Day of Judgment,” and by other canonical readers as maliki, with a short vowel, “King of the Day of Judgment.”9 The difference is one letter (an alif) and a clear shift in sense—owner versus king. Muslim scholars reasonably treat these as complementary: God is both. But it is a difference of meaning, not merely sound, and it sits in the chapter every Muslim recites in every unit of every daily prayer.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: What the Differences Actually Look Like
text: Surah 3:146 describes prophets and their followers in battle. In the Hafs text the relevant word is written with an alif, qatala (“[many a prophet] fought”); in the Warsh tradition it is read qutila (“[many a prophet] was killed”).10 This is a genuine difference of meaning—fighting alongside the prophet versus being slain as a martyr—yet both are read from a single consonantal skeleton, since every canonical reading conforms to the one ‘Uthmanic rasm. That is significant in the other direction: it shows the variation is not always a trivial matter of accent, but can change what the verse says even where the written skeleton is identical.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: What the Differences Actually Look Like
text: The most consequential example concerns ritual law. Surah 5:6 lays out the rules of ablution (wudu) before prayer, including how to treat the feet. The key word, arjulakum (“your feet”), is read in two canonical ways differing by a single vowel: in the accusative case it parallels “wash your faces and hands,” yielding “wash your feet”; in the genitive case it parallels “wipe your heads,” yielding “wipe your feet.”11 This is not a nuance of beauty. It is two different ritual obligations, and the divergence tracks a real difference in practice between the Sunni and Shia traditions of how ablution is performed. A second example, Surah 2:222, turns on whether a husband may resume relations with his wife once menstrual bleeding has ceased or only after the full ritual bath—again a legal fork that the schools of law debated, resting on a difference of verb form.12

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: The Mainstream Muslim Explanation, Stated at Full Strength
text: Before assessing any of this, the traditional Muslim account deserves to be heard in its strongest form—not a caricature, but the case as a thoughtful Muslim scholar would actually press it.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: The Mainstream Muslim Explanation, Stated at Full Strength
text: First, the variety is divinely authorised, not a human accident. The seven-ahruf hadith shows the Prophet himself sanctioning multiple recitations, and the Quran (39:23) calls itself “a Book... mathani”—understood by some as confirming its multiple consistent modes. The qira’at are therefore revelation, not corruption: God gave His word in a way that flexed to the dialects and tongues of the early Arabs, “so recite whichever is easy for you.” Variation here is a mercy, an ease, woven into the revelation by design.13

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: The Mainstream Muslim Explanation, Stated at Full Strength
text: Second, the readings are transmitted by tawatur—mass transmission. A report is mutawatir when it is conveyed by so many independent chains at every link that collusion or error becomes inconceivable. The traditional claim is that each canonical reading was recited by vast numbers of Muslims in an unbroken chain back to the Prophet, so that the readings carry the same epistemic certainty as the consonantal text itself. On this view the qira’at are not the residue of scribal confusion but a living oral tradition of unmatched rigour, sustained by a community that memorised the entire text generation after generation.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: The Mainstream Muslim Explanation, Stated at Full Strength
text: Third, and crucially, the differences complement rather than contradict. Where one reading says “Owner” and another “King,” both are true and the pair enriches the meaning. The qira’at, on this account, are a feature of the Quran’s inimitability (i‘jaz): a single text bearing multiple layers of legitimate sense, all flowing from one source. Far from undermining preservation, the readings are the preservation—evidence of a text guarded so carefully that even its authorised variants were tracked and named.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: The Mainstream Muslim Explanation, Stated at Full Strength
text: This is the account the tradition presses at its strongest, and it deserves a full and fair hearing before any reply — which is exactly what the next section gives it.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: Weighing the Explanation
text: Several parts of this account can simply be conceded, and a Christian should concede them gladly. The variety is rooted in the tradition’s earliest layer—the ahruf hadith is in Bukhari, not a later invention. Most differences are minor. Many readings genuinely are complementary in the way described. And the Arabic consonantal text is, by the standards of ancient texts, impressively stable. None of that is in dispute. The question is whether the popular conclusion—one perfectly identical, letter-for-letter text, miraculously preserved—follows. Three points suggest it needs qualifying.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: Weighing the Explanation
text: The system is humanly constructed, not self-evidently given. If the qira’at were simply the seven ahruf handed down whole, one would expect the tradition to know clearly what the ahruf were and how the readings map onto them. Instead, as Ibn al-Jazari himself records, the tradition preserves dozens of incompatible theories of the ahruf, and the relationship between the ahruf and the qira’at remains unsettled.4 The number seven that Ibn Mujahid fixed upon in the tenth century was, even contemporaries complained, partly a numerical echo rather than a derivation—and the canon then grew to ten and was discussed as fourteen. A revelation whose authorised readings had to be selected, debated, and expanded by named scholars across three centuries is not the same thing as a text that arrived complete and self-authenticating.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: Weighing the Explanation
text: “Complementary” is the right word for synonyms, not for a legal fork. The complementarity defence works well for “Owner” and “King”: both are true of God, and the pair enriches. It works far less well for Surah 5:6. “Wash your feet” and “wipe your feet” are not two facets of one truth; they are two different commands, and a worshipper cannot do both at once in the way the readings specify. Here two canonical readings yield two incompatible ritual obligations from what is supposed to be a single perfectly transmitted divine text. One may hold that God authorised both practices—but that is a different and larger claim than “one identical text,” and it is the claim the popular dawah argument quietly drops.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: Weighing the Explanation
text: The tawatur claim is exactly where modern scholarship presses. This is the most technical point and must be stated carefully. The traditional guarantee of perfect oral preservation is that every canonical reading is mutawatir. Yet Shady Nasser, examining the actual chains of transmission, argues that the system of readings “failed to meet the conditions of tawatur” as the legal theorists themselves defined them: at decisive junctures the chains narrow to one or two named transmitters—technically ahad (singular), not mass-transmitted—creating what Nasser calls a paradox between the certain transmission of the written mushaf and the far less certain transmission of its oral recitation.14 If that analysis holds, then the readings are not guaranteed by the kind of mass transmission the popular claim invokes, and the question of which readings are canonical becomes, at least in part, a matter of later scholarly judgment—which is precisely what the canonisation history shows.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: The Honest State of the Scholarship
text: Fairness requires giving the strongest reply the last word before the conclusion, and naming where the dispute genuinely stands. The tawatur question is contested, not settled. Traditional Muslim scholars have sophisticated rejoinders to Nasser: they distinguish tawatur in the early generations (where the readers were many) from the later named “bottlenecks,” which they treat as a documentary convenience rather than the real channel of transmission; and they argue that the conditions for tawatur should be assessed at the level of the reading-community, not the isnad as written. A careful critic should label this a live scholarly debate, not a knockdown. Nasser is making a serious, well-documented academic case; he is not the unanimous verdict of the field, and many Muslim specialists in ‘ilm al-qira’at disagree with him.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: The Honest State of the Scholarship
text: It is also worth naming the academic on the other side of the meaning question. Adrian Brockett, in his St Andrews study comparing the Hafs and Warsh transmissions in detail, concluded that while the differences are real and worth cataloguing, their effect on the overall meaning of the text is limited—the two transmissions, he argued, are close enough that neither tells a substantially different story.15 Brockett is a sympathetic witness for the modesty of the claim being made here: the readings differ, sometimes in meaning and law, but they do not produce two different Qurans in the sense of two different messages. That is exactly the line this essay walks. What the evidence unsettles is the perfect-identity showpiece, not the substantial integrity of the book.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not Establish
text: So how many Qurans are there? The honest answer is layered. In the sense the popular argument intends—one letter-for-letter, dot-for-dot identical text—the picture is more complicated than the slogan: there are multiple canonical readings, certified by Muslim authorities, that differ not only in pronunciation but at times in word, meaning, and even legal obligation, and the system defining them was built by named scholars over three centuries. In the sense that matters most to a believing Muslim—one message, one stable consonantal text, one book—there is indeed one Quran, and it has been transmitted with real care.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not Establish
text: What the qira’at do not establish should be stated as plainly as what they do. They do not show that the Quran has been corrupted into chaos, or rewritten, or that its message is unrecoverable—to claim any of that would be to overstate the evidence badly. What they show is narrower and quieter — but on the popular boast it is a plain no: the specific claim of flawless, identical, miraculous preservation, often offered as the showpiece proof of the Quran’s divine origin, does not hold. It claims more than the Islamic tradition’s own data will bear. The variant readings are evidence of a careful and reverent transmission—but a human, historical one, with the marks of human scholarship on it.

title: The Variant Readings (Qira’at): How Many Qurans Are There?
section: Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not Establish
text: None of this is an occasion for triumph, and it is not meant to embarrass anyone. The point of understanding the qira’at is not to win an argument but to move the conversation to the ground that actually matters. Notice what even a flawlessly copied text would and would not settle: careful transmission can show that a book has been faithfully preserved, but it cannot by itself show that the book is true. So the preservation boast was always the wrong foundation to rest a claim of divine origin on. The real question — worth asking gently, accurately, and with respect (1 Peter 3:15) — was never the manner of the copying, but who God has shown Himself to be, and whether He has entered history to make Himself known. That is where this conversation begins.

title: Does the Qur’an Contain Scientific Miracles?
text: One of the most popular arguments in modern Muslim outreach is that the Qur’an contains scientific facts that no one in the seventh century could have known — the stages of the human embryo, an expanding universe, mountains with deep roots, a barrier between two seas — and that this “scientific miracle” (in Arabic, i’jaz ’ilmi) proves the book came from God. On a first hearing it can be genuinely arresting. A verse from the year 620 seems to describe something confirmed only by modern instruments; the coincidence can feel too precise to be accidental. Many sincere Muslims find it deeply persuasive, and they share it because they love God and trust their book.

title: Does the Qur’an Contain Scientific Miracles?
text: It deserves a careful hearing and an honest answer — and this essay gives it one. Weighed on its own terms, the argument does not hold. Not because the Qur’an is a crude or foolish book, but because every example turns out to be one of three things: an idea already available in the seventh century, a vague phrase read backwards after modern science supplied the meaning, or a claim that modern science actually contradicts. Let us take the argument at full strength and see why.

title: Does the Qur’an Contain Scientific Miracles?
section: Where the argument comes from — and where it doesn’t
text: The first clue is the argument’s age. For most of Islamic history, the Qur’an’s claimed “inimitability” (i’jaz) meant its literary perfection — the beauty and force of its Arabic — not its science. The scientific version is a twentieth-century development. It was crystallized by the French surgeon Maurice Bucaille in his 1976 book The Bible, the Qur’an and Science,1 then institutionalized in Saudi Arabia through the Commission on Scientific Signs in the Qur’an and Sunnah, associated with Abdul Majeed al-Zindani,2 and carried to mass audiences by popularizers such as Zakir Naik and the Turkish writer “Harun Yahya.”

title: Does the Qur’an Contain Scientific Miracles?
section: Where the argument comes from — and where it doesn’t
text: That date is not a trivia point; it is the heart of the problem. An interpretation invented after the science it claims to predict cannot be evidence that the text predicted anything. If the meaning of a verse was only discovered once astronomers or embryologists had done the work, then the verse did not deliver the knowledge — the reader imported it. This single structural flaw reappears at every example below.

title: Does the Qur’an Contain Scientific Miracles?
section: The flagship: embryology
text: The showpiece of the whole genre is a passage on human development: “We created man from an extract of clay. Then We made him as a drop (nutfah) in a firm lodging. Then We made the drop into a clinging clot (’alaqah), and made the clot into a lump (mudghah), and made the lump into bones, and clothed the bones with flesh” (Surah 23:12–14). Advocates point to a celebrated endorsement: al-Zindani obtained a statement of admiration from the Canadian embryologist Keith Moore, whose textbook The Developing Human appeared in a special edition interleaved with Qur’anic and hadith citations.3

title: Does the Qur’an Contain Scientific Miracles?
section: The flagship: embryology
text: But the stages the Qur’an lists — drop, clinging clot, chewed lump, bones, then flesh — closely track the sequence taught by the Greek physician Galen in the second century ad, whose staged embryology was standard medical knowledge across the Hellenized Near East and had reached Syriac medicine well before Islam. (The great Arabic translations of Galen came later — and, tellingly, they reused these very Qur’anic terms for his stages.) The historian Basim Musallam, surveying medieval Islamic medicine, concluded that “the stages of development which the Qur’an and hadith established for believers agreed perfectly with Galen’s scientific account… there is no doubt that medieval thought appreciated this agreement.”4 In other words, the content was already in the air the seventh century breathed.

title: Does the Qur’an Contain Scientific Miracles?
section: The flagship: embryology
text: And where the Qur’an differs from modern embryology, it tends to track the ancient picture rather than the true one. The word ’alaqah is the linchpin of the modern claim. Da’wah presentations re-translate it as “leech-like” or “that which clings,” and match it to the way the early embryo implants and clings to the wall of the womb — and this, in substance, is what Keith Moore was shown and praised. But the re-translation is itself a retrofit. In the classical Arabic lexica and the older tafsir, ’alaqah means clotted or congealed blood — the ancient idea of the embryo’s first stage — and the “leech” gloss was reached for in the twentieth century precisely because it fits what embryology had by then discovered. Read in its own century, the word carries the old picture, not the new one. And the order “bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh” describes the skeleton forming first and muscle added afterward — whereas in fact the bones and the surrounding muscle develop concurrently from the differentiating mesoderm, not skeleton-first. The physician William Campbell, who wrote the standard point-by-point reply to Bucaille, pressed exactly this: read as science, the sequence is not ahead of its time but behind the facts.5 None of this makes the passage absurd for its era — it is a competent restatement of the best available seventh-century embryology. That is precisely the point: it is seventh-century, not twentieth.

title: Does the Qur’an Contain Scientific Miracles?
section: Reading modern meaning backwards
text: The second move in the genre is retrofitting — pouring a modern discovery into an old, vague phrase. The favourite case is the expanding universe. “And the heaven We constructed with strength, and indeed, We are its expander (musi’un)” (Surah 51:47). Modern advocates render the last word “expanding it” and hear an echo of Hubble. But the classical commentators heard nothing of the kind: the older tafsir tradition, including Ibn Kathir, glosses musi’un as God’s power and vastness — “We are able,” “possessors of might” — with no thought of cosmic expansion.6 The astronomical reading is a modern overlay laid on a word that meant something else for a thousand years.

title: Does the Qur’an Contain Scientific Miracles?
section: Reading modern meaning backwards
text: The same pattern covers the rest of the standard list. Mountains called “stakes” or “pegs” (Surah 78:7) become plate tectonics and isostasy; iron “sent down” (Surah 57:25) becomes supernova nucleosynthesis; the “barrier between two seas” (Surah 55:19–20) becomes the halocline between fresh and salt water. In every case the Arabic is a vivid, ordinary image a desert people would recognize, and the physics is supplied by the reader. The word for “sent down,” anzala, is used elsewhere in the very same Qur’an for cattle (Surah 39:6) and clothing (Surah 7:26) — and no one reads those as arriving from meteorites. When a word only becomes miraculous in the one verse a debater needs, the miracle is in the debating, not the text.

title: Does the Qur’an Contain Scientific Miracles?
section: The verses the argument leaves out
text: A method that cites only its hits is not doing science; it is scoring a highlight reel. Set beside the “miracle” verses are others that read most naturally as the cosmology of their day. Dhul-Qarnayn travels west until “he found the sun setting in a spring of dark mud” (Surah 18:86). The sky is a solid “protected ceiling” that God holds back from falling on the earth (Surah 21:32; 22:65). The stars are lamps set in the lowest heaven that double as missiles hurled at eavesdropping devils (Surah 67:5; 37:6–10). The heavens themselves are seven, in stacked layers (Surah 67:3). A defender can read some of these perspectivally — as how the world looked to an observer, just as the Bible speaks of the sun “rising” — and that reading is fair enough. But notice what it costs the argument: if these verses merely describe the world as seventh-century eyes saw it, they are not scientific miracles — and neither, by the same measure, are the verses on the other side of the ledger. What you cannot do is bank the verses that flatter modern science and quietly set aside the ones that don’t. Judged by one consistent standard, the Qur’an’s cosmos is the ordinary cosmos of late antiquity.

title: Does the Qur’an Contain Scientific Miracles?
section: The test that passes everything
text: The deepest problem is the method itself. Retrofitting has been applied, with equal “success,” to the Bible, to the Hindu Vedas, and even to secular literature — critics have famously “discovered” relativity and space flight hidden in nursery rhymes precisely to expose the trick. A test that any sufficiently poetic text can pass is not a test at all. If the technique validates the Qur’an, it validates a whole shelf of mutually contradictory scriptures — which means it validates none of them. An argument that proves too much proves nothing.

title: Does the Qur’an Contain Scientific Miracles?
section: Muslim scholars say so too
text: This is not merely a Christian objection lobbed from outside. Some of the sharpest critics of i’jaz ’ilmi are Muslim scientists. The astrophysicist Nidhal Guessoum judges the Bucaille approach methodologically bankrupt, warning that it stakes faith on readings that collapse the moment a “confirmed” interpretation is overturned by the next textbook.7 The writer and physicist Ziauddin Sardar long ago dismissed the genre as apologetic pseudo-science that flatters believers rather than instructing them.8 The scientific-miracle claim is contested within Islam; it is a popular apologetic, not a settled Muslim consensus.

title: Does the Qur’an Contain Scientific Miracles?
section: The verdict — and a better place to stand
text: So the honest verdict is plain, and it should be stated plainly: the Qur’an does not contain scientific miracles. Its “scientific” verses are, on inspection, seventh-century ideas already available at the time (Galenic embryology, the cosmology of late antiquity), vague phrases retrofitted with meaning after the fact, or images that modern science simply contradicts. The argument fails on its own terms.

title: Does the Qur’an Contain Scientific Miracles?
section: The verdict — and a better place to stand
text: It is worth being equally careful about what this does not show. It does not, by itself, settle whether Islam is true — a book can be humanly authored and still say true things about God and morality; that is a separate question, taken up in the other essays in this section. What fails here is one specific proof of divine authorship, not every claim the Qur’an makes.

title: Does the Qur’an Contain Scientific Miracles?
section: The verdict — and a better place to stand
text: And the failure quietly points to something worth noticing about how the Christian faith makes its case. Christianity does not rest on hidden codes that only become impressive once modern science catches up. It rests on a claim that anyone in the first century could check and anyone today can investigate: that Jesus of Nazareth was crucified, was buried, and was raised bodily, and was seen by named witnesses who were willing to die for what they said they had seen (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). That is a public, historical, falsifiable claim — the very opposite of a verse that only turns miraculous in hindsight. In conversation with a Muslim friend, we do not need the science-miracle move, and we should not imitate it; we can point instead to the one event that either happened or did not, in daylight, in history.

title: Does the Qur’an Contain Scientific Miracles?
section: The verdict — and a better place to stand
text: Say all of this gently. Those who share the scientific-miracle argument overwhelmingly do so out of sincere devotion and confidence in their book, and they deserve respect, not ridicule (1 Peter 3:15). The kindest thing we can do is not pretend the argument works. It is to show, honestly and without triumph, why it does not — and then to offer, in its place, a hope that stands on ground you can actually walk on.

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
text: Ask a believing Muslim how she knows that the angel Gabriel first appeared to Muhammad in a cave on Mount Hira, that he migrated from Mecca to Medina in the year we now call 622, that he won at Badr and stumbled at Uhud, that he was gentle with children and stern with hypocrites—and she can answer in vivid detail. The striking thing is where almost none of that detail comes from. It does not come from the Qur’an, which says remarkably little about the events of its prophet’s life, naming him only a handful of times and narrating almost no biography.1 It comes instead from the sira, the prophetic biography—a body of tradition assembled by later Muslims who told the story of the man around whom their scripture had formed.

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
text: This essay asks a single, careful question: how solid is that biographical foundation? It is worth saying at the outset, and saying plainly, what is not being argued. This is not the claim that Muhammad did not exist. It is not the claim that nothing can be known about him. Both of those would overreach the evidence badly. The argument is the more modest and, I think, more honest one: the detailed life of Muhammad that most people—Muslim and non-Muslim alike—take for granted rests on sources that are late, that survive only in edited form, and that were shaped by the theological needs of the communities that preserved them. The right posture toward the specifics, therefore, is one of held-loose confidence rather than certainty.

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: The Sources, and the Gap
text: The earliest connected biography of Muhammad we can name is the Sirat Rasul Allah (“Life of the Messenger of God”) by Ibn Ishaq, who died around 767. Muhammad died in 632. That is already a gap of roughly 120 to 135 years between the events and their first sustained narration—the distance, in our own terms, between the present and the 1890s, recounted by someone working only from what had been passed down.2

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: The Sources, and the Gap
text: But the situation is more delicate still, because Ibn Ishaq’s original work does not survive. Not a single complete copy has come down to us. What we possess instead is a later recension—an edited redaction—produced by Ibn Hisham, who died around 833, fully two centuries after Muhammad.3 Alongside Ibn Hisham, large stretches of Ibn Ishaq’s material are preserved as quotations in the massive universal chronicle of al-Tabari (839–923), whose History of the Prophets and Kings reaches us from the early tenth century and in fact contains some of the fullest surviving extracts of Ibn Ishaq.4 The standard English translation, Alfred Guillaume’s The Life of Muhammad (1955), is itself a scholarly reconstruction: Guillaume stitched Ibn Hisham together with Ibn Ishaq material drawn from al-Tabari and others, attempting to recover a lost original he could only approach at second and third hand.5

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: The Sources, and the Gap
text: Two things follow. First, the chain from event to surviving text is long: oral and early written reports across roughly a century, then Ibn Ishaq, then a redactor or chronicler another forty to ninety years on. Second—and this is the part that gives even sympathetic readers pause—the redaction we depend on was openly selective. In his preface, Ibn Hisham tells the reader that he has left things out: matters he judged would “distress certain people,” reports his own teacher could not vouch for, poems regarded as spurious, and, in Guillaume’s rendering, “things which it is disgraceful to discuss.”6 We are not dealing with a raw archive but with a curated one, and the curator told us so.

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: A Disputed Author, an Impressive Method
text: Ibn Ishaq was also a contested figure within his own tradition. Several major early scholars expressed reservations about him as a transmitter; the celebrated Medinan jurist Malik ibn Anas—founder of the Maliki school of law—is reported to have clashed with him and to have called him a “liar” (kadhdhab) and an “imposter” (dajjal, here in the sense of charlatan rather than the eschatological Antichrist), while others suspected him of relying too readily on Jewish converts and of weak chains of transmission.7 Fairness requires immediately adding the other side of the ledger: many equally weighty authorities defended him, and later hadith scholars often graded his reports as acceptable in biography even while hesitating over them in law. The point is not that Ibn Ishaq was a fraud—that would be its own overreach—but that the very tradition that preserved him did not regard him as beyond question.

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: A Disputed Author, an Impressive Method
text: And here charity demands real respect for what the Muslim historians achieved. The transmission of the sira was bound up with the sophisticated science of the isnad, the chain of named transmitters appended to a report, which classical scholars scrutinized with extraordinary care. This was not credulous storytelling; it was an early and serious attempt at source criticism, and it has no real parallel in the ancient world. To wave it away would be both unjust and unwise. The difficulty, which Muslim scholars themselves acknowledged, is structural: isnad criticism interrogates the chain of names more searchingly than the content, and a chain can be counterfeited—a problem we treat at length in the companion essay on the hadith.

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: The Seventh-Century Silence—and Its Few Voices
text: If the Muslim narrative sources are late, what about contemporary, seventh-century evidence—the kind a historian most wants? Here the record is thin, and honesty requires saying so in both directions. There is no contemporary documentary life of Muhammad: no inscription he commissioned, no letter in his hand, no dated chronicle written within his lifetime that narrates his career. The earliest Arabic-Islamic documentary traces—coins, an inscription or two, administrative papyri—begin to mention him by name only in the latter decades of the seventh century.8

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: The Seventh-Century Silence—and Its Few Voices
text: Yet the silence is not total, and the most important counterweight comes from outside the Muslim community. A Greek Christian tract called the Doctrina Jacobi nuper baptizati (“Teaching of the Newly Baptized Jacob”), whose setting is a debate of 634 and whose core is usually dated to around 634–640—within a decade or so of Muhammad’s death—refers to “a prophet” who has appeared among the Saracens (the Arabs), proclaiming the coming of an anointed one and holding, it says, “the keys of Paradise.”9 The text is hostile and confused on details, and it does not name Muhammad. But it is powerful evidence that, within a few years of 632, non-Muslims in the eastern Mediterranean already knew that an Arabian prophet had arisen and that his followers were on the move. Other early non-Muslim notices—Syriac, Armenian, and Greek—corroborate the same broad picture across the seventh century.10 These sources do not vindicate the detailed traditional biography; they were not in a position to. What they do, decisively, is anchor the bare existence and rough dating of Muhammad and his movement in testimony nearly contemporary with the events, and independent of the Muslim tradition.

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: The Revisionist Challenge—Stated at Full Strength
text: In the 1970s a group of scholars pressed the source problem far harder than the mainstream had, and their challenge has to be stated at its strongest before it is weighed. John Wansbrough, in Quranic Studies (1977) and The Sectarian Milieu (1978), argued that the Qur’an and the sira alike were not transparent records of seventh-century Arabia but the literary deposit of a sectarian community that took shape considerably later, perhaps in the eighth or ninth century—the sira, on this reading, a body of pious storytelling (he used the term salvation history) generated to anchor scripture in a prophetic life, not a sober chronicle of one.11

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: The Revisionist Challenge—Stated at Full Strength
text: His students Patricia Crone and Michael Cook went further. In Hagarism: The Making of the Islamic World (1977), they proposed setting the Muslim sources almost entirely aside as too late and too tendentious to trust, and reconstructing Islam’s origins from contemporary non-Muslim sources instead—arriving at a startlingly different picture of a messianic Arab-Jewish movement.12 Whatever one makes of the conclusion, the underlying methodological worry is serious and cannot be dismissed: if our narrative sources postdate the events by a century or two and were written to serve later doctrinal needs, on what basis do we trust their particulars? That is a fair question, and it is the engine of this whole essay.

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: The Mainstream Reply—and What the Revisionists Conceded
text: The reply came swiftly and, in the end, largely prevailed—but it prevailed by conceding the moderate point while rejecting the radical one. Critics noted that the non-Muslim sources Crone and Cook leaned on are themselves fragmentary, hostile, and no more obviously reliable than the Muslim ones; building a confident alternative history on them simply trades one set of problematic sources for another.13 Most strikingly, the authors themselves stepped back. Cook stated flatly, “The central thesis of that book was, I now think, mistaken”; Crone, while never abandoning a critical stance toward the sources, likewise distanced herself from the book’s specific reconstruction.14 Wansbrough’s very late dating of the Qur’an, meanwhile, sits poorly with the early Qur’anic manuscript evidence—most notably the Birmingham folios, radiocarbon-dated with high probability to before 645, and other early Hijazi codices—which point to a seventh-century text far earlier than his model allowed.15

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: The Mainstream Reply—and What the Revisionists Conceded
text: Now the steelman of the position this essay ultimately commends—the mainstream historical-critical view—deserves to be put as strongly as it can be, because it is the strongest position in the room. A real Muhammad, an Arabian religious reformer active in the early seventh century who founded the community that erupted out of Arabia within a few years of his death, is about as well established as anything in late-antique history. The convergence is the argument: the Qur’an itself as a primary seventh-century text; the near-contemporary non-Muslim notices; the explosive, datable Arab conquests that demand a galvanizing founder; the early documentary traces; and a Muslim tradition that, however late its written form, preserves a recognizable core. Scholars such as Fred Donner have argued powerfully that the tradition, critically sifted, yields a credible early-seventh-century “Believers’ movement” around Muhammad, and that wholesale skepticism throws out far more than the evidence warrants.16 Oral cultures, moreover, can transmit a stable core of material across generations even where exact wording and chronology drift. The skeleton—Mecca, Medina, preaching, community, conquest—is firm.

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: The Mainstream Reply—and What the Revisionists Conceded
text: I find that steelman convincing, and this essay does not contest it. The error to avoid is sliding from “the sources are late” to “therefore we know almost nothing,” which is precisely the revisionist overreach the field corrected.

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: Where That Leaves the Details
text: But notice exactly what the mainstream view secures, and what it does not. It secures the skeleton. It does not, by the same evidence, secure the flesh—the specific scenes, sayings, miracles, motives, and tight chronology that make up the traditional biography and that believers often hold with great confidence. Those particulars rest overwhelmingly on the late, redacted sira-and-hadith material, not on the early non-Muslim notices or the Qur’an. The cave of Hira, the wording of particular sermons, the dramatized councils before battles, the miracle reports—these come to us through Ibn Hisham’s admittedly pruned recension and the hadith corpus, with all the distance and shaping that implies.

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: Where That Leaves the Details
text: Here the critic should get the last word before the reply. A defender of the tradition will say: granting the late written form, the isnad system and the sheer mass of cross-referenced reports let us recover far more detail than your “skeleton only” verdict allows; you are smuggling in a double standard, demanding of the sira a documentary contemporaneity you would never demand of, say, Alexander the Great, whose main biographers also wrote centuries after him. That is a genuinely strong objection and deserves a genuine answer rather than a dismissal.

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: Where That Leaves the Details
text: The answer is twofold. First, the Alexander comparison cuts both ways: precisely because Arrian and Plutarch wrote so long after Alexander, careful historians do hold the colorful particulars of his life loosely, distinguishing the secure outline from the legendary embroidery—which is exactly the discipline being urged here for the sira. The plea is not for a double standard but for a single one, applied evenly. Second, the isnad method, impressive as it is, scrutinizes chains more than content and can be defeated by a skilled forger; and the tradition’s own admission—that the great bulk of circulating reports were judged unsound, and that the surviving biography was deliberately edited—is itself reason to treat the rich detail as the most vulnerable layer, not the most secure.17 Conceding the secure core is not skepticism; it is the same critical caution every ancient historian practices.

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: The Honest State of the Scholarship
text: Where does the field actually stand in 2026? The radical revisionism of the 1970s has been substantially rolled back—by the early Qur’anic manuscripts, by its own authors’ retractions, and by the implausibility of dissolving Muhammad into a later fiction. There is broad agreement that a historical Muhammad existed and was active in early-seventh-century Arabia. At the same time, the source-critical worry that motivated the revisionists has been absorbed into the mainstream rather than refuted: serious historians now routinely distinguish the well-grounded outline of Muhammad’s career from the layered, tendentious, late-attested detail of the traditional biography, and treat the latter with calibrated caution. Chase Robinson’s standard survey of Islamic historiography stresses just this—that early Islamic historical writing served social and theological functions and must be read with its purposes in view, not as neutral reportage.18 The live debates today are about how much of the detail can be recovered and by what method (the refinement called “isnad-cum-matn” analysis is one promising tool), not about whether Muhammad existed.

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not Establish
text: The source situation establishes, with as much confidence as history allows, that the traditional biography of Muhammad rests on late and theologically shaped foundations: a first life written more than a century after the events, surviving only through a redactor who told us he edited out what might embarrass, and a documentary seventh-century record that is sparse. It establishes that confident, granular claims about the specifics—particular scenes, words, motives, miracles—should be held loosely.

title: The Sira: How Much Do We Really Know About Muhammad?
section: Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not Establish
text: It does not establish that Muhammad is a myth; he is not, and to say so would be to repeat the revisionists’ corrected mistake. It does not establish that nothing can be known; the convergence of Qur’an, near-contemporary non-Muslim notices, and the conquests secures a real man and a real movement. What it does, for the Christian engaging a Muslim friend, is invite something fair rather than triumphal: a single, consistent historical standard applied to both faiths’ founding sources. Apply it honestly, and the New Testament documents—written within living memory, resting partly on eyewitness testimony, and behind them the creed of 1 Corinthians 15:3–7 datable to within a few years of the crucifixion—turn out to stand closer to their events than the sira stands to Muhammad. That is not a weapon to wield over anyone made, as we all are, in the image of God. It is an invitation to follow the evidence together, with gentleness and respect, wherever it honestly leads.19

title: Tawhid and the Problem of Eternal Love
text: Among the ninety-nine Beautiful Names of God in Islam—al-Asma’ al-Husna—is one that any Christian should hear fairly rather than with suspicion: al-Wadud, “the Loving.” It appears twice in the Qur’an, and both times in the warm company of forgiveness: “Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Affectionate” (Surah 11:90), and “And He is the Forgiving, the Affectionate” (Surah 85:14)—where the divine name rendered “Affectionate” is al-Wadud, “the Loving.”1 Many Muslim commentators gloss the root behind al-Wadud—wudd—as love that shows itself in action and constancy, not merely as an inner sentiment.2 No fair description of Islam can call it a religion without a loving God. It confesses one, by name.

title: Tawhid and the Problem of Eternal Love
text: And yet a question waits underneath that lovely name—a question Muslim theologians and mystics have themselves felt and labored over. It is not a slogan or a trap. It is this: if God is eternally and essentially loving, then love seems to require a beloved—and on a strictly unitarian conception of God, who or what did God love before there was anything at all? The question reaches deep into what kind of being God is, and the Christian claim is not that Islam has no answer, but that the Trinity gives the most coherent one. This essay tries to state the problem honestly, to put the Muslim replies at their strongest, and then to show why the eternal communion of Father, Son, and Spirit secures something both faiths want to say—that God is supremely loving—in a way solitary oneness struggles to.

title: Tawhid and the Problem of Eternal Love
section: What Tawhid Affirms
text: At the heart of Islam stands tawhid: the absolute, undifferentiated oneness of God. God is one in essence, one in will, one in worship; He has no partner, no offspring, no internal composition or plurality of any kind. The shortest and most beloved creed of this oneness is Surah 112, al-Ikhlas: “Say, He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent.”3 To compromise this oneness—to associate any partner with God—is shirk, the one sin the Qur’an presents as unforgivable.

title: Tawhid and the Problem of Eternal Love
section: What Tawhid Affirms
text: It is essential to state this carefully and charitably, because the argument that follows depends on representing it rightly. Mainstream Sunni and Shia theology does not picture God as a lonely or impoverished being. God is al-Ghani, the Self-Sufficient, who needs nothing and no one; the creation adds nothing to Him and its absence would take nothing from Him. This divine self-sufficiency—what Christian theologians call aseity—is something Islam and orthodox Christianity hold in common and both hold dear. The whole force of the problem we are about to examine lies precisely there: it is a tension internal to two things Islam wants to affirm together—that God is genuinely loving, and that God is utterly self-sufficient.

title: Tawhid and the Problem of Eternal Love
section: The Argument Stated Carefully
text: The argument is best stated as a dilemma, not a refutation. It runs:

title: Tawhid and the Problem of Eternal Love
section: The Argument Stated Carefully
text: The Christian contention is that horns (a) and (b) cost Islam something it does not want to pay—the perfection and aseity of God—and that horn (c), self-love, while the most promising, does not quite reach what the word “love” most fully means. The Trinity, by contrast, locates an eternal beloved within God: the Father eternally loves the Son in the Spirit. On that view “God is love” (1 John 4:8) is not a description of how God treats creatures but of what God timelessly is in Himself—and creation becomes the overflow of a love already complete, not the occasion on which a solitary God first had anything to love.4

title: Tawhid and the Problem of Eternal Love
section: How the Argument Developed: Richard of St Victor
text: This is not a modern debating point invented to embarrass Muslims. Its classic form long predates the modern dialogue and was first aimed not at Islam but at understanding the inner life of the Christian God. In the twelfth century, the Augustinian canon Richard of St Victor, in his treatise De Trinitate (c. 1170), advanced what has become known as the argument from love. His reasoning, in Books Three and Five, runs roughly thus: God is the supreme good; the supreme good must possess caritas, the highest charity-love, for nothing is better than charity; but no one who loves only himself has true charity, for charity by its nature is directed toward another. Therefore the supreme good must love a beloved who is fully its equal—and, Richard adds in a further step, the perfection of shared love (condilectio) calls for a third who is loved in common. The fullness of love within God is what led Richard to argue for a plurality of persons.5 It is worth being candid about where the argument is strongest and where it strains: the move from a second person to a third is the most contested step, and Richard offers it as fitting rather than strictly necessitated—the love argument on its own reaches at most a duality of persons (binitarianism), and the further step to a Trinity is a claim about love’s fullness, not a deduction the premises compel.

title: Tawhid and the Problem of Eternal Love
section: How the Argument Developed: Richard of St Victor
text: Richard’s argument was a constructive case for the Trinity from within Christian faith; it becomes a comparative argument when set beside any strictly unitarian theology. Its modern champion is the Oxford philosopher Richard Swinburne, who in The Christian God (1994) revives the love argument in analytic dress.
