title: Why Does Mathematics Describe the Universe?
section: The Strongest Objections—Stated at Full Strength
text: Finally, the charge of intellectual cowardice: you have simply found a gap in our understanding and stuffed God into it; one day cognitive science or a final physics will close the gap, and your “explanation” will evaporate, like every gap argument before it.

title: Why Does Mathematics Describe the Universe?
section: The Strongest Objections—Stated at Full Strength
text: This deserves a careful answer, because the worry is legitimate and the history is real. The reply is that the argument here is not of the gap form. A God-of-the-gaps argument says: “science cannot yet explain X, therefore God.” This argument says something different: even with the physics and the cognitive science completed, there would remain the question of why reality is the kind of thing that submits to elegant mathematical law and is legible to mind—a question one level up from any particular scientific result. It is offered as a better overall explanation of a standing feature of the world, competing with naturalism on the same evidence, not as a placeholder for missing data. That is the structure of inference to the best explanation, not of a gap. Whether it succeeds is contestable; that it is not a mere gap-filler is, I think, clear.

title: Why Does Mathematics Describe the Universe?
section: The Indispensability Debate, and an Honest Hinge
text: One technical front deserves naming, because critics rightly raise it. W. V. O. Quine and Hilary Putnam argued that because mathematics is indispensable to our best scientific theories, and we should believe what those theories quantify over, we ought to believe mathematical objects exist.11 This famous indispensability argument is often read as support for a robust realism about mathematics—congenial to the present case. But it is contested precisely at the joints the theist leans on. Penelope Maddy and others have challenged the “confirmational holism” it assumes, and nominalists such as Hartry Field have labored to show that science could in principle be done without quantifying over numbers at all.12 The upshot for us is a needed concession: how real mathematics is, and therefore how deep the applicability puzzle runs, is itself a live and unsettled question among first-rate philosophers. The theistic argument is strongest if mathematical realism is roughly correct; it is weaker if a thoroughgoing nominalism succeeds. That hinge is genuinely disputed, and we should say so.

title: Why Does Mathematics Describe the Universe?
section: The State of the Scholarship
text: Where does the live debate actually stand? Three things can be said fairly. First, the phenomenon is not seriously in dispute: that mathematics is extraordinarily, and often predictively, effective in physics is acknowledged across the board, by atheist and theist alike. Second, the explanation is wide open. Naturalistic proposals abound—Max Tegmark’s bold “Mathematical Universe Hypothesis,” on which physical reality simply is a mathematical structure, is one striking example13—but none commands consensus, and Tegmark’s own view faces heavy criticism. Third, even sympathetic non-theists concede the puzzle points somewhere unexpected: Mark Steiner, in the most rigorous book-length study, argued that the discovery of physics by mathematical analogy yields an “anthropocentric” or “user-friendly” picture of the universe deeply uncomfortable for naturalism—though Steiner himself stopped short of drawing a theological conclusion.14 The theistic reading, advanced by philosophers such as Alvin Plantinga, is one serious option in this field, not a fringe view and not a settled victory.15

title: Why Does Mathematics Describe the Universe?
section: What the Argument Does, and Does Not, Establish
text: It will not do to oversell this. The unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics does not prove that God exists. It does not, by itself, get you to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, let alone to the Trinity or the empty tomb; those rest on other arguments and on revelation. It does not refute a determined naturalist, who can absorb the data as brute fact or bet on a future explanation. And it leans, as we have seen, on a contested view of how real mathematics is.

title: Why Does Mathematics Describe the Universe?
section: What the Argument Does, and Does Not, Establish
text: What it does is more modest and still worth having. It identifies a deep, conceded feature of reality—that the world is rationally ordered and that this order is legible to the rational mind—and shows that this feature is more at home in a universe made by a rational mind than in one that is not. Wigner called it a gift we neither understand nor deserve. The Christian would gently add: a gift, by its nature, implies a Giver, and the most natural reading of a cosmos written in the language of reason is that Reason wrote it. That is not the end of the conversation. But for anyone who has felt the strangeness of an equation foretelling a star, it is a thoroughly reasonable place to begin.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: An Argument as Old as the Church Itself
text: On the first Easter evening, two disconsolate disciples walked the road to Emmaus, and a stranger fell in beside them. "Was it not necessary," he asked, "that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?" Then, Luke tells us, "beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself."1 The risen Jesus did not first appeal to the empty tomb. He appealed to the prophets.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: An Argument as Old as the Church Itself
text: His followers never forgot it. When Peter stood before the Pentecost crowd, he reached for the Psalms (Acts 2:25–31). When Philip met the Ethiopian official puzzling over Isaiah 53, he "told him the good news about Jesus" from that very page (Acts 8:35). Paul "reasoned with them from the Scriptures" in synagogue after synagogue (Acts 17:2–3). The argument from prophecy is not a modern apologetic invention; it is the oldest Christian argument there is, and it deserves to be made well — which means made honestly.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: An Argument as Old as the Church Itself
text: This essay sets aside a popular but flawed version of the argument (the "statistical" case, treated below) and turns instead to the prophecies themselves: what they say, where the New Testament finds them fulfilled, and — crucially — which carry real evidential weight and which do not. A serious case is one that can survive its own footnotes.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: How to Read Prophecy Honestly
text: The first thing a careful reader must grasp is that the New Testament writers use the word "fulfill" (Greek plēroō) in more than one sense, and not always to mean "a prediction came true." Sometimes it means exactly that — a future-tense forecast realized in a specific event. But often it means something closer to "filled full": an earlier pattern, person, or institution reaches its intended completion in Christ. This is what scholars call typology, and a related idea, sensus plenior — a "fuller sense" God intended in a text beyond what its human author consciously foresaw.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: How to Read Prophecy Honestly
text: The classic example is Hosea 11:1, "Out of Egypt I called my son." In Hosea the verse is plainly about the past — Israel's exodus — and contains no future-tense verb at all. When Matthew applies it to the infant Jesus' return from Egypt (Matthew 2:15), he is not claiming Hosea predicted it. He is drawing an analogy: Jesus relives and succeeds in Israel's story.2 To call that a "fulfilled prediction" would be to misread Matthew himself.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: How to Read Prophecy Honestly
text: This honesty matters enormously, because the strength of the prophetic argument is uneven, and pretending otherwise discredits the whole. So throughout what follows, prophecies are flagged: strong ones concern matters outside any individual's control or staging (birthplace, lineage, the manner and timing of an execution under Roman law); weaker or typological ones are real and meaningful but could in principle be arranged, or were not predictions in their original setting. The cumulative case rests chiefly on the strong ones.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: A Catalogue of the Prophecies
text: Long before any town or tribe is named, the Hebrew Scriptures open a single thread and slowly draw it tight. In the garden, God tells the serpent that the woman’s offspring will one day strike the serpent’s head even as the serpent strikes his heel (Genesis 3:15) — words that Christian readers from the earliest centuries took as the first, faint announcement of a deliverer to come. This is a trajectory, not yet a falsifiable prediction; its force is only that the promise then narrows, generation by generation, from the whole human family toward a single line.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: A Catalogue of the Prophecies
text: The expected deliverer is mapped genealogically with increasing precision. He is the "seed" of Abraham, through whom "all the families of the earth shall be blessed" (Genesis 12:3; 22:18) — applied to Christ in Galatians 3:16. He comes from the tribe of Judah: "The scepter shall not depart from Judah... until tribute comes to him" (Genesis 49:10), echoed in Revelation 5:5. He is of the line of David, to whom God promised an everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 9:7; Jeremiah 23:5), a claim the Gospels press hard (Matthew 1:1; Romans 1:3). Strength: lineage is outside an individual's control, and the New Testament's confident appeal to it — in a culture that took genealogical descent with great seriousness — is notable (though the two Gospel genealogies, Matthew 1 and Luke 3, differ in ways that are a genuine difficulty, not merely a matter of scholarly debate—the proposed harmonizations, such as Luke giving Mary’s line or a levirate-marriage explanation, are possible but contested—though the datum that carries the weight here, a public claim to Davidic descent in a culture that took genealogical descent with great seriousness, does not depend on resolving them).

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: A Catalogue of the Prophecies
text: Micah names the town: "But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah... from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel" (Micah 5:2), fulfilled in Matthew 2:1–6. The Hebrew adds that the ruler's "origin is from of old, from ancient days" — a phrase debated between "ancient lineage" and something more.3 Strength: a specific, falsifiable birthplace; this is one of the strongest data points.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: A Catalogue of the Prophecies
text: The most contested birth text is Isaiah 7:14: "the almah shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." Here we must be candid. The Hebrew ‘almah means a young woman of marriageable age; it does not by itself specify virginity (the more precise word would be betulah). The Jewish translators of the Septuagint, however (Isaiah was rendered into Greek in the second century BC), translated it parthenos, "virgin" — and it is the Septuagint Matthew quotes (Matthew 1:23).4 Moreover, the verse's immediate context is a sign to King Ahaz about a child born in his own lifetime. Many scholars therefore read Isaiah 7:14 as having a near-term referent in Isaiah's day and a fuller messianic sense Matthew discerns in hindsight — a "dual fulfillment." This is a contested, largely typological case, not a knockdown prediction, and it should be presented as such.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: A Catalogue of the Prophecies
text: A forerunner prepares the way: "Behold, I send my messenger" (Malachi 3:1) and "a voice cries: In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD" (Isaiah 40:3), both applied to John the Baptist (Mark 1:2–3). The light dawns in the north: "Galilee of the nations... the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light" (Isaiah 9:1–2), cited in Matthew 4:14–16. The Deliverer is a "prophet like Moses" (Deuteronomy 18:15; cf. Acts 3:22). His ministry brings healing — eyes of the blind opened, the lame leaping (Isaiah 35:5–6) — which Jesus invokes as his credential (Matthew 11:4–5). He teaches in parables (Psalm 78:2; Matthew 13:34–35), and zeal for God's house consumes him (Psalm 69:9; John 2:17). He enters Jerusalem "humble and mounted on a donkey" (Zechariah 9:9; Matthew 21:1–9) — though this is the clearest example of a stageable prophecy, one the Gospels themselves present Jesus as deliberately arranging. Strength: mixed. The forerunner and the geography are reasonably firm; healing and teaching-style are the kind of thing that could be shaped in the telling, so they carry less independent weight.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: A Catalogue of the Prophecies
text: Here the texts grow startling. The Suffering Servant of Isaiah 52:13–53:12 is "despised and rejected," "wounded for our transgressions," "like a lamb that is led to the slaughter" who "opened not his mouth," who "makes his soul an offering for guilt," and who is "with a rich man in his death." Isaiah 53:9 even pairs a criminal's death ("with the wicked") and a wealthy burial — answered in Jesus' crucifixion between two thieves and burial in Joseph of Arimathea's tomb (Matthew 27:57–60). The Servant's silence before accusers (Isaiah 53:7) meets Jesus' silence before Pilate (Matthew 27:12–14).

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: A Catalogue of the Prophecies
text: Psalm 22, sung centuries before crucifixion was a Roman practice, opens with the cry Jesus echoed from the cross — "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Psalm 22:1; Matthew 27:46) — and goes on to describe mockery (v. 7–8), thirst and exhaustion (v. 14–15), and lots cast for clothing (v. 18; John 19:24). Then comes verse 16, one of the most disputed lines in the Hebrew Bible. The traditional Masoretic Text reads ka'ari — "like a lion" — yielding the awkward "like a lion my hands and my feet." But a fragment from Nahal Hever (5/6HevPs, 1st century AD) reads ka'aru, and the ancient Septuagint reads ōryxan, "they dug/pierced." The Septuagint (pre-Christian) and a disputed, faded 1st-century AD fragment together suggest a "pierced/dug" reading is at least old and not a Christian invention — though the Nahal Hever fragment is 1st-century AD rather than pre-Christian, and its reading is contested; scholars such as Brent Strawn defend the Masoretic "lion," and the fragment's ink is faded. This verse is genuinely contested; honesty requires saying so, and the broader Psalm does not depend on it. The point about the manner of Jesus' death and burial should therefore rest not on the disputed Psalm 22:16 but on the textually secure Isaiah 53:9—a criminal's death paired with a rich man's burial—which the manuscripts place well before the crucifixion.5

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: A Catalogue of the Prophecies
text: Other passion details: betrayal by an intimate, "my close friend... who ate my bread" (Psalm 41:9; John 13:18); thirty pieces of silver thrown "to the potter" (Zechariah 11:12–13), eerily matching Judas's betrayal price spent on a potter's field (Matthew 27:3–10 — which, candidly, attributes the quotation to Jeremiah, a long-noted difficulty usually explained by scroll-naming convention or a composite citation).6 No bone is broken (Psalm 34:20; cf. the Passover lamb of Exodus 12:46; John 19:33–36); his side is pierced (Zechariah 12:10, "they look on me, on him whom they have pierced"; John 19:34–37).

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: A Catalogue of the Prophecies
text: And there is Daniel 9:24–27, which foretells that "an anointed one shall be cut off" after a span of "sixty-two weeks" following a decree to restore Jerusalem — language Christians have read as timing the Messiah's death before the Second Temple's destruction (the text says the city and sanctuary will be destroyed afterward, which happened in AD 70). But the dating is heavily contested: which decree starts the clock (Cyrus c. 538 BC, or Artaxerxes in 458 or 445 BC?), and whether the "anointed one" is the Messiah, a high priest, or Onias III, are all live scholarly disputes. The passage is suggestive but should not be overclaimed.7

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: A Catalogue of the Prophecies
text: The Scriptures do not end at the grave. "You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption" (Psalm 16:10) — which Peter (Acts 2:25–31) and Paul (Acts 13:35) argue David could not have meant of himself, since David died and decayed. The vindicated one is enthroned: "The LORD says to my Lord, Sit at my right hand" (Psalm 110:1), the Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes most often. And in Daniel 7:13–14, "one like a son of man" comes "with the clouds of heaven" and receives "an everlasting dominion" — the very title Jesus chose for himself.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: The Honest Objections
text: The sharpest objection is this: the Gospel writers knew the Hebrew Scriptures intimately, so what looks like fulfillment may be the writers shaping their narratives to match the texts. This must be conceded for the "stageable" prophecies — a man could deliberately ride a donkey into Jerusalem (Zechariah 9:9), and an author could narrate a detail to echo a psalm.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: The Honest Objections
text: The reply is to lean on the prophecies outside anyone's control or staging: where one is born, what tribe and lineage one belongs to, and the manner and timing of one's death under an occupying empire that alone held the power of capital crucifixion. A first-century Jew could not arrange to be born in Bethlehem of David's line, nor engineer a Roman execution by a method Psalm 22 seems to describe a thousand years early. And the texts are demonstrably pre-Christian: the Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (1QIsaᵃ) — containing Isaiah 7, 9, 35, 40, and all of chapter 53 — is dated by paleography and radiocarbon to roughly 125 BC, well over a century before Jesus.8 No one shaped Isaiah after the fact.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: The Honest Objections
text: Jewish counter-missionary scholars — Rabbi Tovia Singer foremost among them — argue, fairly, that many of these texts were not predictions of an individual Messiah at all in their original setting. Isaiah 7:14 addresses Ahaz; Hosea 11:1 looks backward to the Exodus. Most pointedly, the "Servant" of Isaiah is in several nearby passages explicitly named as the nation Israel (Isaiah 41:8; 49:3), so Isaiah 53, on this reading, depicts suffering, faithful Israel among the nations — not a crucified Messiah.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: The Honest Objections
text: This deserves a real and respectful answer. First, on Isaiah 53: within the song the Servant is "stricken for the transgression of my people" (53:8) — distinguished from the people, which fits awkwardly with a purely collective reading, though its defenders appeal to a righteous remnant suffering for the wider nation. Second, the messianic-individual interpretation is not a Christian imposition: both individual-messianic and collective readings are attested in ancient Judaism — the Targum on Isaiah 52:13 names "my servant the Messiah" — evidence that an individual-messianic reading of the Servant was live in ancient Judaism, even where later interpreters redirected the suffering elsewhere — and the collective-Israel reading became dominant only in later Jewish tradition, a shift many associate with Rashi in the medieval period.9 Christians should hold this point gently. The collective reading is sincere, rooted in Isaiah's own servant-Israel language, and was sharpened in centuries when Jewish communities were suffering at Christian hands. The fair conclusion is that Isaiah 53's referent is genuinely contested, and that the Christian reading is a defensible — not the only conceivable — interpretation. The honest move is to let it strengthen the cumulative pattern, not to wield it as a club.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: The Honest Objections
text: Here is the reframe this essay was built around. In Science Speaks (developed across editions from the late 1950s), mathematician Peter Stoner argued that the odds of one man fulfilling just eight prophecies were one in 1017 — a figure he reached by taking a raw product of roughly 1028 and dividing by the estimated number of people who have ever lived; he put forty-eight prophecies at 1 in 10157. The image is vivid — Texas knee-deep in silver dollars, one of them marked — and it has circulated for eighty years.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: The Honest Objections
text: It should be retired. The probabilities are not real measurements; they are numbers assigned by guesswork ("the chance of being born in Bethlehem is 1 in 280,000," and so on), then multiplied as if independent. A reviewer in The Quarterly Review of Biology charged Stoner with "using only these facts which bolster his hypothesis"; even Stoner's own grandson now concedes the book is of more historical than evangelistic value.10 The method is pseudo-mathematics: precise-looking figures resting on arbitrary inputs. The case for the prophecies does not rest on it, and never needed it. Convergence, not a manufactured probability, is the real argument.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: What the Argument Does — and Does Not — Establish
text: So what is left when the weak links are removed and the contested texts are flagged as contested? A great deal, but stated precisely.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: What the Argument Does — and Does Not — Establish
text: What the prophetic argument does establish is a striking cumulative convergence: a single first-century figure who fits a constellation of expectations — birthplace, lineage, a rejected and suffering deliverer, a death by piercing and a rich man's burial, a vindication beyond the grave — drawn from documents provably older than he was. The most evidentially weighty of these lie outside any human power to arrange. That convergence is not nothing; it is, in the proper sense, remarkable, and it is why the apostles preached it.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: What the Argument Does — and Does Not — Establish
text: What the argument does not establish is a single, knock-down, mathematical proof. It is a cumulative, probabilistic case, the way a verdict is built from many testimonies rather than one. Some "fulfillments" are typological, not predictive. Several key texts — Isaiah 7:14, Psalm 22:16, the dating in Daniel 9, the referent of Isaiah 53 — are genuinely disputed among honest scholars, and a reader is entitled to know that before being asked to weigh them.

title: The Witness of the Prophets: How the Hebrew Scriptures Converge on Jesus
section: What the Argument Does — and Does Not — Establish
text: The prophets, then, do not hand us a proof to end argument; they hand us a portrait, sketched across a thousand years by many hands, that comes startlingly into focus on one face. Whether that focus is coincidence or providence is the question each reader must answer. But the case is strong enough to be worth answering — and honest enough, made this way, to be made "with gentleness and respect" (1 Peter 3:15).

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: An Argument Designed to Survive Disagreement
text: Most arguments for the resurrection of Jesus run into the same wall on the first move. The case begins by quoting the Gospels, and the sceptic answers that the Gospels are precisely what is in dispute — late, biased, theologically motivated documents written by believers for believers. The conversation stalls before it starts. The achievement of the minimal facts approach, developed over four decades by the philosopher and historian Gary Habermas and pressed into its fullest scholarly form by his student Michael Licona, is to refuse that stalemate. Instead of asking the sceptic to grant the reliability of the New Testament, it asks only for a short list of facts that the sceptic almost certainly already grants — and then argues that the resurrection is the best explanation of those.1

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: An Argument Designed to Survive Disagreement
text: This essay is the overview of the resurrection case as a whole. It does not re-argue each fact in depth — the empty tomb, the early creed, Paul's conversion, the appearances, the transformation of the disciples, and the conversion of James each have their own dedicated treatment in this library. The aim here is to understand the method: why minimal facts, what the two criteria are, how the inference to the best explanation works across the whole set, and — crucially — where serious critics say the method strains. The strength of the argument is also the source of its sharpest objections, and both deserve a careful hearing.

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Two Criteria
text: A "minimal fact," in Habermas's sense, is not simply a fact he finds persuasive. It is a fact that satisfies two deliberately demanding tests. First, it must be strongly evidenced — typically by multiple independent lines of testimony. Second, and this is the distinctive move, it must be accepted by the great majority of scholars who study the subject, including the sceptical ones — atheist, agnostic, Jewish, and liberal scholars, not only evangelicals.2 The second criterion is doing the rhetorical work. It means that whatever survives the filter is common ground; the believer and the unbeliever can argue about its explanation without first having to settle the inspiration or even the general reliability of Scripture.

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Two Criteria
text: Habermas's claim to know what the consensus is rests on an unusual project. Since the mid-1970s he has compiled a running bibliography of academic writing on the resurrection in English, French, and German, tracking how scholars come down on roughly 140 sub-questions. That bibliography now contains on the order of several thousand sources.3 From it he distils the facts that command near-universal assent. The list is usually given as four to six items; in its standard form it runs: Jesus died by crucifixion; his disciples sincerely believed he rose and appeared to them; the persecutor Paul was converted by what he took to be an appearance of the risen Jesus; the sceptic James, Jesus' brother, was likewise converted; and — added with an explicit flag that it is more contested — the tomb was found empty. In his stricter methodological statements Habermas is sharper still: he has never counted the empty tomb as a Minimal Fact at all, since it does not command the near-unanimity the others do, filing it instead among a broader list of "Known Historical Facts" on which he applies the criteria more leniently.4

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Two Criteria
text: The first fact illustrates the method's discipline. That Jesus died by Roman crucifixion is attested by all four Gospels, by Paul, and — outside the Christian sources entirely — by the Jewish historian Josephus and the Roman historian Tacitus, who called the new movement a "pernicious superstition" and had no motive to flatter it.5 This is why even John Dominic Crossan, co-founder of the Jesus Seminar and one of the most sceptical figures in the field, can write that Jesus' execution "is as sure as anything historical can ever be."6 Habermas does not cite Crossan because Crossan is friendly; he cites him because Crossan is hostile, and the concession therefore counts. That is the engine of the whole approach — letting the opposition supply the premises.

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Two Criteria
text: The point is worth pressing, because the crucifixion is the load-bearing fact and sceptics probe it hardest. Beyond the Christian writings, a widening circle of non-Christian sources refers to the execution — though they do not all carry the same weight, and the honest presenter keeps the distinction sharp. Josephus and Tacitus state it outright (the Josephus notice carries later Christian embellishment, but its core reference to the crucifixion under Pilate is widely accepted as authentic). The satirist Lucian of Samosata mocks the Christians for worshipping "the man who was crucified in Palestine." A Syriac letter attributed to Mara bar Serapion appears to allude to the Jews putting to death their "wise king," though it never names Jesus and the identification is a scholarly inference rather than a certainty. And the Babylonian Talmud records that "Yeshu" was "hanged" on the eve of Passover — a hostile Jewish memory of an execution, even if "hanged" is not simply Roman crucifixion and the reference's identification is debated. So the accurate summary is not that five sources "narrate" the crucifixion but that two of them — Josephus and Tacitus — state it, while Lucian, Mara, and the Talmud presuppose or allude to it. None was friendly to the movement.7

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Two Criteria
text: The bedrock is not merely that Jesus was crucified but that he died — and a persistent minority theory, the "swoon" or apparent-death hypothesis, disputes exactly that, proposing that Jesus survived the cross, revived in the cool of the tomb, and was mistaken for one risen from the dead. Two considerations tell decisively against it. The first is medical. Roman crucifixion killed by asphyxiation, blood loss, and shock, and it was carried out by professional executioners with every incentive to confirm death. A detailed 1986 study in the Journal of the American Medical Association reviewed the physiology and concluded that interpretations "based on the assumption that Jesus did not die on the cross … appear to be at odds with modern medical knowledge."8 Nor is this merely theoretical. Josephus records that during the siege of Jerusalem he recognised three of his own acquaintances among a group being crucified and successfully begged the Roman commander Titus for their release; they were taken down at once and given the best medical care available — and even so, two of the three died.8 If even men deliberately rescued in mid-crucifixion and tended by physicians could not reliably be saved — two of those three still died — then the suggestion that a Jesus scourged, crucified, speared in the side, and sealed in a tomb quietly recovered on his own, with no rescue and no medical care at all, is deeply improbable. The second is historical, and it was pressed not by an apologist but by the arch-sceptic David Friedrich Strauss. Writing in 1879, Strauss ridiculed the theory: a man who "had stolen half-dead out of the sepulchre," who "crept about weak and ill" in desperate need of bandaging and care, could not possibly "have given to the disciples the impression that he was … the Prince of Life."9 A battered survivor would have drawn pity and a physician, not the worship of a conqueror of death. The swoon theory has to make the disciples' explosive conviction rest on a scene that would have produced its opposite.

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Earliest Report: The Creed Paul Received
text: If the crucifixion is the bedrock, the earliest report of what the first disciples proclaimed is the true foundation of the positive case — and it is not a Gospel written decades later but a formula older than any of them, embedded in a letter that even the most sceptical scholars date to the early-to-mid 50s. Writing to the Corinthians, Paul hands on what he explicitly says is tradition he had himself received:

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Earliest Report: The Creed Paul Received
text: The verbs "delivered" and "received" are the technical vocabulary of passing on fixed oral tradition, and the passage's balanced clauses, its non-Pauline phrasing, and its Semitic features have persuaded scholars across the spectrum that Paul is here quoting a formula he did not compose but inherited — one that predates his letter by years. John Kloppenborg's careful analysis is representative in concluding that the core is a pre-Pauline formula, even while he is more cautious than some about confident claims for its precise Aramaic wording, its Jerusalem origin, and its very earliest dating.11

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Earliest Report: The Creed Paul Received
text: How early? The chain is short and each link is firm. Jesus was crucified around AD 30. Paul, by his own account, was converted within a few years of that — most reconstructions place his conversion one to three years later — and he tells the Galatians that three years after his conversion he went up to Jerusalem and stayed with Cephas (Peter), also seeing James the Lord's brother, the two men the formula names as recipients of appearances.12 Whether Paul first received the creed at his conversion or on that Jerusalem visit, the tradition traces back to within roughly two to five years of the crucifixion — and its content back earlier still, to the community that coined it. That is why critical scholars reach for unusually strong language. Ulrich Wilckens judged that the formula "goes back to the oldest phase of all in the history of primitive Christianity"; Walter Kasper held that the creed was already "in use by AD 30"; and J. Murphy-O'Connor represents the wide agreement that Paul is quoting received tradition rather than composing it — a cluster of judgments gathered in Gary Habermas's survey of the field.13 The window is far too narrow a gap for a legend to fill.

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Earliest Report: The Creed Paul Received
text: The most striking feature of the second minimal fact — that the disciples sincerely believed the risen Jesus had appeared to them — is how far across the ideological spectrum it is conceded, and on the historian's own terms rather than the believer's. Gerd Lüdemann, an atheist New Testament scholar, wrote that "it may be taken as historically certain that Peter and the disciples had experiences after Jesus' death in which Jesus appeared to them as the risen Christ."14 E. P. Sanders, among the leading historical-Jesus scholars of his generation, was equally blunt: "That Jesus' followers (and later Paul) had resurrection experiences is, in my judgment, a fact. What the reality was that gave rise to the experiences I do not know."15 The Anglican scholar Reginald Fuller called the disciples' Easter faith "one of the indisputable facts of history" and held that the historian "must … postulate an 'x'" to explain it — remarking, of the appearance to Jesus' sceptical brother, that "if there were no record of an appearance to James the Lord's brother in the New Testament we should have to invent one."16 Even Bart Ehrman, no ally of the apologetic case, grants that "it is a historical fact that some of Jesus' followers came to believe that he had been raised from the dead soon after his execution."17 Habermas sums up the pattern: "perhaps no fact is more widely recognized than that early Christian believers had real experiences that they thought were appearances of the risen Jesus."18

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Earliest Report: The Creed Paul Received
text: It is essential to be precise about what these concessions do and do not grant, because the point is easily abused. Not one of these scholars is here conceding, as a matter of historical argument, that Jesus rose from the dead. Lüdemann, Sanders, and Ehrman each propose or leave open a naturalistic explanation of the experiences, and to enlist any of them as a witness to the resurrection itself would flatly misrepresent them. What they concede is narrower — and still remarkable: that the earliest followers really did have experiences they took to be encounters with a living Jesus, and that the tradition reporting it is astonishingly early. That conceded ground is the starting line the argument reasons from, never the finish line it claims to have already reached.

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Earliest Report: The Creed Paul Received
text: It is also why Paul is arguably the single most valuable witness in the entire discussion. His testimony is early; it is written in his own hand rather than reported at second or third remove; and it comes from a former enemy of the movement he now died proclaiming. When he lists the appearances in 1 Corinthians 15 he is naming men he had personally met, and his account of his Jerusalem visits in Galatians 1–2 shows a gospel he received independently of the Jerusalem apostles yet which they publicly endorsed — not a modern-style audit of anyone's memory, but powerful evidence that the message Paul preached and the message of Peter and James were one and the same from the start.19

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: From Facts to Resurrection: The Inference
text: The minimal facts argument is not a deduction. It is an inference to the best explanation, the same form of reasoning a historian or a detective uses: among the live hypotheses, which one accounts for the whole body of data with the most explanatory scope and power, the least strain, and the fewest unsupported assumptions? Licona's 2010 monograph, The Resurrection of Jesus: A New Historiographical Approach, makes this explicit, borrowing the criteria for adjudicating hypotheses from the philosophy of history — explanatory scope, explanatory power, plausibility, degree of being ad hoc, and illumination — and applying them as a working historian would to any contested event.20

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: From Facts to Resurrection: The Inference
text: The argument's force is cumulative. No single fact, taken alone, forces the resurrection. An empty tomb by itself admits of theft or relocation. Visionary experiences by themselves admit of hallucination. What the naturalistic alternatives struggle with is the conjunction. The strongest form of the visionary objection is not the private individual hallucination but the well-documented phenomenon of shared bereavement and religious visions — the kind Bart Ehrman presses, citing collective experiences such as Marian apparitions, where many people sincerely report seeing a figure together. That deserves a direct answer. Two features resist it: first, the appearances include people with no grief and no prior expectation — Paul, a hostile outsider actively persecuting the movement, and James, whose family is remembered as thinking Jesus out of his mind, and who did not believe during the ministry21 — whereas bereavement visions arise among those already devoted to and longing for the one they have lost; and second, no documented apparition tradition on record has produced a community that concluded a particular person had been bodily raised and then proved willing to suffer and die proclaiming it. The stolen-body hypothesis might explain an empty tomb, but it cannot explain why the disciples would suffer, and in documented cases die, for what they would then know to be a fraud, nor why Paul, attacking the movement from the outside, would convert. The legend hypothesis founders on chronology: the resurrection was being preached in Jerusalem within a very few years — on the early Christian account, within weeks — and, as the creed examined above shows, the tradition itself traces to within a few years of the crucifixion, far too early for legend to have done its slow work.

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: From Facts to Resurrection: The Inference
text: The argument, then, is that each rival explanation can cover one or two facts but breaks on the others, while a single hypothesis — that Jesus actually rose — covers all of them at once. Licona's conclusion is stated with care: "Jesus' resurrection from the dead is the best historical explanation of the relevant historical bedrock."22 Note the wording. He claims the best explanation, reached by ordinary historical method, not a mathematical proof.

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: From Facts to Resurrection: The Inference
text: Timothy and Lydia McGrew have pressed this underlying structure furthest, treating the empty tomb, the disciples’ appearances, and the separate conversions of the outsider Paul and the sceptic James as causally independent lines—so that a single naturalistic mechanism (one shared hallucination, one stolen body, one growing legend) would have to misfire in each unrelated channel at once. From their case this essay takes only that qualitative independence, not the probabilistic calculation they attach to it, which—with Licona—it declines (Timothy McGrew and Lydia McGrew, “The Argument from Miracles: A Cumulative Case for the Resurrection of Jesus of Nazareth,” in The Blackwell Companion to Natural Theology, ed. William Lane Craig and J. P. Moreland [Oxford: Wiley-Blackwell, 2009], 593–662.)

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: From Facts to Resurrection: The Inference
text: It is worth naming the move precisely, because critics sometimes treat it as a sleight of hand. The philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce called it abduction — a third mode of reasoning alongside deduction and induction, with the form: "The surprising fact, C, is observed. But if A were true, C would be a matter of course. Hence, there is reason to suspect that A is true."23 That is exactly the shape of the resurrection argument: the disciples' transformation, Paul's conversion, the empty tomb and the rest are the surprising facts; a real resurrection would make them a matter of course; hence there is reason to suspect it. And here is the honest difficulty. Stated crudely, that pattern is the textbook fallacy of affirming the consequent — "if A then C; C; therefore A" — because some other cause might produce the same facts. Peirce did not hide the weakness: writing in 1878 he granted that this kind of inference "is a weak kind of argument," one that "often inclines our judgment so slightly toward its conclusion that we cannot say that we believe the latter to be true; we only surmise that it may be so."24

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: From Facts to Resurrection: The Inference
text: What turns a weak surmise into a reasonable conclusion is not a change in logical form but the weighing of rivals. A bare abduction entertains one hypothesis; a disciplined inference to the best explanation entertains all the live ones and asks which accounts for the whole body of data with the most scope and the least strain — and, crucially, which eliminates the causes that are simply not adequate to the effect. This is ordinary historical method. The historian, reasoning as Peirce did from "numberless documents and monuments" to the real existence of a Napoleon he had never seen, reaches a person or an event as the only supposition that explains the traces it left behind.25 Applied here, the theft, hallucination, and legend hypotheses are not waved away; each is shown to be causally inadequate to some part of the evidence — which is what the section below examines. The comparative move blunts the affirming-the-consequent worry without dissolving it entirely, since one can always ask whether the true explanation is one no one has yet proposed; that is why the argument leans on the facts even critics grant rather than on any single inference. What it delivers, in the end, is the kind of verdict a jury delivers: not deductive certainty, but the best account of the evidence.

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Strongest Objections
text: The minimal facts approach is popular, and popularity has made it a target. The serious objections do not dispute that Jesus was crucified or that the disciples believed they saw him. They attack the method — and an honest survey has to state them at full strength.

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Strongest Objections
text: The most formidable critic here is not a village atheist but Dale Allison, one of the most respected New Testament scholars alive, whose 2005 Resurrecting Jesus and 2021 The Resurrection of Jesus: Apologetics, Polemics, History treat the evidence with unusual rigour — and who remains, by his own account, genuinely undecided. Allison grants much of the data. His objection cuts deeper than any single fact: he argues that the inference from the facts to the resurrection cannot be made independently of the worldview the investigator brings to it. "Probability," he writes, "is in the eye of the beholder."26 Whether the resurrection is the best explanation depends in part on one's prior estimate of whether such a thing can happen at all — and that prior is not itself settled by the historical data.

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Strongest Objections
text: This is the strongest objection in the literature, and it should be conceded as far as it goes. The minimal facts do not, by themselves, compel assent from someone whose background convictions assign a vanishingly small prior to any miracle — the point David Hume pressed in 1748 and which Allison restates with modern rigour.27 The honest reply is not to deny this but to reframe what the argument claims. It does not claim to coerce the committed naturalist. It claims that, if one is open to the possibility that God might raise the dead, the historical evidence then makes the resurrection the most reasonable explanation of an otherwise baffling set of facts. The argument removes the historical excuse for unbelief; it cannot remove the metaphysical one, and it should not pretend to. Allison himself, notably, judges the resurrection appearances and the empty tomb to be better evidenced than most sceptics allow — he simply will not take the last step on historical grounds alone. The point to see is that what stays his hand is a metaphysical prior, not a gap in the historical evidence — which is exactly this argument's contention: the history is not what is holding the honest inquirer back.

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Strongest Objections
text: A second objection targets the second criterion directly. When Habermas says a fact is "accepted by the majority of scholars," two distinct challenges follow. The philosopher Robert Greg Cavin questions whether the inference itself — from the agreed facts to the conclusion that a miracle is the best explanation — is sound.28 But inference to the best explanation is simply the standard tool for reconstructing any contested past event, and the resurrection is being judged by the very criteria — explanatory scope, power, and being less ad hoc — that historians apply to any hypothesis whatever; it is not being handed a special exemption. On inspection Cavin's worry, like Allison's, resolves into the prior probability of a miracle — the metaphysical dispute this essay openly concedes history alone cannot settle — rather than a flaw in the inference form itself. And the historian Richard Carrier, among others, presses the count directly: which scholars, counted how? Habermas's bibliography is not a randomised survey; it is a compilation of those who have chosen to publish on the resurrection — a population that may over-represent the religiously committed. A widely circulated statistical critique by members of the Global Center for Religious Research argued that the underlying dataset is opaque and that the consensus claims, especially the figure that some three-quarters of scholars accept the empty tomb, cannot be independently verified from what Habermas has published.29

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Strongest Objections
text: This is a fair methodological warning and the figures should be handled with the corresponding caution. The empty-tomb percentage in particular — drawn from Habermas's 2005 article in the Journal for the Study of the Historical Jesus — is his own tally of the literature he has read, not a poll, and critics are right that it cannot be audited.30 Habermas himself has answered this line of attack on two fronts. First, the head-count was never what bears the weight: of his two criteria, he holds the demand for strong, multiply-attested evidence to be "by far the most crucial," since that is what actually establishes historicity, while the survey of scholarly opinion is only a secondary check that "may be mistaken or it could change."3 The consensus figure is not the proof; it shows only that the believer is not asking anyone to accept something none but conservatives grant. Second, whatever bias his catalogue carries runs the opposite way from the one alleged: he deliberately over-collected the most radical writers — including non-credentialed mythicists and naturalistic theorists whom mainstream scholars "rarely even footnoted" — so that, by his own account, his tally leans toward the sceptical end rather than the devout.3 Neither point makes the underlying dataset transparent, and the call for an auditable count stands; but together they blunt the charge that the consensus is merely an artefact of a sample skewed toward the religiously committed. Two further considerations point the same way. First, the strongest minimal facts do not depend on a contested headcount at all: that Jesus was crucified and that the disciples sincerely believed they had seen him alive are conceded by named sceptics — Crossan, Lüdemann, Ehrman — on the merits of the evidenceSee the evidenceThe evidenceSourceJohn Dominic Crossan, Jesus: A Revolutionary Biography (HarperSanFrancisco, 1994), p. 145: “That he was crucified is as sure as anything historical can ever be.” Crossan is a co-founder of the Jesus Seminar; the disciples’ sincere belief that they saw Jesus alive is granted on the same terms by critics including Gerd Lüdemann and Bart Ehrman.Who holds itNot a believers’ huddle: the crucifixion and the disciples’ sincere experience are granted by named non-Christian and sceptical scholars on the merits of the evidence, apart from any survey. (The essay flags the empty tomb as the more contested fact, and is careful not to inflate “majority” into “virtually all.”), quite apart from any survey. Second, the empty tomb is precisely the fact Habermas flags as more disputed, and a careful presentation of the argument should treat it as the soft point in the chain rather than as a settled premise. The case is strongest when it leans on the facts the critics themselves grant, and weakest when it inflates "majority" into "virtually all."

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The Strongest Objections
text: A subtler worry, pressed from within friendly scholarship as well as from outside, is that some items on the list smuggle in more than the consensus actually concedes. "The disciples believed they saw the risen Jesus" is nearly universally granted; "they saw group appearances," as the creed reports, is granted by fewer; and "the tomb was empty" by fewer still. This tiering is not merely a critic's complaint; it is built into the method by its most rigorous practitioner. In his 2010 study Licona counts only three facts as historical "bedrock" — the crucifixion, the disciples' appearance-experiences, and Paul's conversion — and expressly relegates the conversion of James and the empty tomb to a lower tier of facts he calls "second-order," to be weighed only where the bedrock leaves a question undecided. Tellingly, he sets James aside not because the datum is doubted — the scholars who grant it range from atheist to conservative — but only because too few specialists have written on it to establish the near-unanimity his own criterion demands.20 The honest version of the argument keeps these tiers distinct, building first on the genuinely common ground and only then arguing — separately and openly — for the more contested items. Where presenters blur the tiers, treating every fact as equally bulletproof, they hand the critic an easy and deserved rebuttal. The method's integrity depends on its restraint.

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The State of the Scholarship
text: Where does the live debate actually stand? On the foundational data, there is genuine and broad agreement: across the spectrum, scholars accept that Jesus was crucified and that his followers had experiences they sincerely interpreted as encounters with the risen Christ. That much is not seriously contested. What is contested is everything downstream — the cause of those experiences, the historicity of the empty tomb, and above all whether history can license the supernatural conclusion at all.

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: The State of the Scholarship
text: The naturalistic alternatives remain on the table and are defended by serious people. Gerd Lüdemann argued for visions rooted in guilt and grief; Bart Ehrman appeals to well-documented bereavement visions; Allison holds the question open. None of these scholars thinks the disciples were lying, and the apologist should not either — the experiences were real to those who had them. The dispute is about their source. The minimal facts argument contends that no naturalistic mechanism yet proposed accounts for the whole set — the crucifixion, the early and group experiences, the conversion of a persecutor and a sceptic, and the empty tomb — without straining badly somewhere. Its critics contend that the resurrection hypothesis strains worse, because it requires a miracle. That, in the end, is the real fault line, and it is a philosophical one as much as a historical one.

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: What the Argument Does and Doesn't Establish
text: The minimal facts argument is best understood as a carefully bounded instrument. It establishes that a small set of facts about the death and aftermath of Jesus is firmly grounded and broadly conceded, and that the most natural explanation of those facts together — for anyone not antecedently committed to ruling miracles out — is that Jesus rose from the dead. It does this without asking the sceptic to grant biblical inspiration, biblical inerrancy, or even the general reliability of the Gospels. That is a genuine and unusual achievement, and it is why the approach has reshaped how the resurrection is argued in the last forty years.

title: The Minimal Facts Argument: Building the Resurrection Case on Ground Even Sceptics Concede
section: What the Argument Does and Doesn't Establish
text: What it does not do is force the conclusion on someone whose worldview assigns no room to the act of God. The most candid statement of that limit comes from the other side. The process philosopher Charles Hartshorne—a non-Christian who did not accept the resurrection—reflected on the 1985 debate between Gary Habermas and the atheist Antony Flew and granted that he could neither explain away the evidence Habermas pressed nor agree with Flew’s denial of it, before naming the real obstacle: “My metaphysical bias is against resurrections.”31 It does not prove the resurrection in the way a theorem is proved; it makes it the best explanation, which is the most any historical argument about any event can claim. And it depends, at its contested edges — the empty tomb, the precise scope of the consensus — on premises that the honest advocate must label as more disputed than the rest. Habermas and Licona, at their best, say exactly this. The argument's power is that it begins where even the critic stands; its limit is that the last step, from "best historical explanation" to "and therefore God acted," is one the evidence invites but cannot compel. Habermas is emphatic on a final point that is easy to miss: the whole approach is an apologetic strategy, not a verdict on the trustworthiness of Scripture. It is, in his words, "not a prescription for how a given text should be approached … or how a sermon is written," and its deliberate restriction to what critics grant "should never be concluded" to indicate "a lack of trust in Scripture … Nor should it cause others to question or doubt their beliefs." The minimal-facts case is a bridge built to be crossed from the sceptic's side; the believer who already trusts the Gospels has simply been handed one more reason to — a corroboration, not a new foundation.2 As the apostle whose own conversion is one of the minimal facts would put it, the case is to be made "with gentleness and respect" (1 Peter 3:15) — confident in how far the evidence reaches, and candid about where argument ends and trust begins.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
text: Imagine a courtroom in which the verdict is fixed before the first witness is sworn. However many people testify, however sober and consistent and unmotivated to lie, the judge has ruled in advance that their testimony cannot be heard, because it concerns a kind of event that—he has decided beforehand—simply does not happen. That is precisely the posture many take toward the central claim of the Christian faith. When the resurrection of Jesus is raised, a great many thoughtful people do not weigh the evidence and find it wanting; they decline to weigh it at all, because they hold that a miracle is either impossible or, whatever the testimony, never something a reasonable person could believe.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
text: If that verdict is sound, the rest of the case is moot. There is no point examining an empty tomb or an early creed if resurrection has been ruled out at the door. So before any historical question can be honestly opened, one prior question must be faced: is there a good in-principle argument that miracles are impossible, or never rationally believable? This essay is about that question, and only that question. Its thesis is deliberately modest: the two classic attempts to shut the door—Baruch Spinoza’s argument that miracles are impossible, and David Hume’s that they are never credible—both fail. If they fail, the door is open. Whether any particular miracle actually walked through it is a separate, historical inquiry, taken up elsewhere.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: Stating the Question Carefully
text: Two questions must be kept rigorously apart. The first is a question of possibility: could a miracle happen at all? The second is a question of actuality: did this or that specific miracle happen? These are answered by different means. Possibility is settled by philosophy—by asking whether the very concept is coherent and whether the universe is the kind of place open to such an event. Actuality is settled by evidence—by testimony, documents, and the ordinary tools of history. Spinoza and Hume both attempt to settle the actuality question a priori, in advance of any evidence, by reasoning from the nature of law itself. That is the move this essay contests.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: Stating the Question Carefully
text: It is worth stating plainly what will not be argued here. Nothing below shows that any miracle has occurred; nothing below establishes the resurrection, or that miracles are common, or that every wonder reported in Scripture happened as told. The claim is narrower and, precisely because it is narrow, more secure: the a priori bar is illegitimate, so miracle claims must be examined case by case on their evidence rather than dismissed at the outset. Removing the roadblock is not the same as completing the journey—but you cannot begin the journey while the roadblock stands.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: What a Miracle Is—and Is Not
text: Careless definitions have done more to confuse this debate than any argument. A miracle, in the classical sense, is not simply a very strange or very rare event; a stunning coincidence is not a miracle, and neither is a phenomenon we cannot yet explain. Nor is it best described as nature “breaking down.” The most defensible definition is that a miracle is a special act of God who transcends the natural order—an event that would not have occurred had nature been left to its own resources. Strikingly, the atheist philosopher Antony Flew, no friend of theism for most of his career, framed a miracle in just such terms: as something that would never have happened if nature had been left to its own devices.1 The concept, then, is not incoherent even to those who reject it; the dispute is over whether such an act is possible and whether it ever occurs.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: What a Miracle Is—and Is Not
text: One further point of care, kept deliberately light and shared across the Christian traditions: a miracle in the biblical sense is not a bare display of power but a sign—an act tied to a message and a messenger, meant to authenticate a word from God. This essay does not adjudicate which miracles are genuine, nor when or whether they occur today; those are questions on which sincere Christians differ. The point here is only conceptual: a miracle is God acting purposively within a world he made, not a random rupture in the fabric of things.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: Descriptions, Not Prescriptions
text: The decisive move in the whole debate is a distinction about what a law of nature is. (The metaphysics of laws is treated at length in a companion essay;2 here only one facet matters.) A law of nature, on the most defensible account, is a description of how things regularly behave, not a prescription that dictates what must happen—and even those who hold that laws genuinely govern take them to govern only how things go when nothing interferes. The law of gravity does not compel a stone; it tells us, accurately, how unsupported bodies do in fact move when nothing interferes. That last clause is everything. The regularities hold when nothing interferes—and agents interfere constantly.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: Descriptions, Not Prescriptions
text: Consider an outfielder catching a falling ball. He does not repeal the law of gravitation; the law describes exactly what the ball would do left to itself, and it goes on describing that even as his glove intervenes. A finite agent, by introducing a new causal factor, produces an outcome the regularity alone would not have produced, without abolishing the regularity in the slightest. If a finite mind and hand can do this within nature, an infinite Mind who authored nature is hardly barred from doing the same on rare occasion and for a purpose. A miracle, so understood, is not the violation of a law but the introduction of a cause the law never claimed to exclude. This is why the loaded word “violation”—which both Spinoza and Hume lean on—quietly smuggles in the conclusion it is meant to prove.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: The Closed Box and the Open One
text: Underneath Spinoza’s argument—and the popular “science has disproved miracles” slogan—lies an assumption rarely stated: that the physical universe is a causally closed system—a sealed box in which nothing acts except other things inside the box. (Hume’s subtler, purely epistemic version does not depend on this; it is taken up in the next section.) On that assumption, of course, no miracle can occur, because there is no one outside to act. But whether the box is closed is not a finding of science; it is a metaphysical commitment. Naturalism assumes closure; theism holds that the universe is open to the God who made it. And here is the pivot: whether the universe is a closed system is exactly the question in dispute between the theist and the naturalist. To assume closure and conclude that miracles are impossible is to argue in a circle—to help oneself to the very premise the theist denies. If a God capable of creating a universe exists at all, the possibility of his acting within it follows almost trivially; the one who made the box is not trapped inside it.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: Spinoza: Miracles as an Absurdity
text: The bolder of the two arguments is the older. Benedict de Spinoza, writing in his Tractatus Theologico-Politicus of 1670, held that miracles are not merely unbelievable but impossible. His reasoning, reconstructed fairly, runs like this: the laws of nature are the eternal, necessary decrees of God; whatever happens follows necessarily from those laws; therefore an event contrary to the laws of nature would be an event contrary to God’s own nature, which is absurd. Spinoza states it without flinching: “Nothing, then, comes to pass in nature in contravention to her universal laws, nay, everything agrees with them and follows from them, for whatsoever comes to pass, comes to pass by the will and eternal decree of God.”3 He concludes that “a miracle, whether in contravention to, or beyond, nature, is a mere absurdity.”4

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: Spinoza: Miracles as an Absurdity
text: Stated at full strength, the argument has real force: if the laws of nature genuinely are immutable and inviolable, then by definition nothing can violate them, and a miracle so defined is a contradiction in terms—like a married bachelor. One cannot simply wave this away.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: Spinoza: Miracles as an Absurdity
text: But it does not survive inspection, for two reasons. First, and fatally, it begs the question by definition. Spinoza builds inviolability into the meaning of “law of nature” and then discovers, unsurprisingly, that laws cannot be violated. But whether the regularities of nature are absolutely immutable—impervious even to their Author—is precisely what is in dispute. Define laws as descriptions of nature’s ordinary course, and the argument evaporates: a description of what usually happens is not breached by an unusual act, any more than the outfielder breaches gravity. Second, Spinoza’s conclusion was already contained in his metaphysics. He was a pantheist who famously identified God with Nature itself—Deus sive Natura, “God, or Nature”—so that there simply is no God who transcends the natural order and could act upon it from without.5 Given that God, miracles are indeed impossible; but that is not a discovery about miracles, it is a restatement of pantheism. Against a theist who affirms a transcendent Creator, Spinoza’s argument has no purchase; it refutes a position no theist holds.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: Hume: Miracles as Never Credible
text: The argument that actually shapes the modern mind is subtler, and more formidable. David Hume, in Section X of his Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), conceded the ground Spinoza had over-claimed. He did not try to prove miracles impossible. He argued instead that no testimony could ever make belief in one reasonable—an epistemological argument, not a metaphysical one, and all the stronger for its restraint.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: Hume: Miracles as Never Credible
text: Hume begins with a principle few would reject: “A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.”6 He then defines a miracle as “a violation of the laws of nature” and presses the consequence: “and as a firm and unalterable experience has established these laws, the proof against a miracle, from the very nature of the fact, is as entire as any argument from experience can possibly be imagined.”7 The whole weight of human experience of nature’s regularity stands, he says, against any report of its breach: “as a uniform experience amounts to a proof, there is here a direct and full proof, from the nature of the fact, against the existence of any miracle.”8 From this he draws his celebrated maxim, offered in Part II as “a general maxim worthy of our attention”: “That no testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle, unless the testimony be of such a kind, that its falsehood would be more miraculous, than the fact, which it endeavours to establish.”9 In practice, Hume thought, such testimony never arrives; the witnesses to miracles are too few, too credulous, too eager, and too apt to found new religions, for their falsehood ever to be more astonishing than the wonder they report.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: Hume: Miracles as Never Credible
text: This is a genuinely powerful argument, and it deserves to be felt before it is answered. It appeals to the same evidential caution that makes us doubt a tabloid headline; it does not deny God or the possibility of the supernatural outright; and it seems only to ask the believer to be consistent about weighing evidence. It has persuaded serious philosophers ever since, and any reply that treats it as foolish has not understood it.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: Where Hume’s Argument Breaks Down
text: Yet for all its polish, the argument fails—and it fails in three distinct places.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: Where Hume’s Argument Breaks Down
text: First, the premise that the evidence for the regular is always greater than the evidence for the rare is simply false. A single well-attested, unrepeatable event can be rationally believed on adequate testimony; the frequency of an event and the strength of the evidence for it are two different things. We accept, on good testimony, that a particular golfer once made a hole-in-one, without demanding that he repeat it, and without weighing against his witnesses the countless times balls have not gone in. More tellingly, the naturalist’s own worldview affirms events believed to have happened exactly once—the origin of the universe and the origin of life among them. These are, on the standard scientific picture, unrepeated and in some sense unrepeatable; yet no one thinks it irrational to believe they occurred. If unique events can be rationally believed elsewhere, Hume’s blanket rule cannot be right. The Humean will reply that a miracle is not merely rare but contrary to the whole uniform run of experience—a stronger charge than mere infrequency. But that objection was met above: a miracle introduces a new cause into the ordinary course of things; it does not breach the regularity that holds when nothing interferes, and so it does not carry the maximally low prior the objection assumes.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: Where Hume’s Argument Breaks Down
text: Second, on its strongest reading the argument argues in a circle. Hume’s claim that “a firm and unalterable experience” stands against every miracle assumes what it needs to prove. How could one know that experience is uniformly against miracles unless one already knew that every miracle report, past and present, is false? But that is the very conclusion in question. C. S. Lewis pressed exactly this point: if we assume in advance that all reports of miracles are false, then of course experience is uniform against them—but we are then reasoning in a circle, having smuggled the conclusion into the premise.10 To label experience “uniform” is not to report a finding; it is to prejudge every disputed case at once.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: Where Hume’s Argument Breaks Down
text: Third, the argument weighs the evidence the wrong way. Hume, in effect, piles the entire mass of ordinary experience against the specific testimony for a specific event, and concludes the testimony must lose. But that is not how rational assessment of a particular claim works. The right method is not to add up how often the extraordinary fails to happen, but to weigh the specific evidence for this claim—the number, independence, and reliability of the witnesses, their access to the facts, their motives. Here the most striking witness is not an apologist at all. John Earman, a distinguished philosopher of science and no friend of theism, subjected Hume’s essay to a rigorous probabilistic (Bayesian) analysis in a study pointedly titled Hume’s Abject Failure. Earman concludes that Hume’s argument, where it is original, is largely without merit, and that Hume overlooked how multiple independent witnesses can, in principle, make even a highly improbable event credible.11 That verdict, from a secular philosopher of the first rank, is worth more than a shelf of sympathetic defenders.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: The State of the Scholarship
text: It would be triumphalist, and false, to say the debate is over. Hume’s essay remains one of the most discussed pieces in the philosophy of religion, and it retains able defenders. J. L. Mackie, in The Miracle of Theism, offered a careful reconstruction of Hume’s reasoning and judged that the balance of probability will almost always lie against accepting a miracle report—a serious case, honestly made, that any responsible treatment must reckon with.12 The live dispute is not whether miracles are worth taking seriously as a concept—that much is now widely granted—but how to weigh testimony for extraordinary events, and how high the prior improbability of a miracle should be set.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: The State of the Scholarship
text: What has genuinely shifted is the collapse of the confident a priori dismissal. Richard Swinburne’s work argued decades ago that there is no good reason to rule out miracles in advance and that historical evidence for them can carry real weight.13 And the weight of recent scholarship, reflected in reference surveys of the field, is that Hume’s argument does not establish its sweeping conclusion; even critics of miracles increasingly rest their case on the assessment of particular evidence rather than on Hume’s general maxim.14 The center of gravity has moved from “miracles are impossible or never believable” to “let us look at the evidence in each case”—which is exactly where the honest inquirer wanted the conversation to be.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not Establish
text: The argument of this essay is a door-opener, not a proof. It does not show that God exists—that case is made elsewhere, from the beginning of the universe, its fine-tuning, and the moral law. It does not show that any miracle has occurred. It certainly does not show that the resurrection happened; that is a historical claim, to be tested by the ordinary evidence of the empty tomb, the early creed, and the transformed witnesses.15 What it establishes is this and only this: neither Spinoza nor Hume has given a sound in-principle reason to refuse the evidence a hearing. Spinoza’s argument begs the question and presupposes a pantheism no theist accepts; Hume’s rests on a false premise, a hidden circle, and a mistaken method of weighing.

title: Can Miracles Happen? Answering Hume and Spinoza
section: Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not Establish
text: If God exists, miracles are possible; if miracles are possible, then whether one occurred is a question for the evidence, not for a rule laid down in advance. The believer need not claim more than that—and need not claim less. The courtroom that fixes its verdict before hearing the witnesses is not being rigorous; it is being closed. The reasonable thing, and the honest thing, is to unbar the door and let the testimony be heard. Those wishing to press on to the historical case will find it taken up in the companion essays on the minimal facts of the resurrection and the empty tomb.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
text: In the garden of Gethsemane, on the last free night of his life, Jesus of Nazareth fell on his face and prayed: “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). It is one of the most searching scenes in all of Scripture—the Son of God in anguish, sweating as it were great drops of blood, asking for another way and then surrendering his will to his Father’s. And it raises a question that, once you see it, you cannot un-see: to whom is he praying?

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
text: For most Christians the answer is obvious: the Son is speaking to the Father.
