But there is an old and earnest tradition, rejected by the church since the third century, that cannot accept that answer at face value—because it holds that the Father and the Son are not two who can speak to one another, but one and the same divine person wearing two different faces. This is modalism, and the question of Gethsemane is, in miniature, the whole argument between it and the historic faith.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: What Modalism Claims
text: Modalism is the teaching that God is a single divine person who is revealed in three modes, roles, or manifestations. Its ancient forms were usually pictured as successive—as Father in creation and the giving of the law, as Son in redemption, and as Holy Spirit in the life of the church—while its leading modern theologian, David Bernard, holds that the one omnipresent God can manifest himself in all three at once. On either view there are not three who are God; there is one who is God, appearing under three titles—as a single actor might play three parts, or as one man may be at once a father to his children, a son to his parents, and a husband to his wife.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: What Modalism Claims
text: The motive behind the view should be stated accurately: modalism is trying to guard the oneness of God. The Shema of Israel is uncompromising—“Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4)—and modalists fear that talk of three persons smuggles in a second and third God by the back door. They would rather say there is one God, full stop, who has worn three masks across the drama of salvation. That instinct—jealousy for monotheism—is not a vice. It is half of the truth the doctrine of the Trinity is built to protect.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: What Modalism Claims
text: The historic church has nonetheless judged modalism to be a serious error, and given it a string of names. In the early centuries it was called monarchianism (from the concern to protect God’s sole monarchia, his single rule), and more specifically modalistic monarchianism or Sabellianism, after Sabellius, a teacher active in Rome in the early third century. Because it makes the Father the one who suffers on the cross—there being no distinct Son to do the suffering—it also earned the mocking label Patripassianism: “the Father suffers.”1

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: What Modalism Claims
text: We know the early modalists mostly through their opponents, which calls for some caution about details. Noetus of Smyrna and a figure named Praxeas taught, according to the church fathers, that the Father himself was born of the virgin and suffered on the cross. The decisive early reply came from Tertullian of Carthage, whose treatise Against Praxeas (c. AD 210–213) is one of the first sustained defenses of trinitarian distinctions. Tertullian’s verdict was withering: “By this Praxeas did a twofold service for the devil at Rome: he drove away prophecy, and he brought in heresy; he put to flight the Paraclete, and he crucified the Father.”2 It was Tertullian who gave Latin theology its enduring formula—one substance, three persons (una substantia, tres personae)—and who insisted the three are distinct “not in condition, but in degree＊Order, not rankIs sayingTertullian's word is gradus, “step” or order: the persons are distinct in their order of relation (Father, Son, Spirit) within one substance.Not sayingNot that the Son or Spirit is God to a lesser degree. The creedal faith this essay defends holds the three co-equal and co-eternal, one in substance and power.; not in substance, but in form” (Against Praxeas 2).3 Sabellius was excommunicated at Rome around AD 220, and modalism was repudiated across the church well before the Councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381) gave the Trinity its creedal shape.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: What Modalism Claims
text: Modalism is not merely a museum piece. Its largest modern form is Oneness Pentecostalism, which emerged out of the “New Issue” controversy among American Pentecostals around 1913–1916, when some came to baptize converts “in the name of Jesus” alone rather than with the triune formula of Matthew 28:19. The movement’s largest body is the United Pentecostal Church International (UPCI), and its most influential systematic theologian is David K. Bernard, the UPCI’s general superintendent, whose book The Oneness of God (1983) is the standard scholarly statement of the position.4

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: What Modalism Claims
text: It is worth being precise and fair about what Bernard and the UPCI actually hold, because Oneness theology is more nuanced than its caricature. Bernard affirms one God, the absolute deity of Jesus Christ, and rejects the charge that he denies the threeness of biblical language. His claim is that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are real and meaningful—but as “manifestations, modes, offices, or relationships” of the one God, not as three distinct persons.5 Crucially, Bernard locates the deity of the Son in the indwelling Father: “the Son” refers to God-as-incarnate, while the prayers and submissions of Jesus express the relationship of his genuine humanity to the deity dwelling in him. It is held by many people who are sincere and devout, and it should be engaged, not sneered at (1 Peter 3:15) — engaged, that is, as the serious error the rest of this essay shows it to be.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: The Texts Oneness Believers Press
text: The Oneness case is built from Scripture, and a fair hearing means stating its best texts at full strength before answering them.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: The Texts Oneness Believers Press
text: The absolute deity of Jesus. Oneness theology leans first on passages that exalt Christ as fully God. “In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9). If all the fullness of deity is in Jesus, the argument runs, what is left over to be a separate person called the Father? Add Isaiah’s great messianic oracle: the child to be born is called “Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6). Here, the Oneness reader says, the Son is named Father outright—Scripture itself collapses the distinction.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: The Texts Oneness Believers Press
text: The unity sayings of John. Then come Jesus’ own words. “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). And to Philip: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father… Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John 14:9–10). On the Oneness reading these are not careful statements of two-in-one-essence; they are plain identifications. To see Jesus is to see the Father, because Jesus simply is the Father made visible.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: The Texts Oneness Believers Press
text: The one name in baptism. Finally, the baptismal evidence. Jesus commands baptism “in the name”—singular—“of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). Yet the apostles, who heard that command, baptized “in the name of Jesus Christ” (Acts 2:38; cf. 8:16; 10:48; 19:5). For Bernard the conclusion is irresistible: the single name behind the three titles is Jesus, because Father, Son, and Spirit are one God whose saving name is Jesus.6 This is the steelman, stated at full strength so that it can be answered at full strength.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: The Biblical Case for Three Distinct Persons
text: The historic reply does not retreat one inch on the points modalism cares about. Orthodoxy insists, with the Nicene Creed, on one God, and on the full and equal deity of the Son and the Spirit—“true God from true God.” Both sides confess one God and call Jesus God — but Oneness locates the deity of the Son in the indwelling Father, so that “the Son” refers to God-as-incarnate. The real question is whether the one God is a single person or three coequal, coeternal persons who share one undivided being. And here the texts that resist modalism are not a verse or two but the structure of the New Testament itself.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: The Biblical Case for Three Distinct Persons
text: Begin where modalism is weakest: scenes in which all three are on stage simultaneously. At Jesus’ baptism, the Son comes up out of the water, the Spirit descends upon him like a dove, and a voice comes from heaven—“This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:16–17). Three distinct presences, at one moment, with one of them speaking about another. A single actor can change masks between scenes; he cannot wear all three at once and converse across them. Successive modes cannot share one scene; persons can act together. Modern Oneness theology replies that the omnipresent God can manifest himself in heaven, in the dove, and in the man Jesus at once. But omnipresence explains how one person can be in three places, not how he can address himself: one person cannot, in the same moment, speak from heaven to another as “my beloved Son” and be the Son who is spoken of—three in relationship, not one in three places. And manifestation cannot absorb John 17: the glory the Son “had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5) was not a manifestation to anyone.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: The Biblical Case for Three Distinct Persons
text: The deepest evidence is the prayer life of Jesus, of which Gethsemane is the sharpest case. “Not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39) is a real will yielded to another real will＊Distinct persons, one divine willIs sayingThe incarnate Son, a person truly distinct from the Father, genuinely submits — the whole point against modalism: Father and Son are not one person wearing masks.Not sayingNot that the Father and Son are two separate divine wills, still less two gods. The one God has one undivided will; in Gethsemane it is the Son's genuine human will freely yielding to the divine will he eternally shares with the Father.. The Oneness reply, which we should answer rather than caricature, is that the genuine human nature of Jesus is here addressing the deity indwelling him—flesh speaking to the Spirit within a single person. The decisive answer is the high-priestly prayer of John 17, because it reaches behind the incarnation altogether. There the petitioner asks for “the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5), and says “you loved me before the foundation of the world” (John 17:24). The one praying speaks of a relationship that obtained before any human nature existed to do the addressing—so the petitioner cannot be the human nature speaking to the indwelling deity; he is the pre-existent divine Son, asking the Father to restore a shared glory the two of them knew before creation. Love between Father and Son before the world began is not a manifestation to anyone; it is eternal interpersonal fact—the very thing a mode can never be. Oneness teachers reply that this glory existed only in God’s plan. But Jesus does not say he was foreknown; he says he had glory “with you” before the world existed (John 17:5)—a shared possession, not a place in a plan. (The phrase “before the foundation of the world” in 17:24 is used elsewhere of God’s foreknowing purpose—Ephesians 1:4; 1 Peter 1:20—so the weight rests on 17:5.)

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: The Biblical Case for Three Distinct Persons
text: Jesus himself counts persons. Challenged on whether his self-testimony is valid, he appeals to the Mosaic law that requires two witnesses: “I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me” (John 8:17–18). On the modalist accounting—one person in two roles—that is a single witness testifying twice, and Jesus’ own argument collapses. It works only if Father and Son are genuinely two. (If the reply is that the two are Jesus’ deity and his humanity, the law Jesus invokes counts the testimony of two people (John 8:17)—and natures do not testify; persons do.) The Father also speaks to the Son and of the Son—at the transfiguration, and at “Father, glorify your name,” answered by a voice from heaven (John 12:28).

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: The Biblical Case for Three Distinct Persons
text: Finally, the sending of the Spirit. Jesus promises “another Helper” (John 14:16). The Greek is allos, which often (though not always, in New Testament Greek) means another of the same kind—and the context bears that out: the Spirit teaches, reminds, and bears witness as Jesus did (John 14:26; 15:26). The Son will ask the Father, and the Father will give the Spirit; later the Son himself sends the Spirit “from the Father” (John 15:26). A king does not petition himself to send himself, and a mode is not “another” Helper at all. The grammar of sending presupposes a sender and a sent who are distinct. So too the risen Christ stands “at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:55–56), where Stephen sees not one but two—Jesus standing beside the glory of God. A right hand requires someone whose right hand it is.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: Answering the Oneness Texts
text: None of the strong Oneness texts, read in context, actually requires modalism—and several positively resist it.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: Answering the Oneness Texts
text: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). The word for “one” here is neuter (hen), not masculine (heis). Jesus does not say “the Father and I are one person”; he says we are one thing—one in unity, power, and purpose. This is exactly how the church has always read it: a statement of shared being between two who are distinct, not of identity. And the immediate context confirms it—a verse earlier Jesus distinguishes “my Father, who has given them to me” from himself (John 10:29).

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: Answering the Oneness Texts
text: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). The next verse interprets it: “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 14:10). Seeing the Son reveals the Father not because the Son is the Father but because of their mutual indwelling—the Son is the perfect image and revelation of the Father (cf. Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:3). Crucially, the very same discourse has the Son praying to the Father, being sent by the Father, and returning to the Father. A reading of John 14:9 that erases the distinction cannot survive its own chapter.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: Answering the Oneness Texts
text: “Everlasting Father” (Isaiah 9:6). The Hebrew is ’abi·‘ad, literally “Father of eternity.” In Semitic idiom “father of X” commonly means the source, possessor, or characteristic bearer of X—as Jabal is “the father of those who dwell in tents” (Genesis 4:20), and as Eliakim the steward is to be “a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem” (Isaiah 22:21) without being their parent. The title casts the Messiah as the eternal one, the fatherly source and everlasting protector of his people—a role-title in a list of role-titles (“Wonderful Counselor,” “Prince of Peace”).7 It names what the Son is to his people, not which person he is. Trinitarian theology has always held that the three persons share every divine perfection—eternity included—while remaining distinct persons.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: Answering the Oneness Texts
text: “The fullness of deity” (Colossians 2:9). This text the orthodox affirm without reservation: Jesus is fully and completely God. But “in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” tells us that Christ lacks nothing of Godhood; it does not tell us that there is no distinct person of the Father. The full deity of the Son is precisely what Nicaea defends—and the same Paul who wrote Colossians 2:9 opened the letter by thanking “God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Colossians 1:3).

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: Answering the Oneness Texts
text: Baptism in Jesus’ name (Acts 2:38). The Oneness case leans hardest on this text, so it needs a full answer. “In the name of Jesus Christ” in Acts is most naturally read not as a liturgical formula competing with Matthew 28:19 but as a description of Christian baptism—baptism into allegiance to Jesus as Lord, marking converts off from John’s baptism and from the synagogue. Luke records varied wording (“in the name of the Lord Jesus,” “in the name of Jesus Christ”), which tells against a fixed verbal formula. And the inference Oneness draws—that Father, Son, and Spirit are therefore one person—simply does not follow: that three share one name can equally express the unity of three persons in one God, which is how the church has always read Jesus’ striking singular “in the name” in Matthew 28:19.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: The Strongest Objection, and the Honest Reply
text: The deepest Oneness challenge is not exegetical but theological, and it should be given in its most pointed form. It runs: be honest—three persons who love one another, send one another, and submit to one another are three gods by any working definition. Oneness took the Shema seriously; you embroidered it. Your “distinct persons” always slides, in practice, into tritheism. This is a serious objection, and it must not be waved away. Its ablest contemporary exponent, the analytic philosopher Dale Tuggy (author of the “Trinity” entry in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy), presses a version of it not toward Oneness modalism but toward a strict unitarianism in which God is the Father alone—which is a reminder that whatever answers the “three gods” charge must not, in doing so, collapse the three back into one person.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: The Strongest Objection, and the Honest Reply
text: The reply turns on what actually makes for many gods. Polytheism counts gods by separable essences—Zeus and Poseidon are two because they have two distinct natures, two wills, divisible turf, and can act against one another. The persons of the Trinity have one undivided divine essence, one will, one power; nothing is parceled out among them. This is why the church rejected tritheism wherever it appeared, and why the Athanasian Creed insists on “neither confounding the persons, nor dividing the substance.” The Son is not a second instance of deity; he is the one God, eternally the Son. To refute modalism by drifting into tritheism would simply trade one error for its opposite—and the same Scripture that forbids collapsing the persons forbids dividing the being. The reply here answers the tritheism charge, not the further philosophical puzzle of how one being is three persons—which the essay concedes below it does not claim to dissolve.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: The Strongest Objection, and the Honest Reply
text: Here the deepest cost of modalism comes into view, and it is not arithmetic but the gospel. Scripture reveals that God did not become loving when he made the world: “God is love” (1 John 4:8), and the Father loved the Son “before the foundation of the world” (John 17:24), in the glory the Son “had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5). The Trinity lets those texts stand together, so that God’s love neither waits on creation nor divides the God who is one; modalism has no eternal Beloved to point to. And the salvation the gospel offers is precisely adoption into that communion—to be brought, by the Spirit, into the Son’s relationship with the Father (Romans 8:15–17; John 17:21). On the modalist account there is no eternal Father–Son communion to be brought into. In saving the oneness, modalism spends the relationship that the gospel exists to share.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: The State of the Question
text: Among historians and theologians across the confessional spectrum—Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant—there is no live dispute that modalism falls outside Nicene orthodoxy; that judgment was settled in the third and fourth centuries and has never been seriously reopened. The genuinely live conversation is elsewhere. First, there is real and respectful scholarly engagement between trinitarian and Oneness Pentecostal theologians—seen in the official Oneness–Trinitarian Pentecostal Dialogue (2002–2007) sponsored by the Society for Pentecostal Studies, and in critical assessments by Gregory Boyd (a former Oneness believer) and others—over exegesis, church history, and what counts as biblical monotheism.8 Second, within orthodox theology itself there are vigorous debates about how to state the doctrine: how strongly to press the social-trinitarian language of three “centers of consciousness” (defended by Cornelius Plantinga and others) versus the classical-theist caution that such language risks the very tritheism modalism warns against. Critics of social trinitarianism—including Brian Leftow and Karen Kilby—argue that overemphasizing the distinctness of the persons concedes too much to the modalist’s complaint.9 That internal debate is healthy, and it shows the Oneness concern is taken seriously even by those who reject the Oneness conclusion.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: The State of the Question
text: Honesty also requires conceding what the Trinity does not claim to do. It does not dissolve the mystery. The doctrine states the data—one God, three distinct persons, full equality—and rules out the failed solutions (modalism on one side, tritheism and Arian subordinationism on the other); it does not pretend to comprehend how one being is three persons. The analogies all limp: water’s three states are actually modalism (the same water, usually one at a time); three men sharing humanity are actually tritheism. The orthodox confess a reality that exceeds every illustration, and they should say so plainly.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: Conclusion
text: Modalism holds fast to one true thing—that there is one God—and any answer that loses that truth, or the full deity of Jesus Christ, has answered badly. But both sides call Jesus God in different senses: Oneness locates the deity of the Son in the indwelling Father. So modalism is a serious error, as the historic church has judged. It secures the oneness at a price Scripture will not let it pay: it must turn the Son’s prayers into soliloquy, the Father’s voice at the Jordan into ventriloquism, and the eternal love of Father for Son into nothing at all. The biblical data are stubborn. Three are present at the baptism; the Son prays to the Father, real address to one who is really other; the Father bears witness as a second witness; the Spirit is sent, asked for, and given, “another” of the same kind.

title: Answering Modalism: One God in Three Persons
section: Conclusion
text: The doctrine of the Trinity does not invent these distinctions; it reads them off the page—while refusing, just as firmly, to let them multiply into three gods. One God, undivided in being; three coequal, coeternal, genuinely distinct persons, eternally in love. That is the needle modalism cannot thread and the gospel cannot do without. To the Oneness believer who fears for monotheism, the trinitarian says: your jealousy for the one God is honored, not abandoned—come and keep it, and keep the Father’s love for the Son as well.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
text: From 1941 through early 1944, a young Lithuanian Jew named Avraham Tory kept a secret diary in the Kovno ghetto — later buried in crates beneath an unfinished building and recovered after the war — recording what the Nazis were doing to his people. He did not write that the murders violated a German statute or offended his preferences. He wrote as though something had been broken in the fabric of the world itself — as though the killing of innocents was wrong whether or not anyone agreed. Most of us read such testimony and feel the same thing. We do not think the Holocaust was wrong for the Allies and acceptable for the SS. We think it was simply, objectively wrong.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
text: That intuition is the engine of the moral argument for God's existence. The argument does not claim that unbelievers are wicked or that one must read Scripture to know that cruelty is evil. It asks a narrower and stranger question: if such moral facts are real — true independently of anyone's opinion — what kind of universe must we live in for that to be so?

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Argument and Its History
text: In its most widely circulated form, associated with the philosopher and apologist William Lane Craig, the argument is a tidy syllogism:

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Argument and Its History
text: 1. If God does not exist, objective moral values and duties do not exist.＊The ground of morality, not who is moralIs sayingThe claim is that objective moral duties — real obligations binding independently of human opinion — need a foundation beyond human preference; without God there is only opinion.Not sayingNot that atheists cannot be moral, cannot tell right from wrong, or are wicked. The essay affirms that unbelievers live morally and grasp that cruelty is evil. 2. Objective moral values and duties do exist. 3. Therefore, God exists.1

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Argument and Its History
text: It is valid: if both premises are true, the conclusion follows. Everything rides on the premises. Craig draws a useful distinction. Values concern what is good or bad; duties concern what is right or wrong — what we are obligated to do. And by objective he means, precisely, independent of human opinion.2 The claim is not that moral views vary across cultures (they do), but that beneath the variation some things are really, mind-independently wrong.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Argument and Its History
text: The argument is old. Immanuel Kant, in the Critique of Practical Reason (1788), argued that practical reason commits us to the "highest good" — perfect virtue crowned with proportionate happiness — and that since we are obligated to pursue it, we must postulate God and immortality as the conditions that make its realization possible. Kant was careful: he did not claim God is the basis of moral obligation, which for him rested on the autonomy of reason itself.3 The contemporary argument is bolder than Kant's, and its most sophisticated grounding comes not from Craig the popularizer but from the analytic philosopher Robert Merrihew Adams, whose 1999 book Finite and Infinite Goods is the scholarly anchor of the whole project.4

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: Premise 2: That Some Things Are Really Wrong
text: Begin with the second premise, which is in some ways the easier. Do objective moral values and duties exist?

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: Premise 2: That Some Things Are Really Wrong
text: Most people, on reflection, are far more certain that torturing a child for fun is wrong than they are of any philosophical theory that might be marshaled to deny it. This is the method of reflective intuition: just as we trust our sensory experience of the physical world absent a defeater, we are within our rights to trust our moral experience absent a defeater. We apprehend the wrongness of the Holocaust the way we apprehend the reality of the past — not by argument but by a basic, non-inferential moral perception.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: Premise 2: That Some Things Are Really Wrong
text: Philosophers have a name for a belief held this way: properly basic — accepted not on the basis of some prior argument but directly, as a deliverance of experience, the way we accept the reality of other minds or of the past. This is the epistemology of Alvin Plantinga's "reformed" tradition, and it reframes the burden of proof. As the atheist philosopher Louise Antony put it in her debate with Craig, any argument for moral skepticism will have to be built out of premises less obvious than the moral truths it is trying to deny — so the skeptic's footing is always less secure than the conviction he means to unseat. One would have to be more certain of a clever theory than of the wrongness of torturing a child, and few honest people are.5

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: Premise 2: That Some Things Are Really Wrong
text: The reality this premise names is not only a philosopher's abstraction; it presses hardest exactly where evil is most concrete. C. S. Lewis, looking back on his years as an atheist, noticed that his strongest argument against God — that the universe is cruel and unjust — had quietly assumed the very thing it denied: "a man does not call a line crooked unless he has some idea of a straight line" (Mere Christianity, Book II, ch. 1). To condemn the world as unjust is already to measure it against a real standard of justice that does not bend to anyone's opinion. Few have pressed that point more unforgettably than Rachael Denhollander, the first of the many women and girls to testify against the sports physician Larry Nassar. Facing him at his 2018 sentencing, she said she could name what he had done evil "because the straight line exists" — "not measured based on your perception… nor mine" — and on that same ground she both asked the court for its fullest justice and offered him forgiveness. Neither the condemnation nor the mercy would have meant anything if the wrong had not been objectively, mind-independently real. That is premise 2 spoken from inside one of the worst places a person can stand — and it is the same standard the argument from evil leans on when it presses the reality of suffering against belief in God.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: Premise 2: That Some Things Are Really Wrong
text: This is not a uniquely religious claim. It is shared by a large camp of secular moral realists — philosophers like Erik Wielenberg, Russ Shafer-Landau, and David Enoch — who agree wholeheartedly that some acts are objectively evil. So premise 2 is, if anything, common ground. The interesting fight is over premise 1: granting that morality is objective, what grounds it?

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: Premise 1: What Grounds the Moral Law?
text: Here we must be scrupulously clear, because this is where the argument is most often caricatured. The claim is not that atheists cannot be good, cannot know right from wrong, or lack moral sincerity. They plainly can and do — often putting believers to shame. The claim is about ontology: about what, at the deepest level, makes moral facts true. An atheist can read the moral law as fluently as anyone; the question is who, if anyone, wrote it.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: Premise 1: What Grounds the Moral Law?
text: The theist's answer comes in two layers. Values are grounded in God's own nature: God is not a being who happens to be good but Goodness itself — the standard, "the Good" in person, after which all finite goods are patterned. Duties arise from the commands that flow from that nature. This is the heart of Adams's modified divine command theory. In his 1973 essay "A Modified Divine Command Theory of Ethical Wrongness" and again in "Divine Command Metaethics Modified Again" (1979), Adams argued that moral wrongness consists in being contrary to the commands of a loving God — not the commands of just any conceivable deity.6 In Finite and Infinite Goods he developed the value side: finite things are good insofar as they resemble the infinite Good, which is God.7 On this picture, the moral order is neither an accident nor an invention but a reflection of the character of the One who is.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Euthyphro Dilemma
text: No discussion is honest without Plato's ancient trap. In the Euthyphro, Socrates asks: is the holy loved by the gods because it is holy, or holy because the gods love it? Translated to monotheism: Is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good?

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Euthyphro Dilemma
text: Both horns wound. Grab the first — good because commanded — and morality looks arbitrary: had God commanded gratuitous cruelty, cruelty would be good, which seems monstrous. Grab the second — commanded because good — and goodness is a standard above God, to which even He answers; God becomes a moral middleman, and the atheist's question returns: why not skip God and go straight to the standard?

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Euthyphro Dilemma
text: The standard theistic reply, sharpened by Adams and others, is that the dilemma is false because it omits a third option. God neither invents the good by fiat nor consults a standard outside Himself. God's own necessary nature is the Good. His commands are not arbitrary, because they necessarily express His character — He cannot command gratuitous cruelty, not because a higher law forbids it, but because such a command would contradict what He essentially is. And the good is not independent of God, because it just is God's nature. The dilemma assumes the standard must be either God's will or something external; the theist locates it in God's being.8

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Euthyphro Dilemma
text: This is a strong reply, and it is the standard move among theists. But it is not cost-free, and honesty requires saying so. Critics such as Wes Morriston (“God and the Ontological Foundation of Morality,” Religious Studies 48, no. 1 [2012]: 15–34) press that "God's nature is the Good" may quietly relocate rather than dissolve the dilemma: why is God's nature good? If the answer is "because being loving, just, and so on is good," then goodness seems definable apart from God after all; if the answer is "because it is God's nature," the charge of arbitrariness creeps back in.9 The theist can respond that "good" and "God's nature" are necessarily, not contingently, identical — like "water" and "H₂O" — so the question "why is God's nature good?" is as confused as "why is water H₂O?" The exchange continues; it is live, not settled.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Strongest Objection: Wielenberg's Godless Normative Realism
text: The most formidable secular challenge today comes from Erik Wielenberg of DePauw University, who debated Craig in 2018. In Robust Ethics: The Metaphysics and Epistemology of Godless Normative Realism (Oxford, 2014), Wielenberg argues that objective moral truths exist as brute, necessary, non-natural facts — they require no foundation outside themselves, God included.10 Moral properties, on his view, are objective, non-natural, irreducible, and causally inert; that "torturing the innocent for fun is wrong" is simply a necessary truth, true in every possible world, full stop.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Strongest Objection: Wielenberg's Godless Normative Realism
text: Let us steelman this. Wielenberg presses a tu quoque the theist must feel. The theist says, "moral values are grounded in God's nature, and that's where explanation stops." Wielenberg says, "moral values are grounded in necessary moral facts, and that's where explanation stops." Both bottom out in something brute and unexplained. If the theist may help himself to God as a necessary stopping point, why may the atheist not help himself to moral facts as necessary stopping points? Indeed, Wielenberg argues, his view is more economical — one fewer entity.11

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Strongest Objection: Wielenberg's Godless Normative Realism
text: The theist's honest reply is twofold. First, on parsimony: a single personal ground (God) that unifies values, duties, moral knowledge, and the obligatory force of morality may explain more than a sprawling plurality of free-floating ethical facts — and explanatory power, not bare entity-counting, is the right measure. Second, and more pointedly, it is hard to see how an impersonal, causally inert fact could generate a genuine obligation or accountability. Duties seem to be owed to someone; commands require a commander. Wielenberg's reply — that obligations can be grounded in the value of persons without a commander — is serious, and the theist grants that his account is internally consistent. What the theist claims is not that Wielenberg's view is incoherent but that it is less explanatorily satisfying: it asks us to accept obligations that float, owed to no one. Reasonable philosophers disagree about whether that cost is fatal. This is the honest state of the debate: on a bare count of entities Wielenberg's ledger is shorter — a point apologists too rarely concede — but that is the wrong ledger, because a free-floating fact owed to no one cannot generate the very thing morality is: an obligation, owed to someone, for which we can be held to account.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Darwinian Dilemma — Which Cuts Both Ways
text: A second objection targets premise 2 by attacking our access to moral truth. In her landmark paper "A Darwinian Dilemma for Realist Theories of Value" (Philosophical Studies 127, 2006, pp. 109–166), Sharon Street argues that our moral intuitions were shaped by natural selection to promote reproductive fitness, not to track mind-independent moral truth.12 If so, the realist faces a dilemma: either deny that evolution shaped our values (empirically untenable) or admit it did, in which case the staggering coincidence that fitness-tracking intuitions also happen to track moral reality cries out for an explanation the realist cannot give. Our confident sense that the Holocaust was evil might be just a well-engineered survival heuristic.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Darwinian Dilemma — Which Cuts Both Ways
text: Two things must be said. First — and this is crucial — Street's argument is not an argument for theism; she is herself an anti-realist, and her dagger is aimed at secular moral realism above all. It therefore wounds Wielenberg at least as badly as it wounds anyone, since his causally inert moral facts cannot have shaped our evolving brains. Second, the theist has a reply ready to hand: a God who designed our cognitive faculties to apprehend the moral order He authored gives a non-coincidental reason why our intuitions track truth. (Wielenberg himself answers Street with a "third-factor" account, on which our faculties both track moral facts and help explain why those facts are instantiated; so the honest claim is not that no secular reply exists, but that a designing mind explains the fit more economically.) That is a point in theism's favor. But candor demands the concession that the theist who leans on this reply has not proved moral realism; he has shown that if realism is true, theism explains our access to it better than naturalism does. The realism itself still rests on the intuition of premise 2 — an intuition the debunker has at least dented.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Darwinian Dilemma — Which Cuts Both Ways
text: Two further replies are worth adding. First, the debunker's empirical premise — that our specifically moral beliefs were fixed by natural selection — is shakier than it is usually made to sound. The biologist Jeffrey Schloss, reviewing the evolutionary literature, finds robust accounts of cooperative behaviors but no settled account of our moral beliefs, and least of all of costly altruism toward those who can never repay us.13 Second, pressed to its limit the debunking strategy consumes itself: if natural selection tuned our faculties for survival rather than truth, that verdict engulfs every belief we hold — including belief in evolutionary naturalism itself. This is the nerve of Plantinga's evolutionary argument against naturalism — a reply his critics vigorously contest, but one that turns the debunker's own premise back on him; the theist, at least, holds that God fashioned our minds to find the truth, moral truth included.14

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Is/Ought Firewall: Can Nature Tell Us to Protect the Weak?
text: There is a sharper, more unsettling form of premise 1 that the abstract debate with Wielenberg can obscure. Set the metaphysics aside for a moment and ask a blunter question: does the natural world, on its own, give us any reason to protect the weak at all? The most honest answer came from a thinker who despised the Christian one. Friedrich Nietzsche saw with perfect clarity that the ethic of compassion — the conviction that a society is measured by how it treats its weakest — is not what nature teaches. In The Anti-Christ he wrote that "pity thwarts the whole law of evolution, which is the law of natural selection," and laid it down as a first principle that "the weak and the botched shall perish… and one should help them to it."15 This is precisely the view the moral argument exists to reject — but Nietzsche states it without flinching, where gentler naturalists look away, and that candor is worth learning from.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Is/Ought Firewall: Can Nature Tell Us to Protect the Weak?
text: For in one narrow sense he was right: protecting the weak is "anti-nature," a standing rebellion against the logic of selection. His error was not the description but the inference — the silent leap from is to ought. That natural selection describes what tends to happen, the strong outlasting the weak, is a fact about biology. That we therefore ought to help the weak perish is not a fact about biology at all; it is a value smuggled in under cover of the description. David Hume named the fallacy: no catalogue of what is the case, however complete, entails by itself a single claim about what we ought to do. Nature can tell us what survives; it is silent on what deserves to. To read any command out of the bare process — whether Nietzsche's command to let the weak perish, or our own conviction that we must never — is to appeal to a standard the process itself does not contain.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: The Is/Ought Firewall: Can Nature Tell Us to Protect the Weak?
text: And that is the point. Nearly everyone, believer and atheist alike, holds with deep conviction that the weak do have a claim on the strong — that the child, the disabled, and the dying are owed care precisely when they can offer nothing in return. Yet that conviction cannot be read off nature, because nature, left to itself, points the other way. It requires a standard above the natural order — which is just what premise 1 asserts: real duties, binding on us regardless of what survival would counsel, need a ground beyond the world of fact. Here the argument leans on no contested intuition; it rests on the firewall between fact and value that Hume made explicit — the very firewall Nietzsche, no friend of theism, breached at exactly the cost this section has traced. What it points to is still thin — a moral order that transcends nature, not yet the God of the creeds — but it is a real signpost, and it points up.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: What the Argument Does, and Does Not, Establish
text: Suppose the argument succeeds. What has been shown? Not the Trinity, not the resurrection, not the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in any detail. The conclusion is thinner: there exists a transcendent ground of objective morality — a moral lawgiver whose nature is the Good. That is a long way from the full Christian God, and the careful defender says so plainly. The moral argument is one strand in a cumulative case; it points toward a personal, good, necessary being, and leaves to other arguments — cosmological, historical, revelational — the work of filling in the portrait.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: What the Argument Does, and Does Not, Establish
text: Nor does the argument impugn the goodness of unbelievers. Let it be said once more, emphatically: atheists can be morally excellent, morally wise, and morally sincere. The question was never whether one can be good without believing in God, but what makes goodness real for believer and unbeliever alike. A child can read by sunlight without knowing what the sun is.

title: The Moral Argument for God: Where Do Right and Wrong Come From?
section: What the Argument Does, and Does Not, Establish
text: What remains, after every concession, is the original intuition — and its strange weight. When we say the murder of innocents is wrong, we mean it is wrong in a way that does not bend to opinion, culture, or power. The theist offers an account of why that should be so: because reality is, at its root, personal and good. The secular realist offers a rival account: because some truths simply are. Between these the argument does not coerce; it invites. As 1 Peter 3:15 counsels, the invitation is best extended "with gentleness and respect" — confident that the One who is the Good has nothing to fear from an honest question.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
text: Strip away every theological commitment, every confession of faith, and one stubborn question remains: can we know anything about Jesus of Nazareth as a figure of history? Skeptics have sometimes answered no — the Gospels, they say, are believing documents written by partisans, and partisans cannot be trusted. Yet most historians, including many who hold no religious faith, do think we can recover a historical core. One of the chief tools that made this possible is deceptively simple. It says: when the same fact about Jesus turns up in sources that did not copy from one another, that fact is harder to explain as later invention. This is the criterion of multiple attestation, and learning to use it well — knowing both its power and its real limits — is part of becoming a serious reader of the evidence.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: What the Criterion Claims
text: The principle is one historians use everywhere, not just in religious studies. If two reporters who never spoke to each other describe the same event, their agreement is unlikely to be a coincidence; the simplest explanation is that something happened. Applied to Jesus, the criterion holds that a saying or deed attested in two or more literarily independent sources is more likely to be historical than one found in a single source, because independent agreement pushes the tradition back behind both sources, toward a common origin.1

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: What the Criterion Claims
text: John P. Meier, whose multi-volume A Marginal Jew is the most exhaustive modern treatment, ranks multiple attestation as one of five "primary" criteria, alongside embarrassment, discontinuity, coherence, and Jesus' rejection and execution.2 He frames it as a question: is it more plausible that early Christians independently invented the same material in Mark, in the source called Q, in Paul, and in John — or that the material goes back to Jesus? Meier adds a refinement worth keeping: attestation can be multiple not only in sources but in forms — when a motif appears across different literary genres (parable, miracle story, aphorism, dispute), the independence is even harder to dismiss as a single source's editorial habit.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: What the Criterion Claims
text: The criterion did not fall from the sky. An early formal articulation is often credited to the Cambridge scholar F. C. Burkitt in his 1906 work The Gospel History and Its Transmission, at the close of the so-called "First Quest."3 It was developed further by C. H. Dodd in his work on the parables and Kingdom sayings, and it became a standard instrument of the "Second Quest" associated with Norman Perrin and others in the 1950s and 60s.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: The Independent Source Streams
text: The whole method depends on a prior, contestable judgment: which sources are actually independent? Here is where the criterion borrows from a century of source criticism. On the dominant "Two-Source" hypothesis, Mark is the earliest Gospel; Matthew and Luke each used Mark plus a second source of sayings, conventionally labeled Q (from the German Quelle, "source"); each evangelist also had material unique to him, called special-M (Matthew's own) and special-L (Luke's own). Many scholars treat John as drawing on traditions substantially independent of the Synoptics, though this is itself debated. To these literary streams scholars add the pre-Pauline traditions — creedal formulas and sayings Paul says he "received" and "passed on" (1 Corinthians 15:3–5; 11:23–25), which predate his letters of the 50s — and a handful of non-Christian sources, principally the Jewish historian Josephus and the Roman historian Tacitus.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: The Independent Source Streams
text: Independence is argued, never simply assumed. Where Matthew and Luke reproduce Mark almost verbatim, that is not independent attestation; it is copying. The criterion only does work where agreement cannot be explained by literary borrowing. This is why the most secure results come from material crossing genuinely separate streams — say, Mark and John, or the Synoptics and Paul, or Christian and non-Christian sources.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: The Independent Source Streams
text: That Jesus was crucified under the prefect Pontius Pilate is about as close to bedrock as ancient history offers. It is in Mark and the passion traditions behind all four Gospels; it is in the pre-Pauline confession Paul cites; and — crucially — it is in two hostile or neutral outside witnesses. The Roman senator Tacitus, writing around AD 116, reports that "Christus, from whom the name had its origin, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus."4 Josephus, in a passage whose Christian-sounding phrases are widely judged to be later additions but whose core most scholars accept, likewise records that Pilate condemned Jesus to the cross.5 A non-Christian Roman with no motive to flatter Christianity confirming the same execution that Christian creeds confess — that is multiple attestation across the widest possible independence.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: The Independent Source Streams
text: Whatever one concludes about the supernatural, the reputation of Jesus as a healer and exorcist is multiply attested to a striking degree. Healing and exorcism stories run through Mark, the Q material (the Beelzebul controversy, where Jesus is accused of casting out demons by the prince of demons, appears in what most scholars treat as independent Markan and Q forms — the so-called Mark-Q overlap, though the reality and extent of such overlaps is itself contested), special-M, special-L, and John, across narrative and saying alike. Even his opponents, on this evidence, did not deny the deeds — they reattributed them to dark powers, which is itself a backhanded form of attestation. Meier devotes a full volume to the miracle traditions, and a broad range of scholars — Meier, E. P. Sanders, Geza Vermes, Graham Twelftree, and the skeptic Bart Ehrman among them — agree that Jesus was, at minimum, widely regarded as a worker of cures and exorcisms in his own lifetime.6

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: The Independent Source Streams
text: Jesus' link to John the Baptist is attested in Mark, Q, John, and Josephus, who describes the Baptist independently of any Christian source.5 The disturbance Jesus caused in the Temple precincts is found in the Synoptics and, placed at a different point in the narrative, in John. E. P. Sanders built his influential reconstruction on a short list of facts he regarded as almost beyond dispute — including that Jesus was baptized by John, was a Galilean who preached and healed, caused a controversy in the Temple, and was crucified by Roman authority.7 These are not the conclusions of apologists; they are the working assumptions of mainstream, often secular, scholarship — and multiple attestation is part of why.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: Attestation Never Works Alone
text: Multiple attestation is one instrument in a set, and it is strongest when its findings are confirmed by the others. Two of Meier's five "primary" criteria work directly alongside it. The criterion of embarrassment asks whether a tradition would have been awkward or costly for the church that preserved it: material later Christians plausibly found awkward, yet kept anyway, is not easily explained as their own invention — though the criterion turns on our reconstructing what the earliest church found embarrassing, which we infer rather than read off the text. The criterion of coherence pulls in the opposite direction — once attestation and embarrassment have marked out a plausible, provisional core, sayings and deeds that sit naturally with that core gain some credibility by association, though this is the most circular move in the set, sound only insofar as the assumed core is.2 (The classic embarrassing data — Jesus' baptism by John, his shameful execution — are treated in the companion essay on his historicity.) Meier weighs a second, more cautious tier as well, among them the marks of a genuinely Palestinian environment: an Aramaic idiom showing through the Greek, or agricultural, legal, and village customs that had faded by the time the Gospels were written in the wider Greek-speaking world. Such traces point back toward the earliest layer, though Meier treats them as reinforcing a result already reached rather than proving one on their own.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: Attestation Never Works Alone
text: The most famous criterion is also the most treacherous, and honesty demands saying so before the critics do. The criterion of dissimilarity — Meier's discontinuity, revived within the new quest by Ernst Käsemann and given its systematic "double" form by Norman Perrin — counts a saying as authentic when it is unlike both the Judaism of Jesus' day and the emphases of the later church, on the reasoning that such material could have been borrowed from neither. Used to include, it has a modest place: a distinctive, unexpected datum unlike both settings is at least unlikely to be a mere borrowing — though even this use leans on a confident picture of both Judaism and the early church that we only partly possess. Used to exclude — as a filter that discards whatever Jesus shared with his contemporaries or handed on to his followers — it becomes the most criticized tool in the kit. Dissimilarity is one place the guild's turn against the criteria has concentrated its fire — but that turn, as the next section shows, indicts the whole toolkit, coherence and embarrassment included.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: The Turn Against the Criteria — Steelmanned
text: Here honesty requires a hard pivot. Over the last half-century, and intensely in the last fifteen years, the criteria of authenticity have come under sustained, learned attack from within the guild. A careful reader must hear these objections at full strength.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: The Turn Against the Criteria — Steelmanned
text: The earliest and still one of the sharpest came from the Cambridge scholar Morna D. Hooker. In two essays — "Christology and Methodology" (1971) and the pointedly titled "On Using the Wrong Tool" (1972) — she argued that the criteria cannot deliver what is asked of them. The materials, she insisted, are largely shaped by the scholar's own presuppositions rather than by objective tests.8 Her closing plea was for humility and tentativeness in all our conclusions. Hooker's point about discontinuity in particular is devastating: a criterion that counts as authentic only what is unlike both Judaism and the early church guarantees a Jesus with no real context and no real influence — an impossible figure.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: The Turn Against the Criteria — Steelmanned
text: The more recent and systematic critique appears in the 2012 volume Jesus, Criteria, and the Demise of Authenticity, edited by Chris Keith and Anthony Le Donne.9 Keith's argument is genealogical: the criteria were forged as tools of form criticism, which assumed the Gospels could be peeled apart layer by layer to isolate the earliest stratum.10 But, he argues, the form-critical model has collapsed, and you cannot keep using a tool while rejecting the workbench it was built for. More deeply, the critics deny that we can cleanly separate "authentic" tradition from the interpretation of the early church, because the only Jesus we have is already a remembered, interpreted Jesus — there is no uninterpreted bedrock beneath the layers to be excavated.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: The Turn Against the Criteria — Steelmanned
text: This dovetails with the social- or collective-memory school and the work of Dale C. Allison Jr., whose Constructing Jesus (2010) draws on memory research showing that memory is reconstructive, selective, and prone to conflation.11 Allison's response is telling: he largely de-emphasizes the attempt to authenticate individual sayings, which he regards as unreliable, and instead asks what recurrent patterns and overall impressions the sources press upon us.11 If the tradition has reshaped the details, no criterion can reliably reverse-engineer the original words from a single pericope.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: The Turn Against the Criteria — Steelmanned
text: The force of the cumulative objection is this: multiple attestation can tell you a motif is early and widespread, but earliness is not the same as historicity. A misunderstanding, a community's theological conviction, or a popular legend could circulate widely and independently within a generation. Attestation counts the witnesses; it does not interrogate them.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: The Considered Reply
text: What should be conceded, should be conceded plainly. The critics are right that no criterion is a "precision tool" that mechanically sifts authentic from inauthentic. They are right that the discontinuity criterion is badly flawed, that all our sources are interpreted, and that the older dream of excavating bare facts beneath the theology was naïve. The most defensible position today is not to crown multiple attestation as decisive.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: The Considered Reply
text: But notice what the critics largely do not deny. Keith, Le Donne, and Allison are not mythicists; they affirm that Jesus existed, was baptized by John, gathered followers, was reputed a healer, clashed over the Temple, and was crucified under Pilate. Their quarrel is with using criteria to authenticate this saying versus that one — the verse-by-verse "sayings authentication" enterprise. And here is the irony: when memory scholars defend the secure historical core, they appeal precisely to what Allison calls recurrent attestation — patterns that surface again and again across the tradition.11 That is a cousin of multiple attestation rather than the very same instrument — Allison would resist having his memory-based approach simply relabeled as the source-critical criterion — so the point is best read as a close analogy: attestation operating at the level of the broad portrait rather than the isolated proof-text. The instrument survives in altered form; it changes scale.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: The Considered Reply
text: So the reply is one of demotion, not abolition. Multiple attestation is best understood not as a verdict but as one weighted indicator within a cumulative, memory-aware argument. It is strongest for establishing broad, recurring features of Jesus' career — that he taught in parables, that he was known as an exorcist, that he proclaimed God's kingdom, that he died on a Roman cross. It is weakest, and the critics are right here, when pressed to certify the exact wording of a single saying. Used at the right altitude, with full knowledge of its limits, it remains genuinely useful.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: The State of the Question
text: The field is in flux. Meier and others — and, in a different key, Stanley Porter, who has argued in print for reforming rather than discarding the criteria — continue to defend a chastened use of them; Keith and the memory theorists argue the criteria paradigm has run its course and should be replaced by approaches drawn from social memory and historiography proper; Allison charts a middle way between skepticism and credulity. There is, at present, no consensus method to replace the criteria — which is itself a reason not to discard the better criteria entirely while the alternatives are still being built.

title: Multiple Attestation: How Historians Test the Gospels
section: Conclusion: What It Does and Doesn't Establish
text: The criterion of multiple attestation does not prove that Christianity is true, nor that any miracle occurred, nor that a given sentence left Jesus' lips exactly as printed. It cannot, by itself, separate authentic tradition from early interpretation; its critics, named above, have pressed that point hard. What it does do — modestly, cumulatively, alongside other considerations — is make it very hard to dismiss the broad historical outline of Jesus' life as later fabrication. When Christian creeds, hostile Roman annals, a Jewish historian, and multiple independent Gospel streams converge on the same Galilean teacher, healer, and crucified man, the convergence demands explanation. The honest conclusion is neither triumphalist nor skeptical but disciplined: there was a Jesus of Nazareth, the rough shape of his life is recoverable, and any serious account — of faith or of unbelief — must begin there.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
text: Imagine you are handed an anonymous short story and asked one question: where and when was the author actually from? You could try to catch them on geography or customs—but a clever forger can study a map. There is, however, one detail almost impossible to fake from the outside, because the writer is not even thinking about it: the names. Pick up a British novel set in 1950, and the boys are Brian and Keith and Derek; set it in 2025 and they are Oliver and Noah and Muhammad. No author sat down to research that. The names simply leaked out, carrying the unconscious watermark of a particular time and place. Get them subtly wrong—name a 1950 schoolboy “Jayden”—and a native reader knows at once that the writer was not there.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
text: Now apply that test to the Gospels and Acts. They are populated by dozens of named people: fishermen, tax collectors, women at a tomb, a man who lent his grave. If these books were composed late and far away—Greek legends spun in Rome or Alexandria two or three generations after the fact, as much skeptical scholarship has long maintained—then the names should carry the watermark of that world, not the watermark of early-first-century Jewish Palestine. The remarkable claim of this essay’s argument is that they carry the Palestinian watermark with surprising statistical fidelity. The names are right—and right in a way that is extraordinarily hard to counterfeit.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
text: This is a quieter argument than the case for the resurrection, and a narrower one. It overlaps with, but is not the same as, the fuller case that the Gospels rest on eyewitness testimony; here the focus is on the name data itself as a marker of provenance—of when and where these traditions were really formed. Used honestly, it is a piece of corroboration, not a proof. But it is a surprisingly stubborn piece.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: Stating the Argument Carefully
text: The discipline at work is onomastics, the study of personal names and their distribution. Its founding observation is simple and uncontroversial: the popularity of a given name is sharply local and time-bound. Which names are common, and in what proportions, varies by region, by religious community, and by generation. This is not a contested theological premise; it is an everyday fact any historian of antiquity will grant.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: Stating the Argument Carefully
text: Premise 1: The relative frequency of personal names in a population is local and time-bound, and could not be reproduced by guesswork by an outsider or a much later author. Premise 2: The names in the Gospels and Acts match—in their specific names, their relative frequencies, and their disambiguation habits—the independently attested profile of Jewish Palestine in roughly 330 BC–AD 200, and do not match the different profile of the Jewish diaspora. Conclusion: Therefore the Gospel traditions are best explained as rooted in early Palestinian sources close to the events, rather than as late, geographically distant compositions.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: Stating the Argument Carefully
text: Notice what this is and is not. It is an inference to the best explanation built on a statistical fact, not a deductive proof. Premise 1 is essentially conceded by everyone. The real work—and the real debate—lies in Premise 2 (does the data genuinely match, and how tightly?) and in how far that match licenses the conclusion. We will give both their due.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: How the Argument Developed
text: The argument has a clear pedigree. Its raw material is the labor of the Israeli historian Tal Ilan, whose Lexicon of Jewish Names in Late Antiquity, Part I: Palestine 330 BCE–200 CE (Tübingen: Mohr Siebeck, 2002) catalogued every attested Jewish person of that region and era—drawn from literary texts, Josephus, ossuary inscriptions, and documentary papyri—and tabulated the frequency of their names.1 Ilan was not doing apologetics; she was building a reference work. But she handed later scholars a hard, independent baseline against which any text claiming to depict that world could be tested.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: How the Argument Developed
text: The person who ran that test on the Gospels was the British New Testament scholar Richard Bauckham, in chapters 3 and 4 of Jesus and the Eyewitnesses: The Gospels as Eyewitness Testimony (Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 2006).2 Bauckham took Ilan’s tables and laid the Gospel names beside them. The argument had antecedents—earlier scholars had noticed the “Jewishness” of Gospel names—but Bauckham made it quantitative, and it became the most-discussed plank of a widely reviewed book. It has since been popularized by the Cambridge scholar Peter J. Williams in Can We Trust the Gospels? (2018), who folds it into a broader battery of “local knowledge” tests.3

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: Premise 1: Why Name Frequency Is a Watermark
text: It is worth dwelling on why name distribution is so hard to fake, because the strength of the whole argument depends on it. Three features combine.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: Premise 1: Why Name Frequency Is a Watermark
text: First, names cluster by community and era in ways nobody plans. The fashion that makes “Simon” ubiquitous in one generation and rare in another is an emergent social fact, not a rule anyone consciously follows. You cannot deduce it; you can only absorb it by living inside the population.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: Premise 1: Why Name Frequency Is a Watermark
text: Second, the diaspora pattern differed sharply from the Palestinian one. Among Egyptian Jews, the most common names included forms like Eleazar, Sabbataeus, Joseph, Dositheus, and Pappus—a noticeably different mix, with far more Greek names, than that of Palestine.4 So a writer working in the diaspora would not merely fail to copy the Palestinian list; he would tend to default to the names of his own world. The watermark is not just hard to forge—the forger’s own background actively pulls him away from it.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: Premise 1: Why Name Frequency Is a Watermark
text: Third—and this is the subtlest point—it is one thing to include a few common names and quite another to reproduce their relative frequencies. An author could easily salt a story with “Simon” and “Mary.” What no ancient author had the tools to do was ensure that the second-commonest name appeared about as often as the second-commonest name actually did, and that the rare names stayed rare in roughly the right proportion. There were no frequency tables in antiquity. Reconstructing them took Ilan a modern scholar’s lifetime of cataloguing inscriptions. The pattern can leak out of genuine memory; it cannot be engineered from the outside.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: Premise 2: Do the Gospel Names Actually Match?
text: Here the numbers do the talking, and they are striking. Working from Ilan’s data, Bauckham found that the most popular Jewish male name in Palestine was Simon, followed by Joseph—and these are exactly the top two in the Gospels and Acts. In Ilan’s catalogue of Palestinian men, about 15.6% bore one of those two names; in the Gospels and Acts, about 18.2% of named men do.5 Widen the lens to the nine most popular male names—Simon, Joseph, Lazarus (Eleazar), Judas (Judah), John (Yohanan), Jesus (Joshua), Ananias (Hananiah), Jonathan, and Matthew (Mattathias)—and the fit holds: roughly 41.5% of Palestinian men in the data carry one of these nine, against about 40.3% in the New Testament narratives.6

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: Premise 2: Do the Gospel Names Actually Match?
text: The women’s names tell the same story. The two most popular female names in the Palestinian record were Mary (Mariam) and Salome; in the Gospels and Acts these are again the two commonest. The fit is looser here—about 28.6% of women in the external data bear one of the two, against about 38.9% in the New Testament—but the rank order and the broad shape match.7 The sheer profusion of Marys in the Gospels (the mother of Jesus, Magdalene, the sister of Martha, the mother of James, the wife of Clopas) is not a narrative embarrassment to be explained away; it is precisely what a real first-century Palestinian sample looks like.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: Premise 2: Do the Gospel Names Actually Match?
text: The most elegant confirmation, though, is not a percentage but a behavior. Because a handful of names were so over-common, real first-century Palestinian Jews had a practical problem: in any crowd there were too many Simons and Josephs to keep straight. Their solution was to tag people—by a patronymic (Simon bar-Jonah), a hometown (Joseph of Arimathea, Mary Magdalene), a nickname (Simon the Zealot, Simon the Leper), or a trade. The decisive observation is that the Gospels apply this disambiguation selectively, and apply it to exactly the names that needed it—the over-common ones—while rare names are usually left bare. That is not the behavior of a writer sprinkling in local color. It is the unconscious behavior of a culture that genuinely had too many Simons.8

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: Premise 2: Do the Gospel Names Actually Match?
text: Two independent controls strengthen the case. First, the same profile shows up in Josephus, a first-century Palestinian Jew whose works name hundreds of his contemporaries—an entirely separate sample that yields the same top names and ratios, so the Gospels are matching not one flawed list but a convergent picture.9 Second, and crucially, the Gospels match Palestine specifically. They do not match the diaspora profile. If these were late Greek compositions written far from Judea, that is the last thing we should expect.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: The Strongest Objections, Stated at Full Strength
text: This argument has drawn serious, technically sophisticated criticism, and it deserves to be met at its best.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: The Strongest Objections, Stated at Full Strength
text: The deepest recent challenge comes from Kamil Gregor and Brian Blais, in a 2023 article in the peer-reviewed Journal for the Study of the Historical Jesus, “Is Name Popularity a Good Test of Historicity? A Statistical Evaluation of Richard Bauckham’s Onomastic Argument.”10 Their case is not the lazy “so what, they used Jewish names” dismissal; it is a genuine statistical critique. They argue, first, that the New Testament sample is simply too small for the law of large numbers to do reliable work—a few dozen named people cannot establish a tight statistical fit. Second, they identify what they regard as anomalies: certain names appear in the Gospels at frequencies that, on a closer look, sit awkwardly with the external data. Third, and most pointedly, they contend that Bauckham’s thesis of eyewitness sourcing offers no statistical advantage over a rival model they call “anonymous community transmission”—a story in which the names accrued through a Palestinian Christian community over time, with no need for named eyewitnesses behind them. If a non-eyewitness model predicts the same data, the name fit cannot be evidence specifically for eyewitnesses.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: The Strongest Objections, Stated at Full Strength
text: A second, older objection—and the one that bears most directly on this essay’s narrow claim about provenance—comes from the Oxford scholar Christopher Tuckett, in his review of Bauckham’s book. Tuckett does not deny that the names match Palestine; he calls the book a “tour de force.” His point is sharper. Bauckham wants to conclude that the names could not have been invented from outside Palestine. But, Tuckett notes, what that conclusion really requires is evidence that people outside Palestine were unaware of Palestinian names—and that is exactly the evidence we lack.11 Jews were mobile; Palestinian Jews lived in Rome and Alexandria, pilgrims streamed to Jerusalem, and Josephus himself wrote his Palestinian narratives in Rome for a Greco-Roman audience. The naming knowledge plainly traveled. So a sufficiently well-informed insider—a diaspora Jew steeped in Palestinian tradition—might in principle have reproduced the right names without being a Galilean eyewitness.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry
text: Take the statistical objection first, because the field has now litigated it directly. In 2024 the same journal published a detailed reply by Luuk Van de Weghe and Jason Wilson—the latter a working statistician—arguing that Gregor and Blais’s negative verdict followed from questionable testing choices and data selection.12 Using a chi-squared goodness-of-fit test, they found that the name occurrences in the Gospels and Acts fit their Palestinian context at least as well as the names in Josephus do, and markedly better than names drawn from ancient fiction or modern historical novels. It should be said plainly that Gregor and Blais have in turn replied, and the statistical exchange is ongoing; the weight of this essay therefore rests on the narrow provenance claim, not on the verdict that “the statisticians settled it.” That last comparison is the telling one: the appropriate question is not “is the fit perfect?” (no real sample is) but “does it behave like a sample drawn from the population, or like a sample drawn from an author’s imagination?” On the published evidence, it behaves like the former.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry
text: Two honest concessions are nonetheless owed to the critics. The sample is modest, and Gregor and Blais are right that one should not oversell the precision of any single ratio drawn from a few dozen names; the women’s figures in particular wobble, and individual anomalies are real. And their methodological demand—that the eyewitness hypothesis be tested against rival explanations rather than simply asserted—is exactly the right demand. This remains a genuinely contested area of scholarship, not a settled one; the disputed hinge is precisely how much the statistical fit can bear. What the reply establishes is more modest than “Bauckham wins”: it is that the fit is real and is not plausibly the product of invention. That alone is enough to carry the narrow conclusion of this essay, which is about provenance, not about proving named eyewitnesses stand behind each pericope.

title: Do the Gospel Names Fit First-Century Palestine? The Onomastic Evidence
section: A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry
