No single cause explains three centuries across a whole empire, and one honest caveat belongs up front: the most serious dissenting historian, Ramsay MacMullen, argued that conversion in this period turned less on charity than on public demonstrations of power—healings and exorcisms a pagan could read as a straight contest between gods.9 His is a rival account of the mechanism—one that discounts charity in favour of displays of power—and it is noted, not answered here; but it is no help to the Constantine objection, because whatever exorcism was, it was not imperial power. Three things, then, recur across the sources.

title: How the Church Took Over the Empire
section: Why it grew
text: Twice the empire was gutted by epidemics—the Antonine plague from about 165, and the plague named for Cyprian from about 249—and ancient cities had no capacity for mass nursing. Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria, writing of the second outbreak in a letter preserved by the historian Eusebius, describes Christians staying with the dying, taking their care upon themselves, and perishing in numbers as a result, while frightened neighbours abandoned their own.10 It is a Christian source describing Christian conduct, and should be weighed as such—though flight from plague was ordinary enough that pagan sources record it too, so the contrast is not invented. Stark’s much-quoted claim is that this was not merely admirable but demographically consequential: even elementary nursing can cut mortality sharply, so tended communities lost fewer of their own and won the loyalty of the strangers they had nursed.11 That model rests on modern estimates applied to diseases we cannot securely identify, so it is a plausible argument rather than a proven result. But the behaviour is well attested, and it is the sort of thing that changes how a neighbour thinks.

title: How the Church Took Over the Empire
section: Why it grew
text: Leaving an unwanted newborn outdoors to die or be taken was legal and unremarkable in the Greco-Roman world. Christian texts forbid it from their earliest layer: the Didache bans abortion and the killing of a newborn in the same breath as murder, and the Epistle to Diognetus singles out Christians as people who “marry, as do all… but they do not destroy their offspring.”12 The same communities admitted, without a bar of status, the categories the surrounding cults ranked and rationed—slaves, the poor, women, and non-Greeks—so that a slave and a matron could belong to the same congregation on the same terms. This point is easy to overstate, and careful specialists such as Lynn Cohick have shown that Greco-Roman women had wider social and economic scope than the older caricature allowed.13 So the defensible claim is the narrower, sturdier one: Christian communities were unusually mixed, and membership was not priced by rank. To people the ancient order treated as disposable, that was an astonishing offer.

title: How the Church Took Over the Empire
section: Why it grew
text: Stark’s most durable contribution is sociological rather than statistical: new religious movements grow overwhelmingly along existing relationships—family, household, trade, friendship—rather than through public preaching to strangers.14 The book of Acts shows exactly this, converting whole households at a stroke—Cornelius, Lydia, the Philippian jailer, Crispus—alongside the public preaching it also records. It is an unglamorous mechanism, and it is precisely what produces the steady compounding the arithmetic describes: not a wave, but a web, thickening decade by decade—the faith spreading the way trust spreads, one relationship at a time.

title: How the Church Took Over the Empire
section: The Constantine objection
text: The standard sceptical reply deserves to be stated at its strongest, because in one respect it is right: the real cause of Christianity’s success, it says, is not the mechanisms above but a single political event. In 312 Constantine won at the Milvian Bridge and credited the Christian God; in 313 he and Licinius agreed the settlement conventionally called the Edict of Milan, ending persecution; imperial patronage followed; and in 380 Theodosius made Nicene Christianity the empire’s official religion, with the coercive power of the state behind it.15 On this telling, Christianity did not win the Roman world—it was handed it.

title: How the Church Took Over the Empire
section: The Constantine objection
text: The concession owed here is substantial. Everything after 312 is entangled with state power, and the church’s growth after 380 with the legal suppression of rival worship. The steepest part of the curve in raw numbers is the fourth century; anyone who points to the Christian majority of AD 400 as proof of the gospel’s persuasive force is trading on a period when the state’s thumb was on the scale.

title: How the Church Took Over the Empire
section: The Constantine objection
text: But the objection explains the wrong stretch of the curve, and three facts sit entirely outside the window the state can cover. Pliny’s letter and Lucian’s satire describe a spreading, organised movement in the second century, when no emperor favoured it. Cornelius’s relief roll is an administrative document from an illegal church in 251. And—this is decisive—the state’s own attempts to destroy the church had already failed with the full machinery of empire engaged. Decius’s universal sacrifice order of 250, Valerian’s edicts of 257 and 258, and Diocletian’s persecution from 303 were all spent, and the last was formally abandoned by Galerius in the edict of toleration of April 311—a full year before the Milvian Bridge.16 The state conceded first. By the time Constantine acted, the church already reached into the army and the palace and numbered in the millions; his patronage recognised and accelerated a movement already too big to suppress. The Constantine story does not explain the growth—it reverses cause and effect.

title: How the Church Took Over the Empire
section: The witness of a hostile emperor
text: The sharpest testimony to what had driven that growth comes from the one man with the most reason to deny it—and its date has to be stated rather than blurred, because it is not evidence from the illegal centuries. It comes from fifty years after Constantine. In 362 the emperor Julian—raised Christian, and the last emperor to abandon the faith—set out to restore the old gods, and found he could not. Writing to a pagan priest, he diagnosed why, and the diagnosis is an unwilling tribute: it was that the Christians simply out-behaved the pagans. When the pagan priesthood neglected the poor, Julian observed, “the impious Galilaeans”—his term for Christians—noticed and devoted themselves to philanthropy; it was their care for strangers and for the poor, he complained, that had done most to advance their cause.17 His remedy was telling: he ordered his own pagan priesthood to fund and imitate the very charity he could not defeat.18

title: How the Church Took Over the Empire
section: The witness of a hostile emperor
text: Julian is therefore not a witness to why the church grew in the second and third centuries—he is far too late for that, and it must not be pretended otherwise. But he is a witness to something worth having: an emperor holding the whole apparatus of the state, and using it against the church, judged that the thing he had to defeat was Christian charity, and that his best hope was to copy it. When your fiercest opponent, with an empire at his disposal, concludes that his surest course is to imitate you, he has told you where the movement’s real strength lay.

title: How the Church Took Over the Empire
section: What the growth shows—and where the truth of it rests
text: Two things follow, and they should be kept distinct. The rapid, illegal, person-to-person spread of the church shows that the faith was profoundly attractive and that its people were utterly convinced—convinced enough to nurse plague victims at the cost of their lives, to take in the children a whole civilisation discarded, and to keep confessing the name when a pinch of incense would have bought their safety. The evidence for it is strong, external, and honest.

title: How the Church Took Over the Empire
section: What the growth shows—and where the truth of it rests
text: But it is not, by itself, proof that the gospel is true, and this essay does not offer it as one. Movements can spread quickly and still be mistaken; popularity is not a truth-detector. The case that Jesus actually rose from the dead rests on different evidence—above all the eyewitness testimony behind the early creed Paul hands on in 1 Corinthians 15:3–7, datable to within a very few years of the events—and that case is made at length elsewhere in this Library. What the growth does do is exactly what you would expect if that resurrection claim were true and its first witnesses sincere: a movement that behaved as though it had genuinely met the risen Christ, that could not be bought off or stamped out, and that changed the people it touched.

title: How the Church Took Over the Empire
section: What the growth shows—and where the truth of it rests
text: So the honest takeaway is not a boast but a recognition. The behaviours that carried the church across the empire—staying with the sick, rescuing the abandoned, feeding somebody else’s poor—were not clever strategies for winning an argument. They were what Jesus had told his followers to do, done at cost, by people who mostly left no names, because they believed he had been raised and would one day ask what they had done with it. A tiny, powerless, illegal movement outlasted the empire that tried to kill it—not by force, which it never had, but by love, which it could not stop giving away. And it never stopped: the movement that began among a few thousand in the eastern Mediterranean is today the largest faith on earth, and no longer a Western one — a century ago about two-thirds of Christians lived in Europe, whereas today most live outside it, across the Americas, sub-Saharan Africa and Asia, with sub-Saharan Africa alone projected to hold the largest single share within a generation. That corrects a common modern assumption, that Christianity is a Western or colonial religion; though, like the ancient growth, it settles nothing about whether the faith is true.19 That is a fact of history that still wants explaining, and a good place for a Christian to stand.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: The brother who did not believe
text: Imagine you grew up in the same small house as a man who is now being called the Son of God. You knew him as a child. You watched him at chores and at meals; you saw him irritated and tired; you went to weddings with him. And when he left home to preach, you concluded — along with the rest of the family — that he had lost his mind. The Gospel of Mark records the verdict bluntly: his relatives "went out to seize him, for they were saying, 'He is out of his mind'" (Mark 3:21).1 The Gospel of John is blunter still: "For not even his brothers believed in him" (John 7:5).2

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: The brother who did not believe
text: That man is James, the brother of Jesus. And the historically arresting fact is what happened next. Within a few years of the crucifixion, this same sceptic is not merely a believer but the recognized leader of the mother church in Jerusalem — the man Paul calls a "pillar," the figure who presides over the Jerusalem council, the brother whose ruling the apostles defer to (Galatians 2:9; Acts 15:13-21).3 And around the year 62, according to the Jewish historian Josephus, James was executed by stoning on the order of the high priest Ananus.4 A man who once thought his brother deranged ended his life as a martyr for the claim that this brother had risen from the dead.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: The brother who did not believe
text: What changed him? That is the question this essay presses. A separate essay in this library is devoted to the conversion of Paul, the persecutor (see The Conversion of Paul); here Paul appears only as the second of two hostile witnesses. The depth belongs to James, because the logic that makes both conversions evidentially weighty rests most cleanly on him.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: The logic of the hostile witness
text: In both courtroom practice and historical method, not all testimony is created equal. A witness who confirms what he wants to be true, or what his community expects, is easy to discount; he may be reporting his hopes. But a witness who testifies against his own prior convictions, against his own interests, against everything he had reason to want — that witness carries a special weight. He is, in the legal idiom, a hostile witness, and his agreement is hard to explain away as wishful thinking.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: The logic of the hostile witness
text: This is closely related to what New Testament historians call the criterion of embarrassment: a tradition awkward for the people who preserved it is unlikely to have been invented by them. That the founder's own family thought him mad, and that one of the movement's chief leaders had to be won over from outright unbelief, is not the kind of detail a community fabricates to flatter itself. It is the kind of detail that survives because it is true.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: The logic of the hostile witness
text: Two men anchor the resurrection's hostile-witness case. Paul began as an active persecutor who, in his own words, "persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it" (Galatians 1:13).5 James began as a domestic sceptic. The first had every ideological reason to disbelieve; the second had every familiar, this-is-just-my-brother reason. Gary Habermas and Michael Licona, in their "minimal facts" presentation, list the conversion of James and the conversion of Paul among the small set of data conceded by the great majority of critical scholars, precisely because each is multiply rooted and cuts against the grain.6 The argument is cumulative: no single feature is decisive, but together they make the naturalistic alternatives strain.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: What we actually know about James
text: The case for James rests on a convergence of independent sources, which is what gives it traction.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: What we actually know about James
text: His unbelief during the ministry rests on two independent strands about Jesus' family. Mark 3:21 reports that "his family" set out to seize Jesus, thinking him "out of his mind" — a statement about the family as a whole, not one that names James (though Mark 6:3 names the brothers, James first, elsewhere). John 7:5 is more sweeping: "For not even his brothers believed in him." James's own unbelief is therefore a strong inference from this family tradition rather than a line that singles him out by name — but it is a well-grounded inference, and it passes the criterion of embarrassment with ease: the early church revered James, so a memory of his earlier scepticism is the last thing it would have manufactured.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: What we actually know about James
text: His place among the named recipients of a resurrection appearance is fixed by the oldest piece of Christian tradition we possess. The creed Paul recites in 1 Corinthians 15 — a formula most scholars date to within a few years of the crucifixion (see The Early Creed of 1 Corinthians 15) — states: "Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles" (1 Corinthians 15:7).7 This is not a late legend about James; it is an early, pre-Pauline confession that singles him out by name.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: What we actually know about James
text: Of the individuals the creed names, James is the one whose prior unbelief the Gospel tradition lets us infer — a strong inference from the family's recorded unbelief — which makes his inclusion among the resurrection witnesses the hardest single line in the formula to explain as pious embellishment. A community inventing appearances to lend its message authority had no motive to award one to the founder's estranged, doubting brother; that it did is better explained by memory than by invention.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: What we actually know about James
text: His leadership of the Jerusalem church is independently confirmed by Paul's own letters and by Acts. Paul says that on his first post-conversion visit to Jerusalem, around AD 35-36, he "saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord's brother" (Galatians 1:19), and that James, Cephas, and John were "reputed to be pillars" (Galatians 2:9). Acts shows James presiding at the Jerusalem council and issuing its decision (Acts 15:13-21). The Australian scholar John Painter, whose Just James is the standard monograph on the figure, traces how James moved from outside the circle of believers to its very center — a trajectory that itself demands explanation.8

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: What we actually know about James
text: His martyrdom is recorded by a non-Christian source. Josephus, in Antiquities 20.200, narrates how the high priest Ananus, exploiting a gap between Roman governors around AD 62, "assembled the sanhedrin of judges, and brought before them the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James, and some others... he delivered them to be stoned."9 The overwhelming majority of scholars — including sceptics — regard this passage as authentic, in part because Josephus mentions James only incidentally, to explain why Ananus was deposed, with no Christian agenda to serve.10 A second-century Christian source, Hegesippus (preserved in Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History 2.23), adds a more elaborate martyrdom — James thrown from the temple parapet and then clubbed — and gives him the title "the Just." That account is more legendary in its details and should be cited with care, but the bare fact of a violent death it shares with Josephus.11

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: What we actually know about James
text: Put the strands together and a shape emerges that no single source could fabricate: a sceptical brother, named in the earliest creed as having seen the risen Jesus, who rose to lead the Jerusalem church and died for the conviction.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: What we actually know about James
text: This convergence has not been lost on critics. The Anglican New Testament scholar Reginald Fuller — no partisan of the apologetic case — called the disciples' Easter faith "one of the indisputable facts of history" and held that the historian "must … postulate an 'x'" to account for it. Of James in particular he remarked that "if there were no record of an appearance to James the Lord's brother in the New Testament we should have to invent one." That a sceptical critic reaches for the appearance to explain the conversion, rather than explaining the appearance away, is a fair measure of how hard the conversion of a witness like James is to reduce to grief or wishful thinking.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: The transformation that needs explaining
text: The bare facts are not seriously in dispute. The interpretive question is what could turn a man who knew Jesus intimately, and disbelieved, into a leader willing to die. Here the precision matters, because James is in one respect a harder case than any other witness.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: The transformation that needs explaining
text: The most psychologically respectable naturalistic explanation of the resurrection appearances is the bereavement-vision or grief-hallucination hypothesis: grieving people who loved someone deeply, and who long for that person's return, sometimes vividly perceive the deceased as present. This is a real, documented phenomenon, and we should concede it plainly. But the documented cases turn on a specific variable: they are keyed to yearning — the ache of a bereaved person who longs to see the deceased restored, and whose mind, in effect, supplies what the heart is reaching for. That is the variable James most conspicuously lacks. He is not on record as a devoted follower yearning for his brother's return; he is on record as having thought his brother out of his mind. (Trauma is a separate variable, and the next section takes it on its own terms.) A bereaved disciple primed by longing is one thing. A sceptical sibling, who had three decades of ordinary family knowledge weighing against any temptation to deify Jesus, and no documented wish to see him restored, is quite another.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: The naturalistic explanations, taken seriously
text: Could James, despite his earlier scepticism, have been so shaken by the trauma of his brother's public execution that he hallucinated him alive? The hypothesis is not absurd; trauma and guilt can disturb perception. But it cuts against the grain of what we know. Crucifixion was not merely a death but a shameful, covenant-cursed death (Deuteronomy 21:23; cf. Galatians 3:13). For a first-century Jew, a crucified messianic claimant was a refuted messianic claimant. Nothing about the manner of Jesus's death would have inclined a sceptical brother toward sudden faith; it would have confirmed his doubts. A grief vision must explain not just an experience but a complete reversal of conviction in someone who had no prior wish to believe.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: The naturalistic explanations, taken seriously
text: A sharper objection runs the other way: perhaps James converted not from grief but from opportunity. His brother's movement survived the crucifixion; James, as the eldest surviving brother, stepped in to lead it — a kind of dynastic succession, with the resurrection claim as the family business. Some sceptical and mythicist writers have floated versions of this "dynastic succession" reading, in which James simply inherited the family business.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: The naturalistic explanations, taken seriously
text: The reply turns on timing and cost. Leadership of a persecuted sect of a crucified criminal in early-30s Jerusalem was not a prize; it was a liability. There was no power, wealth, or honor to inherit — only the social shame of being kin to an executed blasphemer and, eventually, a death sentence. Dynastic ambition explains why a man might lead a winning movement, not why a sceptic would join a losing and dangerous one and then refuse to recant under the threat of stoning. And the dynastic reading must still account for the early creed's specific claim — not that James inherited a role, but that the risen Jesus "appeared to James." The succession theory explains the leadership while leaving the conversion, which is the thing to be explained, untouched.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: The naturalistic explanations, taken seriously
text: A third option is the least dramatic: perhaps James was won over slowly — by the disciples' preaching, by reflection on the scriptures, by the moral force of the early community — and the "appearance" of 1 Corinthians 15:7 is a later, stylized way of marking a gradual change of mind. This is the most serious of the naturalistic readings, because it does not require any anomalous experience at all. It is worth saying plainly where the weight lies: for James in particular, the grief or bereavement-vision hypothesis is the weakest of the naturalistic options, precisely because the yearning it depends on is absent. The gradualist reading — and with it the late-interpretation handling of "then he appeared to James" — is the one a fair case must actually beat.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: The naturalistic explanations, taken seriously
text: Two considerations weigh against it. First, the early creed of 1 Corinthians 15:7 does not describe a process of persuasion; it names a discrete appearance, and it is among the earliest tradition we have, leaving little room for a slow legend to form. Second, gradual persuasion does not easily produce martyrs. People are talked into opinions and talked out of them; the willingness to be stoned rather than recant is the mark of a conviction the holder regards as anchored in something he himself encountered, not merely argued into. The gradualist reading can explain a change of view; it strains to explain a death.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: What the argument does — and does not — establish
text: Intellectual honesty requires drawing the line carefully, and critics are right to insist on it.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: What the argument does — and does not — establish
text: First, the sources for James are real but uneven. The Gospel data on his unbelief and the Pauline data on his leadership are early and strong. The Josephan notice of his death is solid. But the vivid Hegesippus martyrdom is later and partly legendary, and even the Josephus passage, while accepted by most, has been questioned by a minority who suspect the words "who was called Christ" of being a later gloss.12 The case for James should lean on the convergence, not on any single embellished narrative.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: What the argument does — and does not — establish
text: Second, and more fundamentally, this argument does not by itself prove the resurrection. What it establishes is that a sceptic became a martyr-leader, and that he and the earliest community attributed the change to an appearance of the risen Jesus. That James was sincerely and radically transformed is well supported. That the cause of his transformation was a literal resurrection is a further inference — the best explanation, the argument contends, of a conversion that grief, ambition, and slow persuasion all fail to capture. But it is an inference, defended alongside the empty tomb, the disciples' experiences, and the conversion of Paul, not a proof standing alone.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: What the argument does — and does not — establish
text: The honest claim is therefore modest and strong at once: the conversion of James is a fact the naturalistic theories handle poorly, and the cumulative case is the better for it.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: The state of the question
text: That James existed, was Jesus's brother, was not a follower during the ministry, led the Jerusalem church, and died a violent death is close to consensus across the scholarly spectrum, from confessional historians like Richard Bauckham — who has written extensively on James and the relatives of Jesus — to sceptics who grant the same facts while disputing their cause.13 N. T. Wright treats the conversion of James, alongside Paul's, as part of the data any historian of Christian origins must explain, not a pious flourish.14 The live debate is not over whether James converted but over why — and there the naturalistic options remain on the table, defended by able critics, even as their proponents must concede how poorly James fits the grief profile their best theory relies on.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: The state of the question
text: Paul belongs in the same conversation as the second hostile witness: the persecutor who became an apostle and martyr, whose own letters preserve his testimony in the first person. His case is developed in its own essay (The Conversion of Paul). Together the two form a pincer: the outside enemy and the inside sceptic, converging on the same claim from opposite starting points, each immune to the explanation that fits the other.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: Conclusion
text: The conversion of James does not, on its own, prove that Jesus rose. It does something narrower and harder to dismiss: it places at the very center of the early church a man whose prior unbelief is embarrassingly well-attested, names him in the oldest creed as a witness to the risen Christ, and follows him to a martyr's death. The naturalistic explanations — grief, dynastic loyalty, gradual persuasion — each illuminate part of the picture and each leave the heart of it dark, because each was designed for a different kind of witness than a sceptical brother who had no wish to believe and every reason not to. That a man who once called his brother mad would die rather than deny he had seen him risen is exactly the sort of fact that gives the resurrection case its grip on serious historians.

title: The Conversion of the Sceptics: James, the Brother of Jesus, as Hostile Witness
section: Conclusion
text: None of this is to sneer at the doubter; James himself was one, and the church that revered him preserved the record of his doubt. The argument is offered, as Peter urged, "with gentleness and respect" (1 Peter 3:15)15 — confident in what the evidence shows, candid about where it stops, and aware that the most powerful witness here is a man who started exactly where the honest sceptic stands today.

title: Did Christianity Give Us Science?
text: Almost everyone knows the story before they know any of the facts. Faith and science are old enemies, locked in a long war: the church against Galileo, superstition against the telescope, dogma dragging its heels while the light of reason advances. It is one of the most confident assumptions a modern person carries, absorbed from cartoons and textbooks long before anyone reads a page of history. And it has a curious feature. The men who actually founded modern science — Copernicus the cathedral canon, Kepler the would-be minister turned astronomer, Galileo the devout Catholic, Newton writing theology by candlelight — would not have recognised the war they are supposed to have fought. Nearly all of them believed they were studying nature because it was the handiwork of God, and said so in the very books that made their names.

title: Did Christianity Give Us Science?
text: That disconnect is not a curiosity at the edge of the subject; it is the subject. Over the last half-century, historians of science — including many with no religious stake at all — have largely abandoned the “warfare” picture as bad history. This essay is about how that picture was built, why the specialists tore it down, and what the more interesting truth turns out to be. It is a historical claim, made carefully, and it will not prove that Christianity is true. It will suggest something smaller and, once seen, hard to unsee: that the supposed enemies were, for most of their history, closer to family.

title: Did Christianity Give Us Science?
section: The war that was invented
text: The “conflict thesis” is not ancient. It has a birthday, an author, and a sequel. In 1874 the American chemist John William Draper published History of the Conflict between Religion and Science, a bestseller that cast the whole of Western history as a running battle between free inquiry and (chiefly Roman Catholic) faith.1 Two decades later the founding president of Cornell University, Andrew Dickson White, gave the thesis its monument: A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom (1896), two fat volumes of the church forever obstructing progress.2 These books were enormously influential. They are also, as history, largely wrong — and specialists now say so bluntly.

title: Did Christianity Give Us Science?
section: The war that was invented
text: The correction is not a fringe Christian complaint; it is the mainstream of the discipline. The historian Ronald Numbers — himself no apologist for religion — edited a landmark collection, Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths about Science and Religion, in which twenty-five scholars dismantle the set-piece stories one by one, from the flat-earth legend to the claim that the church banned human dissection.3 A more recent volume, The Warfare between Science and Religion: The Idea That Wouldn’t Die, edited by Jeff Hardin, Numbers, and Ronald Binzley, traces how a thesis the experts reject has survived so stubbornly in the popular mind.4 The title says it all: the warfare model persists not because the evidence supports it but because it is a useful story. As the historian James Hannam and others have shown at book length, the actual medieval and early-modern record is one of deep entanglement, not combat.5 Historians are wary of every tidy slogan here — and that wariness is exactly what makes their verdict on the warfare thesis worth trusting.

title: Did Christianity Give Us Science?
section: Why science was born here — the careful version
text: If the two were not at war, a harder question follows. Modern experimental science — the self-sustaining, self-correcting enterprise of hypothesis, measurement, and law — took hold decisively in Christian Europe of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Why there and then? This is contested ground, and it must be stated with care: no serious historian thinks Christianity is a sufficient explanation, and the strong slogan “no Christianity, no science” overreaches badly. But a more modest thesis has real scholarly support. Historians such as Reijer Hooykaas and Peter Harrison have argued that certain theological convictions supplied intellectual preconditions that made the scientific enterprise thinkable.6

title: Did Christianity Give Us Science?
section: Why science was born here — the careful version
text: Three convictions in particular. The first is a free Creator. If God made the world by choice rather than necessity, then the world is contingent — it could have been otherwise — and you cannot deduce its workings by pure reason from your armchair, as the Greeks so often tried. You have to go and look. Harrison argues that this “voluntarist” picture of God underwrote the empirical turn: nature must be interrogated, not merely contemplated.7 The second is an intelligible, ordered creation, made by a rational God and open to the minds of creatures made in his image. This is a historical and theological precondition, not a proof of design — the deeper puzzle of why the cosmos is mathematically intelligible at all is taken up in this Library’s essay on the laws of nature. The third, easily missed, is human fallibility. If the fall reaches the reasoning mind, then the individual thinker is not to be trusted alone; knowledge must be checked, replicated, and disciplined against self-deception. Harrison has traced how the doctrine of the fall shaped the experimental method itself, in Francis Bacon and the early Royal Society, as a remedy for a corrupted intellect.8

title: Did Christianity Give Us Science?
section: Why science was born here — the careful version
text: None of this sprang from nowhere in 1600. It rested on a long medieval lineage that the “Dark Ages” caricature erases. The universities — Bologna, Paris, Oxford — were a Christian invention with no exact precedent, and they institutionalised exactly the culture of open, rule-governed argument that science needs. Medieval natural philosophers did real work: John Philoponus in the sixth century criticised Aristotle’s physics and anticipated the idea of impetus; Jean Buridan and Nicole Oresme in the fourteenth pressed it toward inertia and even entertained a rotating earth; Robert Grosseteste and Roger Bacon pioneered the study of optics and experiment.9 It was the philosopher Alfred North Whitehead — no orthodox believer — who put the point most sharply: the very “faith in the possibility of science” that the early scientists took for granted was, he wrote, “an unconscious derivative from medieval theology” and its insistence on the rationality of God.10

title: Did Christianity Give Us Science?
section: The Galileo affair, without the myth
text: And now the trump card. If the warfare thesis has one battle it can always name, it is Galileo — and honesty requires meeting it head-on, conceding what must be conceded. In 1616 the Roman Inquisition’s theologians judged the claim that the sun stands still to be “foolish and absurd in philosophy, and formally heretical,” and Copernicus’s book was suspended on the Index; in 1633 Galileo was tried, made to abjure his view, and confined to house arrest for the rest of his life.11 This was a real injustice and a real error. The Roman Catholic authorities were wrong to condemn him, wrong to bind the interpretation of Scripture to a particular astronomy, and wrong to silence a man for being, as it turned out, right. No Christian account worth reading pretends otherwise. Whitewashing the episode would forfeit exactly the honesty this whole case depends on.

title: Did Christianity Give Us Science?
section: The Galileo affair, without the myth
text: But the clean fable of enlightened science versus benighted faith does not survive contact with the details. Start with the science itself. In 1616 the evidence did not yet favour Copernicus. His 1543 system still used perfect circles and a thicket of epicycles, and it predicted the planets no better than the old Ptolemaic model; and Tycho Brahe’s geo-heliocentric system fit the same observations—including the phases of Venus—while keeping the earth still. There was as yet no stellar parallax, and the physics of a moving earth was unsolved.12 Heliocentrism was vindicated only later, by Kepler’s ellipses and Newton’s gravity. In 1616 the church, having consulted its astronomers, sided with the scientific majority of the day — which is not a defence of the verdict, but it does explode the idea that faith was simply refusing an obvious fact. The conflict, as the leading Galileo scholar Maurice Finocchiaro observes, ran across both institutions: progressives and conservatives in the church and in the academy alike, not a tidy front of religion against reason.13 Jesuit astronomers at the Collegio Romano confirmed Galileo’s telescopic observations; his fiercest opponents included secular Aristotelian professors. The Orthodox writer David Bentley Hart, surveying the same record, calls the affair less a war of science against faith than a collision of egos, personality, and politics — and, awkwardly for the legend, in 1616 it was often the churchmen asking for proof and Galileo asking for assent to a model not yet demonstrated.14 That does not exonerate the church: its error was not caution but jurisdiction — it converted a legitimate scientific reservation into a charge of heresy and bound the reading of Scripture to it. The other name the legend invokes, Giordano Bruno, burned in 1600, does not change the picture: Bruno was condemned for a cluster of theological heresies — among them denying the Trinity, the divinity of Christ, and the real presence in the Eucharist — not for his Copernicanism, which was incidental to his trial.3

title: Did Christianity Give Us Science?
section: The Galileo affair, without the myth
text: Tellingly, every party to the dispute appealed to the same authority on how to read Scripture: Augustine, who had warned twelve centuries earlier that Christians must not make the Bible contradict what reason and observation establish about the natural world, lest they discredit the faith before unbelievers.15 Galileo quoted that very principle. The lesson the episode actually teaches, then, is double-edged, and it cuts against everyone. It rebukes a faith that overreaches its competence and clings to a scientific claim as though the gospel depended on it. And it rebukes the warfare myth that turns one Italian tragedy into a law of history. One thing it is not is a weapon for one branch of the church against another: the error was the Roman authorities’ of that moment, and the honest response is neither anti-Catholic point-scoring nor Protestant self-congratulation, but a shared caution against ever again mistaking the science of the hour for the word of God.

title: Did Christianity Give Us Science?
section: The founders’ own faith
text: What the legend most obscures is the piety of the scientists themselves. Nicolaus Copernicus was a canon of Frombork cathedral, and he dedicated On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres (1543) to Pope Paul III. Johannes Kepler, who had trained for the Lutheran ministry, understood his astronomy as an act of worship — in a phrase long associated with him, the scientist’s task was to think God’s thoughts after him.16 Galileo, a believing Catholic to the end, argued in his 1615 Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina that God had written two books, Scripture and nature, and that they could not finally conflict because both had the same Author; he approvingly cited a cardinal’s quip that the Bible was meant “to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how the heavens go.”17 He was defending Copernicanism as a Christian, insisting that good science and true faith answer different questions.

title: Did Christianity Give Us Science?
section: The founders’ own faith
text: And Isaac Newton closed the greatest scientific book ever written — the Principia — not with an equation but with a doxology. “This most beautiful system of the sun, planets, and comets,” he wrote in the General Scholium, “could only proceed from the counsel and dominion of an intelligent and powerful Being.”18 (Newton’s private theology was in fact heterodox — he privately rejected the Trinity — a reminder that these were individuals, not a party line, and that the argument here needs no one to have been orthodox.) The point is not that their faith proved their physics, nor that they were all orthodox; it is simply that the caricature is false. The people who built modern science were not straining against their religion. Most of them were expressing it.

title: Did Christianity Give Us Science?
section: What this shows — and what it doesn’t
text: Two honest limits keep this argument where it belongs. First, the thesis that Christian theology supplied the preconditions of science is a claim about history, and a contested one; historians rightly resist any monocausal story, and Numbers himself cautions against replacing the old warfare myth with a triumphalist inverse. Take it, then, as the careful historians offer it: not that Christianity single-handedly manufactured science, but that its picture of a rational, contingent, intelligible creation was fertile soil in which the enterprise could take root and last. Second, science was never a solely Christian achievement. It stands on Greek mathematics and logic, and on the Islamic Golden Age, when scholars in Baghdad, Cairo, and Córdoba preserved and advanced Greek learning, invented algebra, and — in Ibn al-Haytham’s optics — pioneered controlled experiment centuries before Europe.19 That story is told, and defended, in this Library’s companion essay on Islam and science; the case here neither needs nor claims a Christian monopoly.

title: Did Christianity Give Us Science?
section: What this shows — and what it doesn’t
text: And — this matters most — none of it shows Christianity is true. That a worldview proved intellectually fruitful is not proof that it is correct; good and true are different things, and the case for the faith rests not on what it built but on whether Jesus rose from the dead, which is argued on its own evidence elsewhere. What the history does dissolve is a barrier: the widespread assumption that a thinking person must choose between the laboratory and the church. The founders of the one were, overwhelmingly, members of the other.

title: Did Christianity Give Us Science?
section: Conclusion: the enemy that never was
text: The warfare between science and religion is not a fact discovered by historians. It is a story sold by two Victorian writers, embraced because it flattered an age, and quietly retired by the scholars who checked it. In its place stands something stranger and better documented: a scientific revolution midwifed in the most Christian civilisation the world had seen, by men who prayed as they calculated, and who thought — rightly or wrongly — that in reading the book of nature they were reading a second scripture from the same hand. The Galileo affair is a genuine scar, and it should be owned without flinching. But one scar is not a war. The next time someone says science and faith are ancient enemies, the honest reply is that the war is the modern invention — and that the people who actually gave us the telescope, the laws of motion, and the ellipse would have found the whole quarrel bewildering.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
text: Twice a day, every day, the observant Jew says the same sentence. It is the first prayer a Jewish child learns and the last words a dying Jew tries to speak: Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai Echad—“Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Martyrs have died with it on their lips. It is the closest thing Judaism has to a creed, and its theme is unmistakable: there is one God, and Israel belongs to him alone.1

title: The Shema and the Trinity
text: So the question is a good and honest one. If God is emphatically, gloriously one—if the central confession of the faith Jesus himself recited is a hymn to divine singularity—then how can Christians turn around and speak of three? Doesn’t the doctrine of the Trinity quietly cancel the very sentence it claims to honor? Many a thoughtful Jewish person, and many a Muslim and Unitarian, has concluded that it does. This essay takes that objection seriously and argues the opposite case: that the Trinity does not deny the Shema but is, in fact, the early church’s own reading of it—and that the most striking evidence comes not from a fourth-century council but from a first-century Pharisee.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: Stating the Question Carefully
text: First, a concession that must come at the start, not the end. Classical Christianity affirms the Shema without crossing its fingers. The Nicene faith confesses “one God”—not three gods, not a committee of deities, not one God plus two junior partners. The doctrine of the Trinity is the claim that the one God exists eternally as three coequal, coeternal persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one in being. It is emphatically not the claim that there are three Gods (tritheism), nor that the one God merely wears three masks at different times (modalism), nor that the Son and Spirit are lesser, created beings (subordinationism). Whatever the Trinity is, it is a doctrine of monotheism. If it were not, it would have failed at the first hurdle.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: Stating the Question Carefully
text: Second, we should be honest about what kind of argument can and cannot be made here. No one should claim that the Trinity is “stated” in Deuteronomy 6:4, as if Moses had a doctrine of three persons in view. That would be reading the New Testament back into a text written centuries before it. The careful claim is more modest and, I think, more powerful: the Shema confesses that God is uniquely one, and that confession does not, by itself, settle the inner life of the one God it names. The Christian conviction is that the same God who said “Hear, O Israel” later revealed himself more fully—and that the apostles, reading the Shema in light of Jesus, found in it not a wall against the Trinity but a doorway.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: A Lexical Argument to Handle With Care
text: Here we must be especially careful, because this is where popular apologetics most often overreaches. The Hebrew word translated “one” in the Shema is echad＊About this wordIs sayingechad is simply the ordinary Hebrew word for “one”; in context it can describe a unity made of parts (“one flesh”).Not sayingIt does not by itself prove plurality in God or the Trinity. That “compound unity” argument is a discredited overreach; the case for the triune God rests on divine identity, not on this one word.. A common apologetic move runs like this: echad means a compound or composite unity, not a bare singularity, because it describes a husband and wife becoming “one (echad) flesh” in Genesis 2:24, or the spies carrying back “one (echad) cluster” of grapes in Numbers 13:23. Hebrew has another word, yachid, for solitary, only-one-ness—and the Shema, the argument concludes, pointedly does not use it. Therefore (so the claim goes) the Shema itself hints at plurality within God.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: A Lexical Argument to Handle With Care
text: That argument proves far less than its enthusiasts suppose, and intellectual honesty requires saying so plainly. The plurality in “one flesh” or “one cluster” does not come from the word echad at all; it comes from the noun it modifies. A “cluster” is a many-membered thing, so “one cluster” is one collection of many grapes—but that tells us nothing special about echad, which simply means “one.” Echad is in fact the ordinary Hebrew cardinal number; it routinely describes things that are emphatically singular, as in “one day” or “one man.” The standard Hebrew lexica treat it as the unremarkable numeral “one.”2 Critics from the Jewish and Unitarian traditions have pressed exactly this point, and on this lexical point the facts are with them: echad does not prove a composite unity, and the echad-versus-yachid contrast cannot bear the doctrinal weight some place on it.3

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: A Lexical Argument to Handle With Care
text: What can be said—and only this—is the negative claim: echad does not forbid internal complexity either. It asserts that YHWH is uniquely, exclusively Israel’s God; it does not legislate on the metaphysics of how many “persons” that one God is. The Shema’s polemic is against the gods of the nations—against having any rival to YHWH—not against later questions about the divine life that no Israelite was yet asking.4 So the word leaves a door ajar. It does not, on its own, walk anyone through it. For that we need to leave the lexicon and go to the New Testament, where a far stronger argument waits.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: The Heart of the Case: Paul Rewrites the Shema
text: The decisive evidence is one of the most remarkable sentences in the New Testament, and its author is the last person you would expect to tamper with Israel’s creed. Paul of Tarsus was, by his own description, “a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee” (Philippians 3:5)—a man who had recited the Shema since boyhood and once persecuted the church for what he saw as its blasphemy. Writing to the Corinthians around AD 53–54, in a chapter explicitly about the danger of idolatry, he sets the gospel against the pagan world’s “many ‘gods’ and many ‘lords’” and then says this:

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: The Heart of the Case: Paul Rewrites the Shema
text: To feel the force of this, you have to hear it as Paul’s first readers did. In the Greek Old Testament that Paul used, the Septuagint, the Shema reads Kyrios ho theos h&emacron;m&omacron;n Kyrios heis estin—“the LORD (Kyrios) our God (theos) is one LORD.” Two divine titles, theos and Kyrios, both naming the one God of Israel; Kyrios in particular was the standard reverent substitute for the unspeakable name YHWH.6 Now look again at what Paul does. He takes the creed’s two words for the one God—theos and Kyrios—and he distributes them: “one God, the Father… and one Lord, Jesus Christ.” He has not added a second deity alongside the Shema. He has reached inside the Shema and placed Jesus within it.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: The Heart of the Case: Paul Rewrites the Shema
text: This reading is associated above all with the British scholar Richard Bauckham, who calls it the New Testament’s “Christology of divine identity,” and with N. T. Wright, who argues that Paul has “redefined” the Shema around Jesus, producing a kind of christological monotheism.7 Bauckham’s central thesis—widely influential, though the divine-identity category is itself debated—is that ancient Jews defined God less by abstract metaphysics than by identity—by who God is and what only God does: God alone is the sole Creator of all things, and God alone is the sovereign Ruler of all things. To include Jesus in that identity is not to make him a second god; it is to confess that the one God of Israel is somehow Father and Son together. As Bauckham puts it, the earliest Christians “included Jesus in the unique divine identity” of the God of Israel.8 Wright, for his part, suggests that Paul, having once prayed the Shema daily as a Pharisee, may have gone on praying this reformulated Shema with the same devotion.9

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: The Heart of the Case: Paul Rewrites the Shema
text: Notice the two things that make this so weighty. First, the who: this is not a Gentile convert centuries later but a trained Pharisee within roughly two decades of the crucifixion. Second, the where: he does it in the middle of an argument against idolatry. If Paul thought he were smuggling a second, lesser divine being into the picture, he would be committing in verse 6 precisely the sin he condemns in verse 5. The natural reading is that he saw no contradiction at all: one God, confessed in the creed’s own words, now known to be Father and Son.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: The Strongest Objection, Stated at Full Strength
text: The traditional Jewish reading of the Shema deserves to be heard in its full strength, not as a foil. For more than two millennia, the mainstream of Jewish interpretation has understood Deuteronomy 6:4 as strict, indivisible monotheism: the LORD is one—one in the plainest sense, without parts, without persons, without a “within.” On this view, the Christian doctrine is not a development of Israel’s faith but a departure from it, and the burden lies entirely on the Christian to explain why the custodians of the creed have always read it the other way.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: The Strongest Objection, Stated at Full Strength
text: The objection can be sharpened on the very text Christians lean on. The leading scholarly critic here is James F. McGrath, who argues directly against Bauckham and Wright that 1 Corinthians 8:6 does not “split” the Shema at all. On McGrath’s reading, Paul confesses the “one God” of the Shema—the Father—and then adds “one Lord, Jesus Christ” alongside that confession, not inside it.10 On this reading, Jesus is the Messiah, the agent through whom God acts, exalted to a unique status—but a distinct figure subordinate to the one God, not a person of that one God. Paul, the objection runs, is doing something thoroughly Jewish: Second Temple Judaism was full of exalted intermediary figures—personified Wisdom, the great angels, exalted patriarchs like Enoch—who do God’s work, even bear God’s name, without being God. Slotting the risen Jesus into that role of supreme agent is striking, but it is not the Nicene Trinity, and reading Nicaea into Paul, on this view, is anachronism.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: The Strongest Objection, Stated at Full Strength
text: This is the objection at its best, and a fair-minded Christian should grant the facts it rests on, though not the inference drawn from them. The agency literature exists. Some Second Temple texts do exalt intermediary figures to dizzying heights. And the grammatical distinction in the verse—all things from the Father, all things through the Son—is genuinely there and must be reckoned with, not waved away.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry
text: Take McGrath’s “alongside, not inside” reading first, because everything turns on it. The trouble is the word Kyrios. In the Shema Paul is unmistakably echoing, Kyrios is not a generic word for a master; it is the Septuagint’s rendering of the divine name itself. So when Paul confesses “one Lord, Jesus Christ,” using the creed’s own divine title and pairing it with the creed’s “one God,” the “alongside” reading faces a dilemma. If “one Lord” means a being who is not the one God—a separate, exalted creature—then Paul has confessed, in an anti-idolatry argument, one God plus one additional divine-but-not-God Lord through whom all things were made. That is not the strict monotheism the objection wants to protect; it is a second power. And if the reply is that an agent could bear God’s name without becoming a second god, grant it: God’s name and functions could be entrusted to a supreme agent, and the worship itself still could not be. The reading that actually preserves monotheism is the trinitarian one: the one divine identity, confessed under both of the creed’s titles, shared by Father and Son.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry
text: What about “through whom”? Doesn’t the preposition cast Jesus as a mere instrument, an intermediary lower than the Father from whom all things come? Here the decisive consideration is creation itself. In Israel’s Scriptures, creating is the act that marks the absolute line between God and everything else: “I am the LORD, who made all things… who alone stretched out the heavens” (Isaiah 44:24). The one through whom all things were made cannot himself be among the things that were made; he stands on the Creator’s side of that line.11 And the prepositions do not, in fact, mark a difference of rank: Paul elsewhere piles all of them onto God without distinction—“from him and through him and to him are all things” (Romans 11:36). The Son is given a creation role that Jewish monotheism reserved for God alone.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry
text: The exalted-agent objection is the strongest, and it must be answered on its own ground. Two things distinguish Jesus from every intermediary figure in the literature. The first is the boundary of worship. As Larry Hurtado has documented in exhaustive detail, the angels of Second Temple Judaism consistently refuse worship and redirect it to God—the angel in Revelation cries “Worship God!” (Revelation 19:10). Yet the earliest Christians prayed to Jesus, were baptized in his name, sang to him, and called on him in worship—a devotional pattern Judaism reserved for God alone.12 The point needs care, because a gesture of homage was not itself the line: Israelites could bow before a king as well as before the LORD (1 Chronicles 29:20), and some texts picture homage to an exalted figure. What Jewish monotheism guarded jealously for God was not the posture of homage but the substance of worship—sacrifice, invocation, prayer. The second is that no intermediary figure was ever placed inside the Shema. Wisdom is praised; Enoch is exalted; but no Jewish writer took the creed of divine uniqueness and wrote a second figure into it. Paul did.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry
text: And the last objection should go to the critic before the reply. McGrath and others can press one more point: even granting your reading of this one verse, you have built a mountain on a single sentence from one unusually creative theologian—hardly a foundation for the Trinity. The honest answer is that the verse does not stand alone. It reads less like a doctrine Paul invented than like a confession he quotes—compact, balanced, assumed as common ground with readers he is correcting on other matters. And the same devotion surfaces in independent streams: the Philippians 2 hymn—widely regarded as pre-Pauline tradition—applies to Jesus the fiercely monotheistic oath of Isaiah 45:23—“to me every knee shall bow”—so that every knee now bows at the name of Jesus.13 The Aramaic-speaking churches, older than any Greek theology, were already crying Marana tha, “Our Lord, come!”, a prayer addressed to Jesus (1 Corinthians 16:22).14 Baptism ran in the threefold name of Father, Son, and Spirit (Matthew 28:19). Paul is not the inventor of this devotion; he is our earliest written window onto a worship that was already there.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: The Honest State of Scholarship
text: Where does the debate actually stand? On the central exegetical question, the Bauckham–Wright reading of 1 Corinthians 8:6 as a deliberate, christological reformulation of the Shema has become widely influential—arguably the dominant reading—among New Testament scholars, supported in their different ways by Hurtado and, more cautiously, by James D. G. Dunn (who speaks of Paul as, in effect, splitting the Shema).15 But it is genuinely contested, not unanimous. James F. McGrath and others continue to argue that “one Lord” is added to, not folded into, the creed; and a wider scholarly literature debates whether “splitting,” “supplementing,” or “brokering” best describes what Paul is doing.16 These are real disagreements among serious scholars, and the trinitarian should name them as such rather than pretend the case is closed.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: The Honest State of Scholarship
text: Two further honesties are owed. The first is to Judaism. The traditional Jewish reading of the Shema is a serious and ancient interpretation, held in good faith by people who love this text as much as any Christian—and on what the verse itself asserts, Christians agree completely: there is one God, and no other. The Christian claim is not that Jews have failed at arithmetic; it is an intra-biblical claim that the one God of the Shema has disclosed more of his life than the verse alone reveals—a claim Jewish readers are entitled to find unpersuasive. The second honesty is historical: the influential thesis of Daniel Boyarin and others, that something like “binitarian” ideas (a second divine figure beside God, as in the “two powers in heaven” debates and Daniel 7’s “one like a son of man,” who comes with the clouds) circulated within ancient Judaism before being branded heresy, is itself debated among specialists and should be offered as a suggestive line of evidence, not a proof.17

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not Establish
text: What, then, has the argument shown? It has not shown that the Trinity is taught in Deuteronomy 6:4; it is not, and claiming so concedes too much to the lexical over-reach we set aside at the start. It has not shown that echad “means” a compound unity; it does not. And it has not refuted the traditional Jewish reading by force of grammar alone; that reading is held in good faith, but grammar alone was never going to decide the question; the case against it rests on what the one God has since disclosed in Christ.

title: The Shema and the Trinity
section: Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not Establish
text: What the argument does establish is this. The Shema confesses one God and does not, by itself, foreclose the question of that God’s inner life. And the earliest Christians—Jewish monotheists to a man, led here by a Pharisee writing against idolatry—did not abandon the Shema when they confessed Jesus as Lord. They recited it, with Jesus inside it. That is the heart of the matter: the doctrine of the Trinity is not a third-party intrusion upon Israel’s creed but the church’s own reading of it—monotheism kept, not monotheism lost. The Christian does not answer the Shema by changing the subject from “how many gods?” The Christian answers, with Paul, that there is one—one God rich enough to be Father, Son, and Spirit. So the honest answer to the question is no: the Shema does not rule out the Trinity, and the objection built on it does not hold. And this is what we hold to be true: the one God exists eternally as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—three coequal, coeternal persons, one God. This argument does not prove that; it clears the charge against it. The positive case rests on revelation and on the historical case for who Jesus was—on whether the carpenter from Nazareth said and did what only God can say and do, and was vindicated by resurrection.

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone
text: Picture a man pushing a stone with a stick. The stone moves because the stick moves it; the stick moves because the hand moves it; the hand moves because the arm, the muscles, the nervous system, the will all conspire in a single present moment. Remove the hand and the whole sequence collapses at once — not eventually, but now. Thomas Aquinas chose exactly this image to anchor the first and most famous of his arguments for God: "the staff moves only because it is put in motion by the hand."1 Everything in his case for God hangs on what kind of series this is. Misread the picture, and you will spend your life refuting an argument Aquinas never made.

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone
text: The Five Ways — the Quinque Viae — occupy a single dense article of the Summa Theologiae (I, q. 2, a. 3), written around 1265–1268. They are not Aquinas's whole natural theology; they are five compressed sketches, each closing with a deceptively casual tag — "and this everyone understands to be God." The real work of identifying that conclusion with the God of classical theism comes in the questions that follow. To read the Five Ways fairly, we must first read them as written, and then defend the strongest of them against its most serious critics.

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Five Ways in Brief
text: The First Way, "more manifest" than the rest, argues from motion — better translated as change. Things change; whatever changes is changed by another; an infinite series of such changers (of the right sort) is impossible; therefore there is a first, unchanged changer, "and this everyone understands to be God."2

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Five Ways in Brief
text: The Second Way runs the same structure on efficient causation: we observe an order of causes; nothing is the efficient cause of itself; the series cannot regress to infinity; so there is a first efficient cause, "to which everyone gives the name of God."3

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Five Ways in Brief
text: The Third Way argues from possibility and necessity (contingency): some things can be or not be — they come to be and pass away. If everything were like that, then at some point nothing would exist, and nothing would now exist either, which is absurd. So there must be something necessary, and ultimately something whose necessity is uncaused — God. (As literally stated, the Third Way faces a well-known quantifier-shift worry — the slide from "each contingent thing can fail to exist at some time" to "there is some time at which all contingent things fail together" is invalid as it stands; the argument rests its weight on the First and Second Ways, with the Third needing repair before it can be leaned on.)

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Five Ways in Brief
text: The Fourth Way argues from degrees of perfection: we speak of more and less good, true, noble; such comparatives imply a maximum, which is the cause of all such perfection in others.

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Five Ways in Brief
text: The Fifth Way argues from governance: natural bodies lacking intelligence act toward an end, hitting their mark regularly; what lacks intelligence cannot tend to an end unless directed by an intelligent being, "and this being we call God."

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Five Ways in Brief
text: The First Way is the paradigm, so we will dwell there. Everything important — and every common error — is visible in it.

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Single Most Important Point
text: Here is the interpretive key, and it is the one most often missed: the causal series Aquinas has in mind does not stretch backward in time to a first event. He is not arguing that the universe must have had a beginning and that the first domino is God. Aquinas, remarkably, did not think reason could prove the universe began at all. In his treatise De aeternitate mundi (c. 1271) and in the Summa itself, he held that the world's beginning is "an object of faith, but not of demonstration or science."4 This put him in open disagreement with his Franciscan contemporary Bonaventure, who insisted the world's temporal beginning could be philosophically proven. Aquinas thought a beginningless universe was philosophically possible; we know it began only because Genesis tells us so.

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Single Most Important Point
text: So the Five Ways cannot depend on a beginning. They concern a different kind of series altogether. Medieval and modern Thomists distinguish two:

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Single Most Important Point
text: A series ordered per accidens ("accidentally ordered") runs through time: a father begets a son, who begets a grandson. Each member, once it acts, no longer needs its predecessor. Abraham can be long dead while Isaac fathers Jacob. Such a series could, for all philosophy shows, regress forever — which is precisely why Aquinas conceded the universe might be eternal.

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Single Most Important Point
text: A series ordered per se ("essentially ordered") operates simultaneously, here and now. The stone's motion depends, at this very instant, on the stick, which depends on the hand. The later members have no causal power of their own; they move only insofar as something is moving them right now. Take away the first member and the entire series ceases instantly. As Edward Feser, the foremost recent defender, puts it, in such a series the intermediate causes are mere instruments; their causal power is "borrowed."5 A series of borrowers with no one who owns the power outright explains nothing — like a paintbrush moving a paintbrush moving a paintbrush, with no hand. This is the series that cannot regress to infinity, and it requires a first member acting now: not a starter long ago, but a sustainer at the foundation of present reality.

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Metaphysics Beneath the First Way
text: Why must whatever changes be changed by another? Aquinas's answer rests on Aristotle's distinction between potency and act. A thing changes when a potential it has becomes actual — cold water becomes hot. But a mere potential cannot actualize itself; the cold water does not heat itself. Something already actual (the flame) must do it. "Nothing can be reduced from potentiality to actuality, except by something in a state of actuality."6 Trace the present chain of actualizers, and you reach something that actualizes without itself being actualized — something with no unrealized potential, pure actuality (actus purus). That, Aquinas argues across the following questions, must be one, immaterial, unchanging, and the source of all being.

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Objections — Steelmanned
text: Bertrand Russell pressed this in his 1927 lecture Why I Am Not a Christian. Crediting John Stuart Mill's Autobiography, he wrote: "If everything must have a cause, then God must have a cause. If there can be anything without a cause, it may just as well be the world as God, so that there cannot be any validity in that argument."7 It is a clean, memorable objection — and it has persuaded generations.

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Objections — Steelmanned
text: But it answers an argument Aquinas did not give. Aquinas never claims "everything has a cause." His premise is narrower: whatever is being changed is being changed by another; whatever is contingent requires a cause. What is purely actual has no potential to be actualized and so needs no actualizer; what is necessary in itself needs no cause. God is not an exception smuggled in arbitrarily — He is the one thing the argument's own logic says cannot stand in the dependent series. To his credit, Russell elsewhere grappled more seriously with these arguments; but the famous one-liner, repeated endlessly, simply misses the qualifier in the premise.

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Objections — Steelmanned
text: David Hume argued that causation is not a rationally intuited necessary connection but a habit of mind: we see one billiard ball strike another and infer a "power," but we observe only constant conjunction. If so, the causal principle behind the Ways loses its self-evidence. Immanuel Kant, in the Critique of Pure Reason (1781), pressed a different line: the cosmological argument, in inferring from a necessary being to the supremely real being, secretly relies on the ontological argument, which Kant thought already refuted — and in any case the categories of cause and necessity apply only within possible experience, not beyond it.

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Objections — Steelmanned
text: These are formidable, and a fully adequate reply requires defending an entire realist metaphysics against empiricism and transcendental idealism — more than any essay can do. The Thomistic response is that Hume's analysis describes how we come to know causal connections without showing there are none, and that the principle "a potential cannot actualize itself" is not an empirical generalization like "fire is hot" but a metaphysical truth about the nature of potency and act. Against Kant, Thomists deny that the argument depends on the ontological proof at all: it argues from features of the world to their required cause, not from a concept to existence. Whether these replies fully succeed is contested, and honesty requires saying so: the dispute is live among serious philosophers.

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Objections — Steelmanned
text: Here is the objection that should keep a Thomist up at night. Aquinas's premise "whatever is moved is moved by another" looks like exactly what Newtonian physics overturned. By the principle of inertia, a body in uniform motion stays in motion with no mover at all. Anthony Kenny, in his careful and skeptical study The Five Ways (1969), pressed the point hard, concluding that the First Way fails in light of modern dynamics, which dissolves the medieval premise that sustained motion needs a sustaining mover.8 If the paradigm Way rests on dead physics, that is a grave problem.

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Objections — Steelmanned
text: Feser's reply, and that of contemporary Thomists, turns on what "motion" means. For Aristotle and Aquinas, motus is not merely local motion (change of place) but any actualization of a potential — change of quality, quantity, substance. Inertia concerns only local motion, and — on this view — even there it does not touch the deeper principle. Inertia, the Thomist replies, describes that bodies persist in motion; it does not explain what grounds the existence of that motion, or of the body, or of the law itself, from moment to moment.9 The Thomist relocates the argument from "what keeps the cannonball moving?" to "what sustains in being, right now, every actualized potential — including the persistence the law describes?" One may judge the reply successful or strained, but it is not a dodge: it reflects what Aquinas meant by change all along.

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Objections — Steelmanned
text: The atheist philosopher Graham Oppy, perhaps the most rigorous contemporary critic, grants the per se / per accidens distinction more than most — but asks whether an essentially ordered series must terminate in a single first member, or whether reality's "causal shape" might simply bottom out in a necessary initial state of the universe with no need for God. Oppy argues that on the plausible naturalistic options — an infinite regress, a contingent brute starting-point, or a necessary one — non-theism is at least as defensible as theism.10

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Objections — Steelmanned
text: The Thomist answers that a brute necessary physical state is not enough: anything composed of parts, or having unrealized potential, still requires actualization and so cannot be the terminus; only something purely actual and absolutely simple can be. Whether the universe could itself be that — purely actual, with no potency — is the crux, and here the argument shades into the full doctrine of divine simplicity. Oppy is owed the last word on the narrow point: he can coherently maintain that the regress stops at a necessary cosmos rather than at God. The Thomist's rejoinder is that such a cosmos, being changeable and composite, fails the very test that forced us up the series in the first place. That exchange, not a slogan, is where the real debate now lives.

title: The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's Five Ways Reconsidered
section: The Objections — Steelmanned
text: Candor demands it: the Fourth Way is widely regarded, even by sympathetic readers, as the weakest. The inference from "there are degrees of goodness and truth" to "there exists a maximum that causes them" looks, as Kenny noted, like a fragile echo of Platonic Forms, and the premise that a maximum in a genus causes all lesser instances strikes many as a dated piece of metaphysics.
