On the Jewish side, Wright's account of resurrection as bodily, collective, and future is widely accepted even by those who reject his conclusions, though critics such as the historian James G. Crossley have argued (in the Journal for the Study of the Historical Jesus) that Wright overstates the historical security of the empty tomb—a genuinely contested claim.20 On the comparative side, the consensus has shifted decisively away from Frazer: following Jonathan Z. Smith's standard reference treatment, the simple "dying-and-rising god as source of Christianity" thesis is now widely abandoned, while it is acknowledged, with Mettinger, that some such figures genuinely existed. What remains contested is not whether the resurrection claim is unusual—that is broadly granted—but what best explains its origin.

title: Was the Resurrection Copied From Pagan Myths?
section: What Uniqueness Does and Does Not Prove
text: We must be exact here, because the temptation to over-claim is real. Uniqueness is not truth. That an idea is unprecedented does not make it correct; novel false beliefs arise all the time. The argument of this essay establishes something narrower but still significant: the resurrection claim cannot be explained away as the predictable product of its Jewish environment, nor as a Jewish edition of a pagan myth, nor as one more tale of a hero taken up to the gods. Each of those reductions fails on the specifics—and the strongest witnesses against them, Smith and Mettinger, are not friends of Christian apologetics.

title: Was the Resurrection Copied From Pagan Myths?
section: What Uniqueness Does and Does Not Prove
text: What this leaves is not a proof but a question, and it is the right question. If the disciples did not get this idea from Judaism, and did not borrow it from paganism, and were not simply pattern-matching available myths—then where did it come from? The Christian answer is that something happened. One may reject that answer. But one may no longer reach for the comfortable verdict that it was, after all, just another old story. It was not. Whatever it was, it was new.

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
text: Every December, in churches across the world, a line is spoken that ought to stop us short: conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary. It is one of the few biographical claims that made it into the creeds at all. The Apostles' and Nicene Creeds skip from birth to death in a single clause about Pontius Pilate, yet they pause to insist on how Jesus was conceived. That deliberateness invites a question worth asking honestly: what exactly do the Gospels claim about the virginal conception, why did the early church think it mattered, and what can the historian responsibly say about it?

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
text: This essay makes a modest case. The virgin birth is a creedal affirmation resting on the testimony of two Gospels. It is not a public event open to investigation the way the crucifixion is. It is held by faith, on the evidence of Matthew and Luke, with reasons—not demonstrated like a theorem. Saying that plainly is not a retreat; it is the only honest place to begin.

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
section: The claim, stated carefully
text: The doctrine is precise, and precision matters because so many objections aim at a blurrier target. The claim is the virginal conception: that Mary conceived Jesus while a virgin, without a human father, by the creative power of God's Spirit. It is not a claim about Mary's perpetual virginity, nor (in the New Testament texts themselves) about a painless or miraculous delivery, nor about the immaculate conception of Mary herself—later developments that should not be confused with the original assertion.1

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
section: The claim, stated carefully
text: Two narratives carry it. In Matthew 1:18–25, Mary is "found to be with child from the Holy Spirit" before she and Joseph "came together," and an angel reassures Joseph in a dream. In Luke 1:26–38, the angel Gabriel tells Mary she will conceive, and she objects, "How will this be, since I am a virgin?"—to which the answer is, "The Holy Spirit will come upon you" (Luke 1:34–35, ESV). The two accounts are widely regarded by scholars as literarily independent: they share almost no wording, sequence their events differently, and cannot easily be derived one from the other.2 Yet across that independence they converge on a striking cluster of agreements—virginal conception, the name Jesus given by angelic command, birth at Bethlehem, descent from David, and the role of the Holy Spirit. Independent witnesses agreeing on a core is the kind of thing historians take seriously, even when they dispute the details.

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
section: The case in depth
text: The strongest positive consideration is precisely that convergence-amid-independence. If Matthew and Luke had collaborated, their agreements would prove little. If they had simply copied a common source, we would expect verbal overlap. Instead we find two writers, working from different angles—Matthew largely through Joseph's experience, Luke largely through Mary's—who nonetheless land on the same astonishing core. Raymond Brown, whose The Birth of the Messiah remains the landmark critical study, treats the virginal conception as one of the few genuine points of agreement between the two infancy traditions.3

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
section: The case in depth
text: A second consideration is the criterion of embarrassment. A pregnancy before the couple "came together" carried, in first-century Judaism, the unavoidable shadow of illegitimacy. Matthew's narrative shows Joseph "resolved to divorce her quietly" (Matthew 1:19)—a detail no early Christian eager to defend Jesus' honor would invent gratuitously. Hostile traditions did in fact seize on the opening: by the second century, charges that Jesus was born of an irregular union circulated, preserved in the pagan critic Celsus and echoed in later rabbinic material.4 A church fabricating a flattering origin story would have had easier options than one that handed its opponents this weapon. The awkwardness is itself a fragment of evidence—not that the conception was virginal, but that something about Jesus' origin was, from very early, in need of explanation.

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
section: The case in depth
text: Third, the doctrine is early. It is not a medieval accretion. Ignatius of Antioch, writing around 107 AD, already lists "the virginity of Mary and her giving birth" among the "mysteries to be cried aloud."5 Within roughly a generation of the Gospels, the virginal conception is simply assumed, not argued for—suggesting it was received tradition rather than fresh invention.

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
section: Isaiah 7:14: handle with care
text: Matthew alone ties the conception to a text: "All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet: 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel'" (Matthew 1:22–23), quoting Isaiah 7:14. This is where the most serious objection lives, and it deserves to be stated at full strength. (The full textual treatment belongs to the companion essay on messianic prophecy; here I summarize.)

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
section: Isaiah 7:14: handle with care
text: In its original setting, Isaiah 7 is a word to King Ahaz of Judah around 734 BC, besieged by a coalition of Syria and Israel. The sign of a child to be born is, on its face, a sign to Ahaz—a near-term assurance that the threatening kings would soon be gone. The Hebrew word Isaiah uses is 'almah, which means a young woman of marriageable age. It does not strictly mean "virgin"; Hebrew has a more specific word for that, betulah. An 'almah was typically presumed unmarried and so presumably a virgin, but the term's focus is youth, not sexual status.6 So the honest thing is to say it plainly: read in Hebrew and in context, Isaiah 7:14 is not by itself a prediction of a virgin birth seven centuries later — and we should not overclaim the verse.

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
section: Isaiah 7:14: handle with care
text: What Matthew quotes, however, is not the Hebrew but the Septuagint—the pre-Christian Greek translation made by Jews, which rendered 'almah with the Greek parthenos, "virgin."7 Matthew did not engineer that rendering; he inherited it. So the fair description is layered: Jewish translators, well before Christianity, chose parthenos; Matthew, reading his Scriptures in Greek and convinced that Jesus fulfilled them, saw in that wording a fit with what he believed had happened to Mary. The best account of his logic is not prediction-and-proof but dual fulfillment: a prophecy that had a real meaning for Ahaz's own day and a fuller resonance that Matthew, looking back through the resurrection, found realized in Christ. On this reading the conviction came first—the church already believed Jesus was virginally conceived—and the text was seen, in hindsight, to illumine it. Isaiah 7:14 is best treated as a window, not a proof. As a standalone argument for the virgin birth, it does not work, and the case should not be hung on it.

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
section: The strongest objections
text: The translation objection. Stated at its best (and it has able Jewish and critical defenders): Matthew built a doctrine on a Greek mistranslation; the Hebrew never spoke of a virgin; the whole edifice is a linguistic accident. I concede the core of this. Isaiah's 'almah is not betulah, and the verse is not a slam-dunk prediction. The reply is narrower than apologists sometimes wish: the virgin birth does not derive from Isaiah 7:14. The earliest tradition rests on the events Matthew and Luke report; Isaiah is cited to interpret, not to generate, the claim. Strip the verse away entirely and Luke—who never quotes it—still reports a virginal conception. So the objection wounds a bad argument, not the doctrine itself.

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
section: The strongest objections
text: The pagan-parallels objection. Critics in the history-of-religions tradition long argued that the virgin birth is borrowed mythology—Mithras, Dionysus, the divine paternity of Augustus, and others. This must be taken seriously, not waved away. The reply turns on a disanalogy that holds up well. The pagan tales, where they involve miraculous birth at all, are overwhelmingly stories of divine impregnation: a god, in some bodily or quasi-bodily form, unites with a mortal woman, who then is no longer a virgin. Dionysus is the offspring of Zeus and the mortal Semele. The Augustus legend has the god Apollo as a physical agent. Mithras, in the Roman cult, is born from a rock, with no woman in the scene at all.8 None of these is a virginal conception—a woman conceiving with no consort, divine or human, by the non-sexual creative act of God's Spirit. The Jewish, fiercely monotheistic setting makes a borrowed divine-consort myth especially unlikely; the last thing a Palestinian Jewish community would import is a god siring children on women. The candid scholarly verdict, even among many non-confessional historians, is that the alleged parallels are too loose and too late to ground a derivation. That said, this is a negative argument—it shows the borrowing thesis is weak, not that the conception occurred.

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
section: The strongest objections
text: The argument from silence. Here the objection bites hardest. Our earliest Christian writer, Paul, never mentions the virgin birth; he says Jesus was "born of woman, born under the law" (Galatians 4:4) and "descended from David according to the flesh" (Romans 1:3)—phrases that neither affirm nor require a virginal conception. Mark, the earliest Gospel, has no infancy narrative at all. John, the latest, opens with a cosmic prologue and never mentions Mary's virginity. So the doctrine is attested in only two of the New Testament's voices, and in the two that wrote infancy narratives at all. The legendary-development thesis—that the virginal conception grew up in the decades between Paul and Matthew/Luke—is a serious historical hypothesis, and Raymond Brown lays it out with notable fairness, concluding that the historicity of the virginal conception cannot be settled by historical-critical methods alone.9 The honest concession: attestation is limited and arguably late, and silence in Paul and Mark is a real datum, not a trick. The measured reply is twofold. First, silence is not denial—Paul wrote occasional letters to churches, not biographies, and had no obvious occasion to discuss Jesus' conception; Mark begins his story at the Jordan as a matter of literary design. Second, the silence cuts less far than it seems precisely because the two writers who did tell the birth story did so independently: their agreement on the virginal conception pushes the tradition back behind both Gospels into an earlier, shared stream rather than a single source one of them invented—though in fairness that shared stream need not reach all the way back to the event itself. The silence is a real datum, and an honest reader will feel its weight—but silence is not denial, and two independent witnesses to a private family matter push the tradition earlier, not later. What the argument from silence cannot do is convert an early, independently attested conviction into a late invention.

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
section: The strongest objections
text: The internal-tension objection. Matthew and Luke do not merely differ; in places they pull against each other. Their genealogies of Jesus diverge sharply—Matthew traces Joseph's line through David's son Solomon to a father named Jacob; Luke runs through David's son Nathan to a father named Heli.10 Their itineraries differ: Matthew has a flight to Egypt; Luke has a return to Nazareth with no Egypt at all. Proposed harmonizations exist—that Luke records Mary's line, or that levirate marriage explains the two fathers—but they are reconstructions, not statements the texts themselves make, and a fair reader should label them contested. What the tensions do not touch, however, is the shared core. Two accounts that disagree on route and lineage yet agree on virginal conception, Bethlehem, and Davidic descent look less like one fabricated story than like two independent memories of the same extraordinary claim, each elaborated in its own way.

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
section: The honest state of scholarship
text: Conservative scholars (e.g., the contributors gathered in studies defending the doctrine's historicity) hold that the convergence and the embarrassment criterion make a virginal conception the best explanation of the data. Critical scholars such as Brown regard the question as historically undecidable and theologically held; others, more skeptical still, judge it a relatively late confessional development. Among Jewish interpreters, the reading of Isaiah 7:14 as a near-term sign to Ahaz, with 'almah meaning simply "young woman," is the mainstream and longstanding view, and Christians owe that reading respect rather than caricature. No purely historical method can adjudicate a private, miraculous event attested by two sources a generation or two after the fact. That is the real limit of the evidence, and it should be stated without flinching.

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
section: What it does and does not establish
text: So what can be said? The virgin birth is not a public, multiply-corroborated event like the crucifixion under Pilate. It is the testimony of two Gospels, early and independent, agreeing on a core that ran against the church's social interest. Those features give it real evidential weight; they do not amount to proof. Isaiah 7:14 is best read as dual fulfillment—a word to Ahaz that Matthew saw illumined in Christ—and not as a predictive demonstration. The pagan-parallel charge fails on closer inspection; the silence of Paul, Mark, and John is a genuine weight on the other side of the scale.

title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14: What the Gospels Claim and What History Can Say
section: What it does and does not establish
text: In the end this is a confession held by faith, on the testimony of two witnesses, with reasons—and that is exactly how the creeds present it. The early church did not think the virginal conception proved Jesus' divinity; rather, having come to believe he was God-with-us, they saw in the manner of his coming a fitting sign that the new thing God did in Christ was, from the very first cell, God's own initiative and not merely ours. "Behold, the virgin shall conceive... and they shall call his name Immanuel"—God with us. The church confesses it as true—“conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary”—and this essay holds it so; the reader is asked only to weigh it as what it is, neither oversold as airtight proof nor dismissed as borrowed myth.

title: Did the First Christians Worship Jesus as God?
text: Somewhere around the year 55, a Jewish follower of Jesus named Paul preserved, untranslated, a prayer his Greek-speaking congregations had received from the first believers in Judea: Marana tha — “Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22).1 He was a monotheist to the marrow, raised on the Shema: “Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). And yet here he is, and the churches before him, calling on a crucified Galilean to come — the way Israel’s Scriptures call on the LORD. That is not a title, or an argument about his nature. It is an act of worship. And it is old.

title: Did the First Christians Worship Jesus as God?
text: This is the question that stands behind the doctrine: not first “how can Jesus be God?” but the plainer, historical one the New Testament scholar James Dunn put as a book title — Did the First Christians Worship Jesus?2 The popular answer is that they did not: that Jesus was revered as a great teacher and only slowly, over generations of Hellenistic drift, inflated into a god to be worshipped — the divinity a late arrival, the worship later still. The evidence points the other way. The devotion is early, it is Jewish, and it crosses the one line Second Temple Judaism guarded most jealously of all.

title: Did the First Christians Worship Jesus as God?
section: What worship meant — and where the line was drawn
text: To feel the force of the evidence you have to see the line clearly, because it is easy to misplace. The line was not the mere posture of homage. Israelites could and did bow low before a king as well as before God — 1 Chronicles 29:20 uses a single verb of prostration for both the LORD and King David in the same breath.3 Bowing, kneeling, honouring: these could be offered to prophets, kings, and angels without blasphemy. What Jewish monotheism reserved for the one God, absolutely and without exception, was not the gesture but the substance of worship — sacrifice, invocation, prayer, the hymn sung to a god. Angels, prophets, and kings could be honoured; they could not be prayed to.4

title: Did the First Christians Worship Jesus as God?
section: What worship meant — and where the line was drawn
text: The New Testament itself draws the line in exactly that place. In the book of Revelation, when John falls down to worship the angel who has shown him the vision, the angel recoils — twice: “You must not do that!… Worship God.” (Revelation 19:10; 22:9). Even the highest created messenger refuses the worship due God alone.5 That refusal is the control case: it tells us precisely what the earliest Christians thought they were — and were not — free to do. And it makes what they did with Jesus all the more startling.

title: Did the First Christians Worship Jesus as God?
section: They gave that worship to Jesus
text: Consider what the sources actually record the first believers doing. They prayed to Jesus. Marana tha is not the homage due a vice-regent; it is an invocation, calling on the risen Lord to come. Stephen dies with a prayer on his lips — “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:59) — entrusting his spirit to Jesus exactly as Jesus had entrusted his to the Father (Luke 23:46). And Paul can define the whole church, in a single phrase, as “all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 1:2), taking up the Scriptures’ own idiom for invoking YHWH by name (Joel 2:32; Romans 10:13).6

title: Did the First Christians Worship Jesus as God?
section: They gave that worship to Jesus
text: They sang to him. The hymn Paul quotes in Philippians 2 gives Jesus “the name that is above every name” and applies to him Isaiah’s oath that to YHWH alone “every knee shall bow” (Philippians 2:9–11, quoting Isaiah 45:23).7 And the worship of Jesus is attested even from outside the church: reporting to the emperor around AD 112, the pagan governor Pliny records that the Christians he interrogated met before dawn and sang “a hymn to Christ, as to a god” (carmen Christo quasi deo, Pliny, Letters 10.96) — hostile testimony that, by the early second century, worshipping Jesus was already the settled, customary practice of the churches Pliny encountered.8

title: Did the First Christians Worship Jesus as God?
section: They gave that worship to Jesus
text: And they worshipped him where they refused to worship anyone else. In Revelation the whole created order sings to “him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb” the same blessing and honour and glory, and the elders fall down in worship (Revelation 5:13–14) — in the very book whose angel twice refuses that worship for himself. Hebrews goes further still: God commands the worship — “Let all God’s angels worship him” (Hebrews 1:6) — in words whose Old Testament source directs that worship to the LORD.9 The Lamb receives what the angel forbids.

title: Did the First Christians Worship Jesus as God?
section: They gave that worship to Jesus
text: Matthew frames the point with a deliberate irony worth pausing on. Early in the Gospel the devil offers Jesus all the kingdoms of the world if he will “fall down and worship” him, and Jesus refuses with Scripture: “You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve” (Matthew 4:10, quoting Deuteronomy 6:13). Worship belongs to God alone; Jesus says so himself. Yet the same Gospel ends with the disciples worshipping the risen Jesus — “and when they saw him they worshiped him, but some doubted” (Matthew 28:17; cf. 14:33) — and Jesus does not refuse it, as the angel of Revelation does. The Greek verb here (proskyneō) can by itself mean no more than homage — the very posture that, as we saw, could be offered to a king — so the force of the scene lies not in the word but in the frame Matthew builds around it: the same Gospel that has Jesus refuse Satan’s proskynēsis by quoting “him only shall you serve” closes with the risen Jesus receiving it from his disciples and answering, not with the angel’s refusal, but with a claim to all authority in heaven and on earth. What Jesus refused to take from the devil, he received from his disciples, without a word of protest.10 The candour of “some doubted” is worth noting: Matthew is not concealing the difficulty. He is recording worship offered, and worship received.

title: Did the First Christians Worship Jesus as God?
section: The decisive point: it was early, not late
text: The one thing a “slow development” story cannot accommodate is the timeline, and the timeline is where this case is strongest. The most explosive evidence is also the earliest. Marana tha is Aramaic — a fossil of devotion in the original language of the Palestinian church, carrying us behind Paul’s Greek to the first Aramaic-speaking believers in Jerusalem in the 30s. The Philippians hymn is widely regarded as pre-Pauline material, older than the letter that carries it (this dating is debated — Gordon Fee argues Paul composed the hymn himself — but the worship of Jesus it expresses stands either way). The historian Larry Hurtado devoted a major study to exactly this question and concluded that a “binitarian” pattern of devotion — worship offered to Jesus alongside God — emerged “amazingly early,” within the first years of the movement, among Jews who would have regarded worshipping any creature as blasphemy.11 The development was in the articulation, not in the worship: the words the church later coined to explain the devotion came slowly; the devotion itself was there at the beginning.

title: Did the First Christians Worship Jesus as God?
section: The strongest objection: was he only a supreme agent?
text: The most serious challenge comes from those who affirm the Bible but deny that Jesus is God by nature — Jehovah’s Witnesses and biblical Unitarians among them. Their key tool is the Jewish principle of agency, the shaliach: “a man’s agent is as the man himself.” An ambassador is honoured, obeyed, even received as though he were the king — without being the king. On this reading everything above is the dignity of a supreme agent: Jesus is honoured because the Father appointed him, addressed as the one who perfectly represents God, given a kind of worship as God’s exalted vice-regent. Much New Testament language of Jesus being “sent,” “given,” and “appointed” fits this naturally, and the reading deserves to be met on its merits, not caricatured.12

title: Did the First Christians Worship Jesus as God?
section: The strongest objection: was he only a supreme agent?
text: But agency has a ceiling, and the worship evidence crashes through it. No shaliach in Jewish thought ever received the cultic devotion — the prayer, the invocation, the hymn offered to a god — that the sources give Jesus. Agency conferred authority; it never conferred that adoration. This is exactly why the angel in Revelation, himself God’s messenger and agent, refuses the very worship the Lamb accepts. An agent represents the sender; he is not prayed to, does not receive the hymn sung “to a god,” does not share the sender’s throne. Even Dunn, whose survey is the most cautious of the major treatments, grants that the earliest devotion is real and must be reckoned with; the question is whether “agency” can bear its weight, and at the altar it cannot. The framework explains the titles and the sending-language; it breaks at the altar.

title: Did the First Christians Worship Jesus as God?
section: “But surely the worship grew over time”
text: The developmental thesis is pressed at its most sophisticated by the agnostic scholar Bart Ehrman, who — it should be said plainly — rejects the crude “Constantine invented it” story and grants that devotion to Jesus began strikingly early. His subtler claim is that early reverence is not yet the later dogma: that an initial “exaltation” devotion grew, over time and reflection, into the full worship of Jesus as God in the same sense as the Father.13 The concession comes first, because part of this is true. The church’s formal vocabulary for what it was doing — the fourth-century language of “one essence” — genuinely did develop later＊What “developed later” meansIs sayingThe technical creedal vocabulary and systematic formulation (Nicaea’s “one essence,” Chalcedon’s “two natures”) came later, as the church’s articulation of what it was already doing.Not sayingNot that the worship of Jesus, or his deity, was a later human invention. The devotion — prayer to Jesus, the hymn sung to him, invocation of his name — is present from the earliest layers we can reach., and no informed Christian need pretend otherwise. But the datum this essay rests on is not the vocabulary; it is the practice, and the practice is in the earliest layer we can reach. Marana tha, the Philippians hymn, the pattern Hurtado documents: these are not the top of a slow climb. They are the bedrock. The refinement was in how the church explained the worship of Jesus, never in whether it offered it.

title: Did the First Christians Worship Jesus as God?
section: What this establishes — and what it does not
text: The reach of the argument should be stated plainly, because overstating it is how a true case turns brittle. It does not, by itself, prove that the worship was warranted — that Jesus is in fact God, and rightly adored. That is the separate work of his resurrection and of his own words and deeds, argued elsewhere in this library. Nor does it hand us the developed metaphysics of the fourth-century councils, which the honest case concedes came later. And the sharpest scholarly framing of the evidence — Richard Bauckham’s thesis that the New Testament writers deliberately include Jesus within the unique divine identity of the one God — is influential but genuinely contested: Dunn, and from another angle James McGrath, question how sharply that boundary can be drawn, and Hurtado himself, broadly an ally, preferred to frame the data as devotional practice rather than in Bauckham’s identity categories.14

title: Did the First Christians Worship Jesus as God?
section: What this establishes — and what it does not
text: What it does establish is enough to dissolve the “slow development” myth. The first Christians — Jewish monotheists who would die before bowing to an idol — prayed to Jesus, sang to him, called on his name, and worshipped him where they refused to worship even an angel; and they did so from the earliest years of the movement, not after centuries of drift. They held, in one breath, that God is one and that the crucified Jesus was to be worshipped. That is not the reverence a great teacher accumulates over generations. It is worship, offered at the start — and worship, in a Jew, is a confession about who God is.
